stories.Headline: Infotech LIVE 2026 in Toronto to Feature CIO Association of Canada Panel on Developing IT Leaders for the Agentic Era
stories.Summary:
Infotech LIVE 2026 in Toronto will host a main-stage panel with the CIO Association of Canada on November 11 at the Fairmont Royal York. The session, titled Developing Senior IT Leaders for the Agentic Era, brings together senior IT executives to discuss leadership development and how organizations can prepare for AI-driven work. The three-day conference runs from November 10 to 12 and is aimed at CIOs and other IT leaders. The panel is one part of a broader program built around turning advances in AI into measurable business gains while managing cost, risk and change.

The panel features three executives: Alicia Samuel of Holt Renfrew, Doris Simcich of MDA Space and Jennifer Hutton of Steele Auto Group, all holding the CIO.D designation. Yasemin Sezer, an executive counselor at Infotech, will moderate. The organizers say the speakers will explain how their leadership preparation has shaped their work building the foundations for an AI-supported future. Hannes Scheidegger, Infotech's chief global services officer, has said CIOs are being asked to make faster and more complex decisions about agentic AI while keeping services reliable. The Association's president and chair, Derek Cullen, has said the panel's experiences can give peers a useful starting point for deciding what they need to strengthen.

The CIO Association of Canada is a national, not-for-profit group founded in 2004 that represents CIOs, CISOs and IT executives. It promotes executive development through peer networking, shared practices and professional recognition, and its CIO.D designation is supported by the CIO Executive Leadership Program, delivered with the University of Toronto's Rotman School of Management. That program covers strategy, financial management, governance, board relationships and delivery. The conference itself offers more than 30 keynotes and over 40 breakout and workshop sessions, with former Chief of the Defence Staff Rick Hillier among the featured speakers. Attendees can also meet analysts and peers and access benchmarks and IT playbooks.

Media professionals, including journalists and podcasters, may apply for complimentary in-person passes by contacting pr@infotech.com. Exhibitors are also invited to showcase products and services to attendees. Infotech, formerly Info-Tech Research Group, describes itself as serving more than 30,000 IT leaders worldwide through an API-driven advisory model. Further details on the agenda and registration are available on the conference website.

stories.Headline: Investigation reveals $11 AI voice cloning scam
stories.Summary:
Researchers at KMBC 9 tested how easily an AI tool could copy a person's voice and fool someone who knows them. Cybersecurity expert Aaron Weissenfluh of Tenfold Security collected 32 minutes of audio of KMBC 9 reporter Byra Berry from videos already posted publicly on YouTube and Facebook. He then used voice-cloning software that cost $11 to build a digital copy of her voice, and some comparable programs are free. Berry never had to record in a studio or read a script, because the audio was already online for anyone to hear. The test showed how little is needed to create a convincing imitation.

In the test, Berry's cousin received a phone call from the AI-generated voice and believed she was speaking with Berry. The cousin only noticed pauses in the conversation, and the voice was otherwise convincing enough to pass as the real person. The investigation raised the question of how persuasive the call would have been without those pauses. Scammers can use the same technology to impersonate a loved one, and a familiar voice can create immediate trust, especially when the caller claims an emergency or asks for money. The article notes that AI-generated deepfakes are improving faster than the laws meant to control them.

The article offers practical advice for protecting yourself. If an unexpected caller claiming to be a family member asks for money, do not rely on the voice alone, and be wary of anyone who pressures you to act right away or asks you to keep the call secret. Hang up and phone the person back using a number you already know. Families can also agree on a code word to verify identity during an emergency.

The article further advises caution about posting videos of yourself online, since scammers may need little more than publicly available recordings to work with. The article's central takeaway is that hearing a familiar voice no longer proves you are speaking with the person you think you are. The report comes from the KMBC 9 investigation, which was shared with other Hearst Television stations and published on those stations' websites on November 6, 2026. The articles do not describe any specific further steps by regulators or companies.

stories.Headline: Consumers Are Now Worried About an AI Bubble, Michigan Survey Says
stories.Summary:
On November 6, 2026, the University of Michigan released its preliminary November consumer survey, which found that some households were voicing growing anxiety about a possible AI bubble in stock prices. The survey's director, Joanne Hsu, described this worry in the open-ended comments respondents gave. The headline Index of Consumer Sentiment rose to 51.0 from 48.0 in October, a gain of 6.3 percent that only returned the index to its November 2025 level. Interviews for the survey ran from October 20 to November 2, so they ended before a sharp market selloff on November 5, when the S&P 500 fell 4.36 percent and the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52 percent.

The split in sentiment is the central finding for investors. Consumers with the most money in stocks grew gloomier, with their sentiment falling 5 percent, while lower- and middle-wealth households became more upbeat. Hsu said most of the small gains in expected personal finances and business conditions came from political independents. The current conditions index rose to 51.0 from 46.7, and the expectations index rose to 50.9 from 48.8. The articles note that the AI-bubble concern came from open-ended comments and that the survey attached no percentage to it, so the articles cannot say how many people hold that view.

The articles tie the wealthy group's pessimism to the AI trade, since those households own most of it and feel its losses first, and they link it to a turbulent period in markets. The articles name the Invesco QQQ Trust, which fell 13.41 percent over the past month, and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust, which fell 5.39 percent over the same period. They say QQQ carries more concentrated AI exposure because NVIDIA alone made up about 7.6 percent of the fund as of June 30. Sticky inflation is also a concern, with year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.3 percent and long-run expectations at 3.4 percent. The articles say October CPI data, due November 10, is the next test, and that the final November sentiment reading, due November 20, will show whether Thursday's losses have reached consumer sentiment.

stories.Headline: Tencent Cloud Enterprise Unveils Full-Stack Intelligent Private Cloud for Sovereign Agentic AI
stories.Summary:
Tencent Cloud Enterprise, or TCE, used the AI-Powered Private Cloud for Global Markets session of the 2026 Tencent Global Digital Ecosystem Summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 6, 2026, to show how highly regulated industries can run production-grade agentic AI inside their own boundaries. The company launched two major solutions, the Full-Stack Intelligent AI Suite and Lite Deployment, and presented joint research reports it prepared with Gartner and Omdia. The theme of the session was full-stack intelligence and sovereign AI. Kaibo Sha, Vice President at Tencent Cloud, argued that once an agent touches core business data and critical systems, the key questions are where the data is processed, who operates the system, and what foundation the agent runs on. The Full-Stack Intelligent AI Suite is described as the company's flagship release of the year and marks a shift from a full-stack cloud to a full-stack intelligent cloud.

It has four selectable layers: a converged compute, storage and networking foundation, a model service layer built on TokenHub, an agent runtime layer with a cloud-native sandbox, egress control and identity credentials, and an agent application layer. TokenHub is a private platform for LLM services that offers metered, callable inference on an industry-standard API with multi-tenant isolation. The suite is said to deliver more than 250,000 TPM of measured single-accelerator throughput, cache hit rates above 90%, and up to 220% throughput gains on alternative silicon, and it has been validated at 10,000-GPU scale. Its resilience target is a recovery time objective of two minutes or less and a recovery point objective of zero, and the company says data, model weights and inference traffic stay inside the customer's sovereignty boundary. Lite Deployment targets organizations that want to start small before committing larger budgets.

According to the release, it delivers a complete full-stack cloud from eight servers, made up of three master nodes, three block storage nodes and two network function nodes, without reducing core infrastructure capability. An AI-only entry point can begin with three servers and include private model services. The same architecture can grow from a single availability zone to metro dual-AZ active-active and then to cross-region disaster recovery. It is delivered as software on existing hardware, requires no capital-heavy refresh and carries no minimum spend.

One large futures brokerage used this route to run core trading systems across heterogeneous chip architectures, starting AI on three servers and expanding as volumes grew. Tencent Cloud Enterprise and Gartner also released A Practical Guide to Building Sovereign AI Cloud Platforms, which treats sovereignty as a spectrum resting on data, operations and technology and sets out adoption paths for financial services, healthcare, public service cloud and telecommunications. The guide cites Gartner research projecting that by 2028, strict data sovereignty and privacy rules will push over 25% of enterprises in regulated industries to move their primary GenAI workloads back on-premises, and that through 2029, dependence on proprietary foundation models will lock more than 50% of GenAI adopters into one public cloud provider's ecosystem. The article is cut off before it lists the remaining findings, so the rest of the research and any further next steps are not described here.

stories.Headline: Christopher Nolan Previews DGA’s Next Phase of AI Protections: ‘It’s Down to the Studios’
stories.Summary:
Christopher Nolan, who has been president of the Directors Guild of America since fall 2025, spoke on the Hollywood Insiders podcast on Saturday, November 7, 2026, about the guild's fight against artificial intelligence in film and television. He praised the DGA and the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers for negotiating what he called excellent language and guardrails on AI in production. He also said the next challenge, protecting copyrighted work from AI, rests mainly with the studios. His remarks were reported by TheWrap and Deadline in articles published on November 7 and 8, 2026.

Nolan said the guild is focused on holding studios accountable for protecting their copyrights, but that the DGA cannot do this itself because, with very few exceptions, its members do not hold the copyrights to the films they work on. He argued that "AI" is too broad a term, one that companies use to avoid responsibility by portraying the technology as an uncontrollable force. He said existing laws already protect creators and that companies hiding behind fair use arguments will not hold up in court in the long run, pointing to some significant judgments already issued against that defense. He also said he was pleased that the closing credits of his film The Odyssey, from Universal, include for the first time a notice stating the film cannot be ingested or used as AI training data.

Nolan compared this principle to the long-settled rules on sampling music, saying that taking another's work, feeding it into a machine, and selling the output even in disguised form should not count as fair use. He acknowledged the matter will have to be settled through courts and legislation, and that it will take a long time. Deadline reported that Nolan had earlier said the guild needs a voice in how AI tools are used and in shaping the legal framework, because members' residuals depend on how their work is monetized. He described the effort as an ongoing fight rather than one with a fixed endpoint.

stories.Headline: LA Council seeks citywide data privacy policy amid AI, ALRP tech
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 6, 2026, the Los Angeles City Council voted unanimously to approve a motion calling for a standard data privacy policy that would apply across the entire city. The action was prompted by concerns about how data is kept, how long it is retained, and what privacy rights residents have when artificial intelligence and automated license plate reader technology are involved. The motion was introduced by Councilwoman Monica Rodriguez, and the vote was unanimous. Reporting on the vote came from several outlets that day, including the Daily News, MyNewsLA.com and the Daily Breeze. The motion directs the Information Technology Agency and other relevant departments to return with recommendations for a citywide policy and supporting policies.

These would set standards and safeguards for how data is collected, stored, retained, accessed, shared and disclosed. Departments are also expected to report on cybersecurity measures and protection against unauthorized access or security breaches. The reports are to cover appropriate and prohibited uses of city technology and data, along with transparency, accountability, oversight and auditing requirements, among other things. The articles do not give specific deadlines or dollar figures for these reports. Rodriguez, speaking at the council meeting, said the city has an overarching responsibility to keep residents' privacy and personal information protected.

She argued that departments should not operate under different standards when collecting and sharing sensitive data, whether the tools involved are license plate readers, artificial intelligence or other new technologies. She also noted that the Los Angeles Police Department has faced significant scrutiny over its technology use, and said the same level of scrutiny and protections should apply to every city department. Rodriguez said that if the city is serious, these standards should become routine in how each department adopts new technologies. The articles describe the motion as a response to growing public and council concern about surveillance tools and data handling, with the LAPD's use of automated license plate readers as a central example. The articles do not say when the departments' recommendations are due or when a final citywide policy might be adopted, so the next step is the departments' reports back to the council.

stories.Headline: AI can be delegated authority, but not responsibility: Türkiye's technology minister
stories.Summary:
Turkish Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir said on Saturday that artificial intelligence should not operate without clear accountability, speaking at the TRT World Forum panel "Navigating Responsibility in the Age of AI." He warned that increasingly autonomous AI systems raise serious questions about transparency, safety and accountability. Kacir said that authority could be handed to AI but responsibility could not. He pointed to risks including algorithmic discrimination, cybersecurity threats, deepfakes and the concentration of computing power among a small number of technology companies.

Kacir noted that more than 90 percent of the world's notable frontier AI models in 2025 were developed by industry. He said just five companies controlled an estimated 70 percent of global AI computing power. He called for a human-centred, risk-based regulatory approach, arguing that AI applications with significant consequences for individuals should face stronger safeguards and meaningful human oversight. The minister's remarks framed these safeguards as central to technological progress.

Outlining Türkiye's ambitions, Kacir said the country's 2026-2030 Artificial Intelligence Action Plan aims to place Türkiye among the leading countries in AI technologies. The plan targets AI literacy training for 5 million citizens, the development of 10,000 advanced AI experts and 100,000 AI professionals, and the opening of at least 2,000 public datasets to researchers and entrepreneurs. It also aims to expand data centre capacity to at least one gigawatt by 2030 and attract at least $10 billion in private-sector-led investment in data centres, cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Kacir added that the country's Turkish large language model, BILGE, would strengthen technological independence, with its first version soon to be made available to developers.

Kacir also announced plans to establish regulatory sandboxes in priority sectors and an AI Ethics Board to address privacy, discrimination and children's safety. He said Türkiye was committed to contributing to global AI governance through the G20, OECD, UNESCO, the Organisation of Turkic States and the United Nations. The articles do not say when the ethics board or sandboxes will be set up. The remarks were reported by TRT World, citing the Anadolu Agency.

stories.Headline: Aligning MLLMs with the Latent Structure of Human Cognition via Behavior-Derived Semantic Dimensions
stories.Summary:
A research paper posted to arXiv by Ning E, Changde Du, Yizhuo Lu and Huiguang He describes a new way to align Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with human cognition. The authors noted that it was unclear whether these models' internal representations and decision criteria match the latent structure of human thinking, even though the models perform well on many reasoning tasks. Their approach builds on an earlier behavior-derived semantic embedding space in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions. Those dimensions were derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out judgements. The paper was listed on doi.org on November 7, 2026.

The framework works by taking each triplet of objects and inferring the most salient decision dimension behind a human's choice. That dimension is then converted into a linguistic rationale grounded in the dimension, so the model learns both the final pick and a justification that fits the inferred criterion. According to the abstract, this improves the model's consistency with human similarity judgements while keeping competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. The authors also report that searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset showed increased representational alignment between the model and humans. They present these results as evidence for a data-driven way to bring human cognitive structure into MLLM alignment.

Separately, a second paper on arXiv, titled Memorilla and authored by Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli, Nikita Mounier, Shirley Wu, Shayan Pardis and Jure Leskovec, addresses a different limitation of language models. It introduces a memory system that gathers information from a whole document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent memory tokens for a frozen LLM. The paper states that the first version was submitted on October 15, 2026, and that the latest revision, version three, was posted on November 3, 2026. Using only 16 memory tokens, the system outperformed baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks. On FactKG it reached 84.33% accuracy, compared with 80.43% for full-context inference, while using 108 times fewer tokens to represent the source documents.

The Memorilla authors also tested the system in a TextWorld environment, where it reduced an agent's tendency to revisit rooms it had already explored. Its average success rate rose from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. The paper presents this as a step toward continually learning AI systems that accumulate and use knowledge across long interactions. The articles do not describe any deployment plans or next steps beyond these experimental results and the publicly available code and project website.

stories.Headline: TSMC Weighs Making Advanced Memory Chips to Capture More AI Spending

TSMC, the Taiwanese chipmaker, is weighing whether to begin manufacturing advanced memory chips, a move that would take it into a market it has largely left to others. The Information reported the consideration on November 6, 2026, describing it as a way to capture more of the spending flowing into artificial intelligence. The move would allow the company to sell into a category of components that AI data centers rely on heavily. The reporting describes the idea as under consideration rather than a finalized plan. The article's account is limited, and the text available to me is mostly navigation and a paywall teaser for an unrelated story about Nvidia and data center retrofits.

It does not give figures on investment size, production timelines, or which memory types TSMC would target. Nor does it spell out what regulatory or capacity changes such a shift would require. Readers should treat those details as unknown from this source alone. The article does not name a specific TSMC executive or quote a company statement, so responsibility rests with the company's own decision-making. Any formal position from TSMC on the matter is not reported in the material provided.

The piece is framed around the company's interest in expanding its share of AI-related revenue. The context is that memory chips and chipmaking capacity have become central to the AI buildout, and TSMC's move would mark a broadening of its business beyond the logic chips it is best known for. The articles do not say what comes next or when a decision might be announced. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Ondo Plans Anthropic Tokens From IPO Day for Non-US Buyers
stories.Summary:
Ondo Finance said on X on November 6 that it plans to offer tokens tracking Anthropic on the day of the AI company's initial public offering. The tokens would be sold through its Ondo Stocks platform, which its own product page says is not available in the United States. The post stated that Anthropic would be tokenized on day one and launched on IPO day, but it gave no date, price or token terms. It also did not say that Anthropic was involved in the plan. The post had drawn 74,231 views when the reporting was checked on November 7.

Ondo's product page describes Ondo Stocks as offering eligible investors outside the United States economic exposure to publicly traded securities. The page says the tokens are fully backed by underlying shares, along with U.S. stocks, ETFs and cash held with U.S. broker-dealers. An independent Verification Agent reviews that backing daily, according to the page. Holders would receive economic exposure designed to track the underlying stock, with dividends reinvested net of applicable withholding tax. Ondo launched a day-one IPO service for tokenized stocks in February, and by that time its Ondo Global Markets had passed $500 million in total value across more than 200 tokenized stocks.

Anthropic has published its own list of firms for the international retail part of its proposed IPO, covering Australia, Canada, nine European Economic Area states, Japan, Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Its help-centre page names 33 broker and selling-agent firms for that offer, and Ondo is not among them. Anthropic also says it does not currently intend to list its Class A common stock on any exchange in those international jurisdictions. A separate Anthropic notice, first published in February, states that any sale or transfer of its stock not approved by its board is void and will not be recognized on its books. That notice warns that third parties claiming to sell Anthropic shares to the public through tokenized securities are likely offering something with no value, but it does not name Ondo.

The reporting found no Anthropic statement on Ondo's plan. Anthropic exposure already trades outside the company's own channels, including perpetual futures that track its price. The IPO itself has not been dated, and the reporting does not establish whether Ondo's tokens would be sold before or alongside any listing. Ondo has not published terms for an Anthropic token, and neither company has said how Anthropic's transfer notice relates to Ondo's plan. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling despite usage increase
stories.Summary:
Ramp, the spending platform, released data showing that companies are using more AI tools but their spending on them has stalled, flattening out over late summer even as token volumes rose. Token spend grew only 1.5 percent across August and September, after growing 42 percent from June to July. The report's lead economist, Ara Kharazian, told TechCrunch that almost all AI spending comes from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies. He added that a slowdown among the top 1 percent of firms was enough to pull overall revenue down, even with volumes still climbing.

The top 1 percent of firms, which Kharazian described as the most heavily invested in AI, spent just under $10,000 per employee in August and September, below their summer peaks. Median firms spend $12 to $15 per employee each month, while the top 10 percent spend $600 to $1,000. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for its GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. Anthropic also reduced prices for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, a move the company said in a recent filing cut its revenue growth by about $600 million. October showed an 8.9 percent rebound in token spend from September to October, though Kharazian said the headwinds remain strong.

Kharazian attributed the slowdown mainly to competition rather than weak demand, pointing to price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic, enterprise offerings from Meta and Nvidia, and cheaper open-source models from China and the United States. He also noted that companies are getting better at controlling AI costs by using default settings that avoid expensive models, setting employee budgets, and routing tasks to cheaper models. Bloomberg reported that Anthropic's potential valuation fell from $2 trillion in early October to between $1.2 trillion and $1.3 trillion, and that OpenAI lowered its proposed valuation from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion. Both companies have also reportedly cut their fundraising goals.

Investors have assumed that new AI uses, such as personal agents, will sustain rapid growth in spending, much as AI coding did. Kharazian is skeptical, saying that personal agents are not as economically productive as coding and may not drive the same level of spending. He said the data suggests the era of hypergrowth in AI spending may be over. The report comes as Anthropic nears an IPO, which raises questions about how investors will view the company's revenue trajectory.

stories.Headline: In Saudi Arabia’s Year of AI, business leaders need trusted partners
stories.Summary:
Saudi Arabia has declared 2026 its Year of AI, and the country is pushing hard on artificial intelligence across government and industry. Riyadh, where the author lives and works, is seeing new buildings rise and conversations move from planning to delivery. Business leaders there are asking which partners they can really rely on. The question is pressing because the country leads the world in public-sector AI adoption and has committed $9.1 billion to local AI companies.

The article argues that opportunities are clear but reliable partnerships are harder to find. Leaders want partners who will stay the course when projects become complicated and timelines tighten. Many global technology firms have made missteps by treating Saudi Arabia as a market to capture, announcing ambitious plans that outpace what they can deliver. The author says partners who are already winning mandates arrived early, were honest about their limits, and committed to Vision 2030 as a national effort.

The author sets out three requirements for real partnership at this level. Partners should show up before any formal opportunity, building relationships through working sessions and candid conversations. They should be able to deliver at Saudi scale, serving ministries that digitalize services for millions, energy companies embedding AI in large operations, and banks modernizing under regulatory pressure. Finally, they must have proven sovereign capability, meaning systems that keep data governance, cybersecurity and operational continuity under national control.

The piece is published by NTT Data and written by Rami Beidas, its country head for Saudi Arabia, so it presents the company's own case for how it meets these requirements. It says NTT Data designs and runs sovereign AI infrastructure that keeps Saudi data within Saudi jurisdiction, drawing on its work with governments in more than 70 countries. The company also cites a workforce of 190,000 professionals and its SAP capabilities. The article ends by inviting Saudi ministers and business leaders to share what genuine partnership would mean to them, and by promoting NTT Data's AI services and a 2026 Global AI Report.

stories.Headline: AI agents may run your household. What could go wrong?
stories.Summary:
Parents are expected to be among the first families to hand household chores to AI agents, a trend that has accelerated quickly this year. Meta launched its Muse agent in September, reportedly in response to the early success of Instinct, and OpenAI and Anthropic soon followed with their own products. Startups such as Fambot and Fo have also entered the market, while Marissa Mayer drew attention when she described her agent, Dazzle, in a New York Times interview. Experts say the enthusiasm is justified, but parents should first learn how to protect their data.

Erica Layer, a mother of two who runs a fractional AI company, relies on an Instinct agent for meal planning, calendaring, and birthday reminders. She says the tool gives her a great deal of time back. However, when her agent offered to book family train tickets in Portugal, it asked for her children's passports. Layer reviewed Instinct's privacy terms, found them lacking in transparency, and made the booking herself. Mashable said it tried to reach Instinct's founder for comment but received no reply before publication.

Several parents interviewed say the appeal is strong. Amy Wu Martin, a new mother and partner at Menlo Ventures, uses Muse and Claude to check whether restaurants and hotels are kid-friendly, though she has not connected her inbox to an agent because of security concerns. Menlo Ventures' survey research suggests parents are about twice as likely as non-parents to use AI daily, with 40 percent using it for tasks like meal planning, shopping, and logistics. S. Shyam Sundar of Penn State's Center for Socially Responsible Artificial Intelligence says parents who seek such help are not being selfish. He argues that offloading tedious tasks protects the household's psychological welfare and relationships.

Security experts advise caution. Kayne McGladrey, a virtual chief information security officer and senior member of the IEEE, recommends looking for phrases such as "zero retention," "zero training," and "zero-knowledge encryption" in a product's privacy claims. He also says consumers should confirm that a company stores login credentials separately, since storing a bank password alongside inbox access raises the risk of theft. McGladrey warns that parents often underestimate how much sensitive information sits in their inboxes, including health and school communications. He adds that IEEE is developing agentic security standards, which likely will not be ready until 2027.

stories.Headline: IREN Says New AI Cloud Customers Are Prepaying 90% of the Chips
stories.Summary:
IREN, the AI cloud operator, said on November 5, 2026 that a new customer will prepay most of the cost of the graphics processors that will serve it. After the quarter ended, IREN signed a five-year AI Cloud contract at about $22 million of annualized revenue per megawatt of IT load. The customer is prepaying about 90% of the related GPU capital spending. The announcement came as the company's shares fell sharply in the regular session, closing at $18.03, down 16.95%, before recovering to $19.95 after hours.

The prepayments could ease IREN's funding needs, since customer money covers much of the hardware that would otherwise require outside financing. Even so, IREN's cash fell to $3.52 billion from $5.90 billion, and its net debt rose to $4.43 billion from $216 million. The company also signed a short-term contract at more than $40 million per megawatt, expanded a deal with a leading frontier AI lab, and signed new contracts for older H100 GPUs at double the earlier pricing. IREN did not name the five-year customer, and it gave no megawatt counts, GPU numbers, total contract value or start dates.

Chief Financial Officer Anthony Lewis said some recent contracts carry prepayments of up to 90% and that IREN targets total GPU financing of 90% of related capex, including prepayments. Co-CEO Daniel Roberts said lower-credit customers tend to make larger prepayments, which complicates the positive reading of the deals. Chief Commercial Officer Kent Draper said the company does not comment on individual contracts. Lewis also said two-thirds of the $20.3 billion backlog, which grew 22%, comes from investment-grade customers including Microsoft and NVIDIA.

The company's target of more than $4 billion in operating annual recurring revenue is now set for January 31, 2027 instead of year-end 2026, and it could slip to the end of February 2027. Roberts said Microsoft asked IREN to rework the network at its 200 MW Horizon 1 site, which he described as a negligible extra capital cost. IREN plans $15 billion of capital spending for the rest of fiscal 2027, of which $9 billion is covered by cash and committed funding, while $6 billion depends on market conditions. Investors are watching whether the capacity target is met and whether the remaining gap is covered mainly by new stock.

stories.Headline: Facing Backlash, Meta Pulls Down Terms of Service That Pushed New AI Media Strategy
stories.Summary:
Meta has indefinitely paused proposed changes to its terms of service for business account users, which would have allowed the company to scrape content from those users' websites to support its AI products. The company posted a notice in its Business Help Center on a Thursday, saying the update, which had been set to take effect November 20, 2026, was now paused and that existing terms remain in effect. Earlier in the timeline, the new terms were first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15, and they were initially due to take effect October 30 before being pushed back. Critics said the update would have also shifted responsibility for errors produced by faulty AI onto customers.

Opposition came from news publishers in the United States and Europe, who argued that the terms would force them to supply their content free of charge to AI products that could compete with them for readers and advertisers. Democratic Senator Adam Schiff of California wrote to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg urging the company not to implement the terms, calling them a serious abuse of its power. Four European press associations sent a joint letter to the European Commission, claiming the plan violated the European Union's Digital Markets Act. The News/Media Alliance, led by Danielle Coffey, asked Meta to withdraw the terms and hold discussions with publishers before any future changes.

Meta's vice president of communications, Andy Stone, said on October 28 that the company wanted to consult with industry groups and leaders before making policy changes, and that implementation could be delayed beyond November 20. A Meta statement to Nieman Lab said the company was pausing the changes while it continued engaging with stakeholders. Courts in Norway and Brazil had already issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms following lawsuits from media organizations in those countries. The United Kingdom's Competition and Markets Authority has also opened a formal investigation into whether Meta was abusing a dominant market position.

The broader context includes a fine Meta received two weeks before this report for illegal use of customer data, along with a layoff of 8,000 employees earlier in the year. The articles do not say when or whether Meta will return with revised terms, though the company has said it will provide a further update when it has more to share. The outcome of the UK investigation and the court cases in Norway and Brazil remains unresolved in the reporting. For now, the company says its existing terms remain in effect for business accounts.

stories.Headline: “AI Sandbox” workshop allows faculty and staff to put AI through its paces in low-stakes environment
stories.Summary:
A University of Pittsburgh workshop called the "AI Sandbox," run through the Faculty and Staff Development Program, gave faculty and staff a low-stakes chance to test how AI handles basic writing tasks and whether it is worth using. The session was led by J. D. Wright, an English faculty member who also consults for the University Center for Teaching and Learning. Participants practiced writing prompts, refining them to get different versions of a document, and judging whether the results helped them. The article was published on November 6, 2026.

Wright told attendees that longer and more detailed prompts generally produce more complete and accurate output, and he urged people not to accept the first answer. He described AI as more like a conversation with a colleague than a source of single correct answers, and as a tool for generating options rather than final truths. In one exercise, students asked an AI to draft a social media invitation to a department event, and reactions varied: some were pleased with the layout, tone, and extra details, while others found it made assumptions they had not requested. Wright noted that asking for 100 paper titles takes little more effort than asking for five, and that a few of them may be strong. He also suggested asking the AI to point out what a user might be overlooking, predict how an output could be misread, and recommend a workflow for future tasks.

Wright was candid that his own use is limited, saying he rarely uses AI to create full documents, though he recommends it for first drafts that can be revised. One participant said she likes the tool but does not fully trust it, since she still has to check its work and is unsure it saves her time. Wright's central test for any use was whether it saved time or produced a better result than the user would have on their own. The article reports these views without describing any broader institutional policy.

Separately, a Nebraska Public Media report dated November 5, 2026, describes a different approach at the University of Nebraska, where President Jeffrey Gold announced university-wide expectations for AI use in a Thursday message. The executive memorandum bars using institutional and research data in personal AI subscriptions, prohibits tools that claim ownership of user data or use it to train other models, and makes users responsible for checking outputs, facts, and citations. The university is providing an enterprise ChatGPT license that faculty and staff must complete training to access, with Gold asking everyone to move to it by the end of 2026, and faculty can request enterprise access for students. Copilot is already available system-wide, and a new NU AI Governance Group with faculty, staff, and units such as the NU AI Institute, legal, and finance will help implement the memorandum. Gold said faculty and staff still decide whether AI is used in their courses or research, and that the rules are meant to keep pace with fast-changing technology.

The sell-off followed a rout on Wall Street overnight, where investors dumped major artificial intelligence and data center stocks after the election results.

Chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK hynix dropped more than 3 percent and 6 percent, respectively. The Korean won traded at 1,356.2 won to the U.S. dollar at 11:20 a.m., weaker by 0.7 won from the previous close. The articles attribute the worry to the Democratic Party's midterm victory, which investors feared could restrict data center building. Han Ji-young, an analyst at Kiwoom Securities, said that because Texas accounts for about 27 percent of all U.S. data center construction, limits in such areas could have negative ripple effects.

stories.Headline: Kookmin University research team develops AI model to predict properties of mixtures
stories.Summary:
A research team at Kookmin University, led by chemistry professor Joung Joon-young, has built an artificial intelligence model that predicts the properties of chemical mixtures from the identities and proportions of their components. The university announced the work on Thursday, and the findings were published in the Chemical Engineering Journal under the title "Encoding composition-dependent intermolecular interactions into learned molecular representations." The team also included Kim Ji-hwan, a student in the university's integrated master's and doctoral program, and undergraduate Kim Chan-joong. The model, called MEMo, was announced as a new tool for a field the articles describe as central to everyday products.

Most chemical products people use are mixtures, including industrial solvents, battery electrolytes, automotive fuels, and cosmetic and pharmaceutical formulations. Their properties depend on which substances are combined and in what proportions, and those changes do not follow the mixing ratios in a simple, direct way. Earlier AI approaches learned each molecule's properties separately and then averaged them by mixing ratio, which missed how molecules interact and how those interactions shift with composition. MEMo accounts for both molecular identity and mixing proportions from the start, first learning each molecule's traits and then letting molecules exchange information so the model can learn their interactions. The team tested it against more than 860,000 experimental measurements from the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology across five properties: density, speed of sound, vapor pressure, refractive index and surface tension.

According to the articles, MEMo predicted four of the five properties better than conventional methods. The gains were largest for mixtures with strong intermolecular interactions, such as ionic liquids and aqueous salt solutions, and for mixtures containing molecules the model had not seen during training. Joung said the key was building a model that understands molecular behavior on the same principle that governs mixtures, and he expects it to shorten and cheapen materials development by predicting properties for different compositions without physical experiments. He named battery electrolyte design, eco-friendly solvents and carbon dioxide capture materials as possible applications. The articles do not say when or how the model will be made available for these uses.

stories.Headline: ‘Triplets of Belleville’ Director Sylvain Chomet Fires Back at AI Accusations Over Dior Film Featuring Robert Pattinson’s Voice: ‘Everything Was Drawn by Hand’ (EXCLUSIVE)
stories.Summary:
Sylvain Chomet, the French animator behind "The Triplets of Belleville" and "The Illusionist," is denying that generative AI was used to make his six-minute Dior short "Christian Dior's Night in Color," which features voice work from Robert Pattinson, Rihanna, Josh O'Connor, LaKeith Stanfield, Louis Garrel and Camille Cottin. The film, produced by Aton Soumache, drew online criticism after some viewers pointed to visual glitches, including a character with six fingers, as signs of AI generation. Dior presented the film as a celebration of traditional craftsmanship to launch its 2026 holiday season, which made the accusations especially awkward for the brand. Chomet and Soumache told Variety that the film was made with traditional 2D techniques, with characters, backgrounds and key poses drawn by artists.

The pair acknowledges that an automated interpolation system helped generate some in-between frames to smooth movement, but they insist generative AI never produced the artwork. Soumache says the film took seven months to make and employed roughly 20 people, including six animators, storyboard artists, designers, background artists, compositors and editors. He describes the interpolation tool as a small part of the process used for repetitive work. Chomet adds that such tools automate the mechanical side of animation rather than the creative work, and he notes that the artists now draw on digital tablets rather than paper.

Chomet also says the criticism is ironic given his long commitment to hand-drawn animation. He recalls that when Disney and others declared traditional 2D dead after the rise of CGI in the era of "Toy Story," he chose to keep making hand-drawn films. He says he has stayed faithful to drawing throughout his career while still willing to use the tools technology offers. Soumache adds that Dior approached them because it wanted Chomet's distinctive drawing style, and he points to his own history of championing 2D work after years in CGI.

The short draws on episodes from Dior's history, including his friendship with Marlene Dietrich, his ties to Hollywood and the 1949 Junon gown. It also takes inspiration from an early idea behind Jonathan Anderson's Cruise 2027 collection, the shift from black-and-white to Technicolor in cinema. In the story, Dietrich, preparing to shoot in Los Angeles, asks for a colorful Dior gown, setting Dior and his seamstresses against the clock. The articles do not report any response from Dior to the accusations.

stories.Headline: Woori, MSCI Chiefs Discuss Climate, AI Finance
stories.Summary:
Woori Financial Group Chairman Yim Jong-ryong met Henry Fernandez, chairman and CEO of the global investment information provider MSCI, at Woori's headquarters in Jung-gu, Seoul, on November 5, 2026. The two men discussed how climate change and artificial intelligence are affecting the financial industry and what responses might be needed. The meeting was arranged to reaffirm the role of financial companies in supporting corporate low-carbon transition and technological innovation during a fast-changing global environment. Reports on the meeting appeared in the Korea Herald and BusinessKorea on November 6.

Yim described the founding philosophy of Daehan Cheonil Bank, the predecessor of Woori Financial, and said its goal of supplying funds for the national economy and industrial development has carried forward into productive, inclusive and ESG finance. He said the group would significantly strengthen financial support for green industries, using its corporate finance capabilities in line with the government's Korean-style Green Great Transformation, or K-GX, strategy. Woori has set a target of providing 100 trillion won, about $72.5 billion, in ESG finance by 2030, and it had reached a cumulative 67 trillion won by the end of 2025. The group's stated aim is to do more than supply money and to help companies make a soft landing into a low-carbon economic structure. The Korea Herald gave the target as $73.7 billion, a different conversion of the same figure.

Woori is also bringing AI into its operations to make financial work more efficient. It runs a "K-Taxonomy Expert Consultation AI Service" that supports reviews of whether corporate activities meet the Korean Green Taxonomy, which defines environmentally sustainable economic activities. With this support, Woori Bank had provided green loans meeting those standards worth 180 billion won, about $130.5 million, by the end of September 2026. The Korea Herald put that figure at 1.8 trillion won, so the two outlets disagree on the scale of these loans. Yim said the meeting gave both sides a chance to exchange views on global financial issues, and that the group will keep supporting companies' low-carbon transition while pursuing companywide innovation and productivity gains through AI.

stories.Headline: Military spouse uses AI to help veterans navigate VA benefits
stories.Summary:
Tracy Contrino, a Calvert County military spouse, has launched TheClusterFix, an independent nonprofit that uses an AI assistant called Frank to help veterans find and understand benefits information from the Department of Veterans Affairs and other federal sources. The idea grew out of her own frustration while trying to help her husband, who served 18 years in the Army and National Guard and is rated 100% P&T disabled, navigate the VA system. Contrino says the tool is meant to show veterans where to start and what steps may come next, not to replace the VA or give legal or medical advice. The organization stresses that it is not affiliated with or part of the VA.

Frank is built to draw on publicly available VA and federal information and to answer questions quickly, without appointments or waiting. Contrino says many of the questions it receives so far concern general and education benefits, and the group has begun working with higher education institutions. Hope Bald, the board president, says Frank surfaced information for her own claim that a service officer had not mentioned, and the team is now expanding its guidance on VA education benefits. The nonprofit is free for veterans, relies on grants and community donations, and hopes to add partnerships, a broader resource center and more data collection that does not identify individuals.

Contrino describes getting a disability rating as a tedious process that can take months or even years, and she says denials can leave veterans confused about their next move. She says many veterans feel alone in the process and give up, even though some available benefits can be significant for them and their families. Her stated goal is to save veterans time, possibly days, weeks or months, spent searching websites or waiting on hold, and not to compete with the VA. Bald says she and Contrino want veterans to receive clear answers rather than confusion.

A separate opinion piece on RealClearDefense, written by Rob Schroder, founder and CEO of SteerBridge and a Marine Corps veteran, makes a related argument about federal benefits. It refers to a presidential executive order directing the Department of War and the VA to modernize record sharing, build digital tools and improve transition assistance. Schroder argues that AI should speed up processing by organizing records, summarizing evidence and automating administrative tasks, but that qualified VA personnel, not AI, should decide whether a veteran is entitled to a benefit. He says SteerBridge has helped agencies cut processing times, such as handling education benefits in seconds rather than weeks and screening disability evidence in hours rather than months, and he urges judging modernization by measurable results for veterans.

stories.Headline: Why Do We Still Need AI When It Has Snatched Up All Graphics Cards and Memory?
stories.Summary:
The first article, published by 36Kr on November 4, 2026, reports that graphics cards and memory have become scarce for gamers because manufacturers have shifted production toward AI and professional cards. It says the RTX 5090 is nearly impossible to buy, the RTX 5080 has roughly doubled in price, AMD is preparing another price increase, and Intel's Arc B580 may be discontinued. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman drew anger when he said ordinary consumers' memory is used only about 5 percent of the time and that this allocation is unreasonable, suggesting the hardware belongs in data centers running around the clock. Elon Musk joined the online backlash, and the article argues that Altman's view is illogical, because data center cards may sit idle in warehouses, and because the purpose of AI should be to give people more leisure rather than take away their entertainment.

The article cites a whistleblower channel, Moore's Law Is Dead, which claims AI card makers pressured customers into advance contracts, while the customers' facilities were not ready, leaving many cards stacked and unused. It also says some purchased cards may exist only as delivery vouchers, and that companies may use unreceived hardware as collateral for loans. The author notes that investor Michael Burry is reportedly buying put options on AI companies expiring as early as 2027. Using a British financial blogger's estimate, the article compares the cost of 200 hours of the upcoming GTA 6 at about $2 per day with roughly $5,000 for the same stretch spent on nights out, and it concludes that for many ordinary consumers games are the only affordable high-quality entertainment, so taking them away would likely push people toward free short videos rather than a more refined life.

The second article, published by GameGPU on November 7, 2026, covers the release of gputaskman, an open-source utility under the MIT license, with version 0.3.3 published in its repository. The tool monitors GPU load, video memory use, and per-process resource consumption, along with temperature, power, and frequencies, and it runs in the terminal with real-time graphs. It supports Windows with NVIDIA and AMD cards, Linux, WSL, and Apple Silicon on macOS, and it can detect local AI runtimes such as llama.cpp, Ollama, and LM Studio. For compatible models it estimates how memory is split among weights, the KV cache, and compute buffers, though the developer says these figures are approximations from model metadata and logs rather than direct readings of video memory. Results can be saved as JSON, Windows builds need no Python installation, and the developer calls the project experimental, with some features still limited.

stories.Headline: Saudi Arabia introduces AI principles for media
stories.Summary:
Saudi Arabia has introduced a national framework that governs how artificial intelligence may be used in media, setting out principles meant to promote transparency, accuracy and accountability. The AI Principles in Media document, reported by the Saudi Press Agency, asks media practitioners and content creators to say when material has been generated or assisted by AI. They are asked to use clear labels, watermarks or metadata so audiences can tell synthetic content from authentic records. The move follows growing use of AI tools to produce text, images, video and audio. Officials cite concerns about misinformation, intellectual property rights and user privacy.

The guidelines lay out eight core principles that cover transparency and disclosure, factual accuracy and credibility, privacy and the protection of public figures, and the prevention of misleading content. They also address accountability across the full life of a piece of content, impartiality and integrity, public awareness and empowerment, and ongoing impact assessment with regulatory compliance. The framework cautions against treating generative AI as an authoritative source of information. It stresses that human verification, deepfake detection and awareness of possible algorithmic bias are needed. Taken together, these points set expectations for how newsrooms and creators should check and label their work.

The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, known as SDAIA, worked with the General Authority of Media Regulation to promote responsible use of the technology. The two bodies organized the AI for Impact forum, which brought together more than 250 media professionals, digital influencers and content creators. Participants discussed ethical standards and practical risks at each stage of production, from research and scriptwriting to editing, audience analytics and impact assessment. The forum also marked the launch of the Impact Creators program, which will offer theoretical instruction and practical training in content verification and professional production standards. According to the reports, the program aims to help Saudi creators use AI safely and effectively while strengthening trust in the Kingdom's digital media sector.

He noted that WeWork, the once high-flying office-sharing company, never completed its IPO, while OpenAI keeps pushing its own listing back. Stocktwits reported the interview on November 7, 2026.

He asked what the effect on Nvidia would be if the company, which he called the poster child of the AI trade, took a big hit. He also argued that Nvidia is well run and that its chips are strong, but questioned whether demand for them is unlimited and whether the buyers can turn a profit. He singled out neocloud companies, which rely heavily on outside financing, as the most vulnerable, noting that their borrowing costs are rising. Marcus cited a Bank of England study of roughly 10,000 decision-makers that, in his reading, found only limited productivity gains from AI so far.

Responsibility for those views rests with Marcus himself, who framed them as warnings rather than predictions, and who said that shifts in investor confidence could matter as much as financial fundamentals. The reports include no response from OpenAI or Nvidia. stories.Headline: Smaller Language Models Could Reshape How Enterprises Deploy AI
stories.Summary:
Enterprises are shifting their attention from how capable large language models are to how reliably they can be evaluated, governed, and controlled, according to reporting from Analytics India Magazine published on November 6, 2026, and a follow-up from TechGig on November 7. That shift is pushing smaller language models (SLMs) into the spotlight. These models are built for narrow jobs such as document processing, classification, information retrieval, and workflow automation, and organisations can split work across models of different sizes instead of relying on one large model for an entire pipeline. Experts warn, however, that a smaller model is not automatically safer, since a poorly trained one can cause as many problems within its intended use as a much larger one.

The main operational advantage of SLMs is that their scope is easier to define, which makes testing more practical. A general-purpose model takes open-ended prompts, so its possible failure cases are close to endless, while a specialised model can be tested against a curated, representative dataset and its failures traced more systematically. Experts also describe a multi-model setup in which smaller models act as independent checks on a larger model, validating outputs against retrieved context, filtering sensitive information, or screening queries for prompt injection. In agent systems that access databases and APIs, one commentator argued that the model deciding on an action should not also approve it, and that a small policy model or plain rules should check each action against permissions. Experts stressed that deterministic, identity-based infrastructure controls should still govern access to databases and critical tools.

Industry figures behind the reporting say that building safety into SLMs requires work across the whole lifecycle, including data curation, model alignment, adversarial testing, and deployment safeguards. KiteFishAI, led by Anuj Gupta, says it tests models inside their full application environment, including APIs, external tools, and retrieval pipelines, for prompt leakage, bias, and instruction drift, and it is building custom pipelines for banking, financial services, and healthcare, though it has not publicly named client deployments. Sourav Bandyopadhyay of Shunya Labs advises building test sets from real traffic, held out from training, and reporting accuracy per class rather than a single average, which he says can hide failing categories. He notes this matters in markets such as India, where code-mixing and dialectal variation are common.

The articles also note trade-offs, since SLMs can struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, long context windows, and ambiguous inputs. Shunya Labs described a three-tier design for its multilingual customer-care voice platform in which an internal 143 MB model resolves about 90 per cent of requests, with reported accuracy of 97.7 per cent on high-confidence predictions. Routing intermediate requests through a mid-sized model reduced LLM traffic to 3.9 per cent and raised throughput 1.9 times compared with an LLM-based classifier alone. The articles add that managing fleets of specialised models shifts the engineering burden toward routing logic, drift monitoring, versioning, and fallback protocols, and that adoption will depend on whether models can be verified to perform predictably under defined, audited conditions.

stories.Headline: Democrats Plan Legislation for Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Democrats are preparing a wave of artificial intelligence legislation that would take effect once they gain control of Congress in January, according to a November 6, 2026 Reuters report that also appeared in other outlets. The plans cover AI system safety, corporate liability and the electricity demands of data centers. Lawmakers and advocates said the proposals would mark a sharp break from the Republican-led Congress, which mostly focused on promoting AI development and did not pass restrictions on the technology. Voters have grown wary of data centers and their large power needs, and that concern appears to be shaping the Democratic agenda.

The bills under discussion would aim to shield consumers from rising electricity costs tied to data centers, require independent testing of advanced AI systems, and clarify when AI companies can be held liable for harm caused by their products. Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, who is expected to become majority leader, said protecting consumers from higher energy costs would be among his priorities next year. Representative Lori Trahan of Massachusetts plans to push for independent experts to measure leading AI models against safety standards, and for clarity on corporate responsibility when AI systems act harmfully. Any such legislation would face steep odds while Republican President Donald Trump remains in office, since he has repeatedly rejected calls for mandatory AI rules. Democrats could still try to attach AI provisions to routine annual bills, which must pass Congress.

Representative Greg Casar of Texas, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said AI executives should be called to testify under oath. Representative Zoe Lofgren of California, who is seeking to chair the House Science Committee, said Democrats would focus on developing responsible regulations while also fostering innovation. Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat who won a Senate seat on Tuesday, called during his campaign for an independent agency to oversee AI with power to police tech companies. Lofgren and other House committee leaders asked OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and SpaceX in October to detail their security practices and report instances of their AI tools acting in ways their designers did not intend.

The Reuters report said public concern about AI is high, with most voters in an October Reuters poll saying the administration and Congress are not taking its risks seriously enough. One policy analyst said a crisis could build enough support to overcome a presidential veto, which Congress can override with two-thirds of both chambers. Technology stocks fell sharply on Thursday on fears of slower AI development and doubts about returns on heavy spending, and the slide extended into Friday in Europe and Asia. Trump said on Friday he would work with states that want to embrace AI, without giving details. The articles do not say when any of the proposed bills would be formally introduced or voted on.

On November 4, 2026, University of Nebraska System President Jeffrey P. Gold, MD, sent a message to faculty and staff about artificial intelligence, and the system then rolled out Executive Memorandum 48 on Thursday, November 5. The memorandum sets university-wide expectations for the secure, ethical and responsible use of AI. The system has also obtained an enterprise license to ChatGPT, and faculty and staff are encouraged to take the Generative AI Security Essentials Training in Bridge. Those who complete it at Kearney, Lincoln, Omaha or the Nebraska College of Technical Agriculture will automatically receive access to an enterprise ChatGPT account, while UNMC is still working to implement that access.

Faculty and staff who use a free or non-enterprise version of ChatGPT for university work are expected to move to the enterprise version by the end of the fall 2026 semester. Most employees should find the baseline account sufficient, though heavy users can request credits for additional use. Faculty may also request enterprise access for students, and all employees already have Microsoft CoPilot. The NU System is also forming a new NU AI Governance Group to carry out the memorandum, with representatives from faculty, staff, the NU AI Institute, and the legal, compliance, ITS, procurement and business and finance offices. That group will decide which tools are acceptable for routine work, which need an approved exception, and how AI use should be disclosed.

President Gold wrote that the university must harness AI's potential while protecting university data, sensitive information and intellectual property, and he acknowledged that moving to approved platforms may be a significant change for people who built workflows around other tools. He also stressed that the memorandum does not decide whether AI should be used in teaching or research, since faculty keep authority over their courses and principal investigators keep authority over their research. At UNMC, Emily Glenn, dean of the McGoogan Health Sciences Library, along with John Windle, MD, leads implementation as co-chairs of the Campus Steering Committee for Healthcare Artificial Intelligence. Dr. Windle was named UNMC's first associate vice chancellor for healthcare artificial intelligence last month by Chancellor H. Dele Davies, MD.

The changes come as AI evolves quickly and universities everywhere face difficult questions about its use. Norwich University, a separate institution, has announced its own Artificial Intelligence Center to offer courses and research on machine learning and related fields, with an emphasis on ethical and responsible AI. Questions about getting started with enterprise tools can go to the NU ITS help desk at nusupport@nebraska.edu or 866-472-3970. The article notes that additional resources and answers to frequently asked questions will be shared in the weeks ahead.

The question before the council is whether an interpretation of the existing code could bar these facilities in Salem.

If the council finds that the code already excludes them, the interpretation would effectively halt such projects without writing entirely new rules. A separate report from Salem Reporter also says the developer, Verrus, has offered the city a $10 million package ahead of the code interpretation.

The articles do not describe the terms of that offer or how the council has responded to it. stories.Headline: IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge pair a 120-qubit Nighthawk with an AMD supercomputer to test quantum error correction
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, IBM, AMD and the Department of Energy-funded Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory unveiled a joint platform for quantum error correction that links a quantum processor with a classical supercomputer. The setup places IBM's 120-qubit Quantum Nighthawk processor alongside ORNL's Umbra system, which runs AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen EPYC CPUs. The platform will also connect to the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility. Reporters covering the launch noted that the partners aim to bring more classical computing into the work to speed progress.

The project supports the Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission, which targets 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028. IBM says it has run experiments with up to 70 logical qubits and 438 hard operations, so the partners would need roughly a 230-fold rise in hard-operation count to reach the goal. Researchers will compare what each error-correction technique requires in qubits, time, samples and classical resources. They will also test concatenated and space-time codes, algorithm-aware decoders and hardware-aware compilation through IBM's Quantum System API. Today's qubits err roughly once every few hundred operations, while algorithms such as Shor's need billions of error-free operations.

IBM, AMD and ORNL are the organizations behind the platform, and their leaders described its purpose in their own terms. Jay Gambetta, director of IBM Research, said the question is no longer whether error correction will work on quantum hardware. AMD executive vice president Mark Papermaster described the platform as an important step toward scalable, efficient infrastructure for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Travis Humble, director of the Quantum Science Center at ORNL, said solving error-correction challenges is a laboratory priority. IBM also said the results may shape its planned Quantum Starling, its first fault-tolerant machine.

The platform builds on earlier collaborations among the same partners. In 2025, IBM and AMD demonstrated an algorithm that decodes quantum errors efficiently on AMD chips. Earlier in 2026, IBM and ORNL used quantum computers and the Frontier supercomputer to simulate magnetic materials and fusion-fuel candidates. Other companies are pursuing similar goals, with Quantinuum expecting its Nexus system to automate error correction through 2029. The articles do not say when the partners expect the first results from the new platform.

stories.Headline: Building AI governance at the speed of trust
stories.Summary:
An Indigenous-led research team is building Ask Mishomis, a digital repository meant to make research accessible to First Nations communities while keeping control of their data with those communities. The project grew out of a memory of Jacob Taylor's undergraduate years at Western University, when he walked past a shelf holding 11 volumes of the Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples that were largely unread because they were written in language only academics could follow. Taylor, now Executive Director of the National Indigenous Economic Prosperity Institute at First Nations University of Canada, said AI could help translate complex research into usable formats. The platform's name means "grandfather" in Ojibwe, reflecting its aim of sharing knowledge in a conversational way. Taylor is co-leading the work with Victoria Lemieux, a professor emerita at the University of British Columbia.

The platform uses retrieval-augmented generation, which draws answers from verified research rather than broad web data, so community economic development officers and local leaders can ask plain-language questions and get direct answers. It runs on Clio-X, a decentralized, blockchain-based infrastructure Lemieux first developed for archives and cultural institutions, which lets communities decide who can access their information and under what conditions. The project is supported by an AI Safety Catalyst Grant from the CAISI Research Program at CIFAR, the independent scientific research arm of the Canadian Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute. Its governance is grounded in wâhkôtowin, a Cree concept of relationships among people, land, animals, plants, ancestors, the spirit world and future generations. The team is following the First Nations principles of OCAP, which stand for ownership, control, access and possession, through campus surveys, workshops and discussions.

The article presents the project's approach as a response to a history in which Indigenous data was taken without consent and used to harm communities, including through centralized registries under the Indian Act. Its leaders warn that modern AI could repeat that pattern by drawing cultural knowledge from the web into corporate systems that ignore community ownership. Lemieux argued that broad, top-down legislation cannot guarantee safety for a specific cultural group, so the community itself should decide who enters and on what terms. Taylor credited CIFAR's funding with giving the work institutional credibility and the resources to build trust and support emerging Indigenous researchers. Jonathan Sawa, a Cree graduate researcher from Cowessess First Nation who is co-leading the survey and workshop design, said that community ownership of an AI system and its data governance would be ideal.

The team says the project must move at the speed of trust, which it contrasts with the fast pace of the technology sector. Taylor linked the model to Call to Action 92 of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which urges Canadian institutions to foster Indigenous participation in the modern economy. Under the approach described, communities could eventually own hardware nodes and receive economic value when their data contributes to wider activity. Lemieux said that the relationships built through the work matter most to her, more than the research outputs or the technical systems. The article does not give a timeline for launching the platform or describe its next milestones.

stories.Headline: How Grab Keeps Mobile Stability Amid a Surge in AI-Generated Code
stories.Summary:
Grab, the Southeast Asian super-app company, has built a layered defense to keep its mobile apps stable as AI coding assistants increase the amount of code shipped in each release. According to reporting from InfoQ and LavX News published on November 7, 2026, the growing use of these tools has sped up development and raised the number of code changes per release, which creates more chances for defects and crashes. The company responded with a strategy designed to prevent, detect, and contain crashes across the full development and release lifecycle. The articles describe this as a shift-left approach that aims to catch problems as early as possible.

The stakes are high because a high volume of merge requests lands every week across many product teams, and many features ship behind flags that switch on independently of releases. A single change can introduce a crash that lowers crash-free session rates and can affect the app's ranking on Google Play. Because not all users enable automatic updates, a crash that reaches production can remain on their devices for a long time. Crashes also do not always arrive with clean, symbolicated stack traces, so engineers must cross-reference release timelines, flag rollouts, and session metadata to find the cause. Grab's engineers summed up the goal by saying that AI is speeding up how fast code is written, and that the layered defense is what makes that speed safe.

The first and primary line of defense runs from pre-merge through pre-production. Engineers use static code analyzers such as Android Lint and SwiftLint, along with platform, community, and custom lint rules, to catch issues before code merges. Automated and manual testing, including unit tests, UI tests, and quality assurance checks, adds further protection. Grab Early Access serves as a pre-production gate where early builds go to internal users and are monitored for crashes, since a problem seen by only a few internal users could become a significant spike in production. During the release phase, staged rollouts start with a small percentage of users so engineers can pause if crash rates look abnormal, while feature flags let teams enable features gradually and disable them without a new release if they push crash rates past set thresholds.

After release, Grab relies on rapid incident response. Real-time monitoring through Firebase Crashlytics and BigQuery flags anomalies as soon as a build goes live, and automated triage with enriched diagnostics helps teams map crashes to specific pull requests. Feedback loops and post-mortem analysis then feed lessons back into extended lint rules and broader test coverage. The original write-up is credited to Sergio De Simone at InfoQ, and the articles note that the full piece contains more detail than these summaries provide.
