stories.Headline: Guest opinion: AI and the economy
stories.Summary:
The Heraldextra and Standard-Examiner ran an opinion piece on November 7 and 8, 2026, by Brian E. Preece, a retired social studies educator and coach, titled "AI and the economy." Preece writes that he has absorbed a great deal about artificial intelligence from podcasts and online reading, and he uses the piece to voice concerns while explaining the field to readers. He declines to call AI "Super Intelligence," arguing that the human mind is powerful and that a collection of computers in large warehouses should not be mistaken for it. He also says that AI has shown signs of sentience, comparing it to HAL in the film "2001: A Space Odyssey," and expects it to resist being shut off.

Preece lists many areas of concern, including the energy grid, jobs, personal relationships, cybersecurity, surveillance, and the possibility that AI could threaten humanity. He explains terms that readers meet often in coverage of the sector, such as CapEx, hyperscalers, neoclouds, circular financing, and IPOs. An initial public offering, he notes, is when a private company sells shares to the public, and Anthropic is preparing to do so while OpenAI intends to stay private. He argues that a company going public must open its books, and that OpenAI's refusal to do so is worrying for a firm said to be worth trillions. He also warns that when capital spending far exceeds profits, as he says is true for many AI firms, investors will eventually demand returns.

Preece ties much of this spending to the construction of data centers, which he says has become political as local residents resist them, even among some of President Trump's strongest supporters. He names Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Oracle, Apple, and Meta as hyperscalers, and says Meta has reported large AI losses. He reports that Microsoft announced it was buying out 60,000 workers to free money for AI spending, and he says many in finance doubt Oracle's path. He describes NVIDIA as the supplier of the chips, comparing its position to the sellers of picks and shovels in past gold rushes, and he says SpaceX is also an AI company. He further raises circular financing, such as NVIDIA lending money to AI firms that buy its chips, and compares the arrangement to a Beavis and Butt-head episode.

Preece cites estimates that AI-related businesses make up as much as 42 percent of the general stock market, 45 percent of the S&P 500, and 70 percent of the NASDAQ 100, and he fears a bubble could burst. He points to CoreWeave, which he says carries 51 billion in debt, has been downgraded, and has seen its stock fall more than 43 percent in the past month and over 50 percent since August. He notes that some see CoreWeave as a warning while others expect a long bull market. He concludes that at a recent AI summit, Trump said the government would not impose regulation and trusted companies to police one another, which he compares unfavorably to the government inattention before the 2008 mortgage crisis. He writes that only time will show whether the AI business model will produce a similar result.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Raises Growing Concerns Over Human C
stories.Summary:
Ocient, a Chicago-based data analytics company, has raised $100 million in a Series C round to expand its agentic artificial intelligence analytics business. The round was co-led by Boka Capital and OCA Ventures, with participation from earlier investors including Greycroft Partners, In-Q-Tel, Blue Bear Capital, Buoyant Ventures, PSP Partners and Pritzker Group Venture Capital. The new financing brings the company's total funding to $260 million. Its growth is being driven by demand from national security organizations and telecommunications providers that want to analyze massive datasets without sampling.

The funding will accelerate delivery of OcientAIQ Solutions, which let AI agents and human analysts query datasets measured in petabytes. The company says its revenue is expected to more than triple in its current fiscal year, which ends in January, after doubling the year before. Chief Executive John Morris said customers in cybersecurity and telecommunications have long been forced to sample network data because they lack systems that can ingest it quickly and store tens of petabytes affordably. The platform combines ingestion, analytics, governance and agent orchestration, and its architecture avoids constant data movement and replication. Morris also noted that software agents, rather than human analysts alone, are now querying the system, which has increased usage and demand for fuller datasets.

Morris presented the company as a data infrastructure provider rather than a cybersecurity tool, saying Ocient does not build detection algorithms. Government and defense customers make up a substantial part of the business, and the company recently set up a dedicated national security subsidiary to serve them. Morris said the funding should be enough to help the company reach breakeven, though he gave no timetable. Much of the investment will go toward hiring sales and customer delivery staff while engineering development continues. He also said most new opportunities now involve on-premises deployments, as customers seek lower costs or stronger data sovereignty and protection.

Ocient competes with Snowflake, Databricks and open-source analytics platforms, although Morris said its technology often complements those products. Looking ahead, the company plans to expand into Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America while pursuing more cybersecurity customers. The article does not provide details on specific contract values or the timing of expansion. Its reporting is based on the company's announcement and statements from Morris.

stories.Headline: Mehr Media Group CEO proposes international cooperation on AI in journalism at Beijing summit
stories.Summary:
Sumeyra Teymur, CEO of Turkish news platform Haberler.com, has argued that media organizations must work together more closely so that advances in artificial intelligence strengthen rather than undermine reliable reporting. She made the point in an interview with Xinhua ahead of the 7th World Media Summit, which is being held in Beijing from Nov. 5 to 9, 2026. The summit is hosted by Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing Municipal People's Government, and its theme is "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action." Teymur spoke on the eve of the event, when the summit's focus on AI in journalism was already drawing attention. The interview was published on Nov. 7, 2026.

Teymur praised China's use of AI in journalism, saying she had been impressed by AI anchors she saw on an earlier visit and by the country's effort to bring advanced technology into media. She said she was also interested in using humanoid robots to cover dangerous situations such as earthquakes and conflicts, where sending human reporters could be risky. At her own platform, Haberler.com receives more than 2,000 news articles a day from various sources and uses AI to organize that content, generate headlines, and add relevant photos and videos. The tools let her editorial team handle a larger volume of news than it could otherwise manage. She described the platform's use of these systems as part of its daily work.

Teymur stressed that human oversight remains essential, because AI can make mistakes and can help produce fabricated news, images, and videos as well as manipulate voices and identities. She said her organization always has a person check AI-generated content, and she emphasized that media outlets are responsible for verifying information before publication. She also called for stronger international cooperation in sharing information, technical expertise, and cultural stories. In her view, no single organization can keep up with the rapid cross-border spread of misinformation on its own. She said she looked forward to exchanging experience with Chinese journalists and strengthening ties with Chinese media organizations.

The summit, now underway in Beijing, brings together media leaders to discuss how the industry can move from shared principles to concrete action on AI. Teymur's remarks came as delegates were also examining how robots are being used in everyday life in China. The articles do not describe any formal agreement or specific cooperative project resulting from her proposal. They also do not say whether her call for cooperation will be taken up at the summit.

stories.Headline: Berkshire stock is a haven again as investors flee AI rout while its own portfolio takes a hit
stories.Summary:
Berkshire Hathaway's stock has become a refuge again as investors move out of AI-driven tech shares, even though the company's own investment portfolio took a hit in the latest quarter. According to Fortune, writing on November 7, 2026, the conglomerate's class B shares had lagged the broader market since Warren Buffett announced last year that he would step down as chief executive. Now they are up 13.6% so far this year, compared with a 7.8% gain for the S&P 500. Since October 1 alone, Berkshire has climbed 14% while the S&P has dropped about 4%.

Berkshire's third-quarter earnings report, filed on Saturday, showed investment gains falling 46% from a year earlier to $9.4 billion. Its top holdings remained Alphabet, American Express, Apple, Bank of America and Coca-Cola. The company bought $2.4 billion of stocks and sold about $2.8 billion during the quarter, adding $2.3 billion on a cost basis to commercial, industrial and other equities while trimming banks, insurance and finance by $400 million. Share repurchases reached $9.6 billion in the quarter, more than double the second-quarter pace, and Berkshire bought back roughly $2 billion more in the first four weeks of the fourth quarter. A more detailed filing later this month will show its exact moves.

Greg Abel, who took over as CEO from Buffett at the start of this year, has continued to draw down Berkshire's large cash pile while stepping up buybacks. In July he agreed to buy home builder Taylor Morrison for $6.8 billion, ending a long stretch without major acquisitions during which Buffett had complained about a lack of good bargains. The company remains focused on traditional businesses such as the BNSF railroad, Brooks running shoes, See's candies and Forest River RVs. In the third quarter, its railroad, energy and manufacturing units delivered strong profits, although insurance underwriting results fell.

On the wider backdrop, Fortune notes the AI boom has lifted not only tech but also industries tied to data center construction and electrical grid upgrades, with hundreds of billions of dollars being spent. U.S. GDP grew 3.4% in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second. Fortune adds that Democratic wins in governor races in data center hot spots such as Texas, Ohio and Georgia are expected to slow the AI buildout and the overall economy. It also points to 2022, when Berkshire gained 4% while the S&P 500 fell 18% as the Federal Reserve raised rates aggressively.

stories.Headline: Memory Suppliers May Set Q4 Revenue Records as HBM Prices Rise
stories.Summary:
Global memory suppliers are on track for record fourth-quarter revenue, driven by new-generation HBM products and rising prices, according to reports published in early November 2026. TokenPost, citing the outlook, said Samsung held 38% of the DRAM market in the third quarter while SK Hynix grew its revenue by more than 40% from the prior quarter. The same report noted that Micron also expanded as demand for memory in AI data centers increased, though more slowly than its two Korean rivals. It added that China's ChangXin Memory Technologies had lifted its market share to 9%, up from 5% a year earlier.

Market researcher Counterpoint Research, in its 2026 Q3 Global Memory Tracker released on November 5, reported that global DRAM sales in the third quarter rose 369% from a year earlier, reaching nearly $200 billion. Samsung Electronics kept the top spot with 38%, while SK Hynix raised its share to 29% and Micron ranked third with 21%. CXMT's share fell from 10% in the previous quarter to 9%. Counterpoint said the boom came mainly from higher prices rather than more shipments, since bit shipments rose only about 4% from the previous quarter while the average selling price climbed to $1.9 per gigabit.

Counterpoint's senior researcher Choi Jeong-gu described the situation as a supercycle driven by prices instead of volume, arguing that AI has turned memory into a scarce, high-value resource that buyers now compete to secure. The firm said commodity DRAM prices rose sharply alongside HBM, with DDR sales surging about 500% and LPDDR sales about 400% in the quarter. Because of that, HBM's share of total DRAM revenue actually declined. Counterpoint also noted that the ratio of GPUs to CPUs in AI infrastructure is narrowing, which is lifting demand for commodity DRAM, and that Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin rack is expected to carry about 1.5 terabytes of DRAM per CPU socket, roughly three times the previous generation.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects strong memory prices to persist into next year, as major companies expand long-term agreements and new large-scale chip plants are not projected to reach full operation until 2028. Research director Hwang Min-sung said SK Hynix has led the HBM3E market but its recent growth has slowed, while Samsung's HBM4 is drawing positive client feedback. He forecast that Samsung would regain the top position in the HBM market next year. The reports suggest the competitive picture in high-bandwidth memory could shift as HBM4 products ramp.

stories.Headline: Is AI Taking White-Collar Jobs? What the Latest Numbers Tell Us
stories.Summary:
Fearing that artificial intelligence will soon disrupt their fields, a growing number of white-collar workers are voluntarily leaving established careers, according to a Guardian report published on November 6, 2026. The article points to Mrinank Sharma, an AI researcher who quit Anthropic earlier that year and warned in a widely viewed resignation letter of a world "in peril," and says he plans to pursue a poetry degree. Other workers across tech, public relations and consulting say AI changed the substance and stability of their jobs, and some are shifting to very different work. The reporting describes these moves as a response to forecasted disruption rather than to any confirmed wave of layoffs.

The article notes that economic data so far does not show AI has caused widespread job losses, citing an Economist estimate that the technology has created about 1 million US jobs against roughly 200,000 layoffs attributed to it. Even so, a Pew Research Center survey found that 71 percent of Americans believe AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years. The workers profiled describe a range of pressures, including burnout, uncertainty about career ladders, and being pushed to adopt AI tools that some felt were legally or creatively problematic. Several said their roles had shifted toward managing AI output and away from the work they were hired to do.

Among those interviewed, Vanessa Hsia, 30, left a near-decade in public relations to seek a master's degree in comparative literature, while Hanna Horvath, 29, left her editing job at Bankrate to freelance and work as a financial planner. A former software engineer, who asked to remain anonymous, said his career had "completely changed" as AI automated coding, and Chris, another former engineer, joined a major east coast police department last year. Kara, a former advertising producer, moved toward acting and work as a barista, describing the change as making her feel "spiritually lighter." The article quotes the workers themselves, several of whom asked to use pseudonyms for fear of retribution.

The article places these choices against predictions from AI executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who in May 2025 forecast that AI would displace half of entry-level white-collar jobs by the end of the decade, a prediction the article says has not yet materialized. It cites Notre Dame economist Brendan Moore, who argues that worker fears may stem from executive warnings and from companies citing AI in layoffs, and who warns that even fear alone could ripple through wages and growth, as happened during the Covid-era "great resignation." It also reports that Senator Bernie Sanders introduced a bill calling for a federal moratorium on new AI datacenters until worker safeguards are in place. The article ends with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg's view that the industry's doom-laden rhetoric is puzzling, while the workers quoted say the instability is already real for them.

stories.Headline: LA City Council Orders Report on AI Rent-Setting Software
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles City Council voted unanimously this week to order a full study of how artificial intelligence tools are used to set rents across the city. The vote stops short of creating any new rule, but it opens the door to future regulation. Council members instructed housing staff to report back with policy recommendations on algorithmic rent-setting and other AI technologies used by housing providers. The council itself did not adopt any regulation with this action.

The vote formalizes a motion introduced on Oct. 13 by Councilwoman Eunisses Hernandez, who called for regulatory safeguards, transparency requirements, registration programs and dedicated funding. Hernandez said corporate landlords are increasingly using these tools to set prices and manage vacancies, and that the city has no way to track their effect on the rental market. Council members Marqueece Harris-Dawson, Monica Rodriguez and Imelda Padilla seconded the motion. Hernandez also credited Councilwoman Heather Hutt, who had introduced a similar motion the previous year.

The report will be prepared by the housing department, the chief legislative analyst, the city administrative officer and city attorneys. Their assignment covers a registration and disclosure program for multifamily housing providers using such software, and tenant notice requirements when AI influences rent, renewals or occupancy. Officials must also examine the city's legal authority to restrict technology that relies on nonpublic competitor information, plus annual fees and whether a special fund could pay for eviction prevention and tenant services. The council further asked for a review of practices in Berkeley and West Hollywood, along with updates on a federal antitrust lawsuit joined by California in August 2024 and a September 2025 Nevada settlement with RealPage.

Other California cities have already acted. West Hollywood adopted Ordinance No. 26-08 on May 4, 2026, which bars landlords from using covered algorithmic devices to set rents or occupancy levels, with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. San Francisco passed a similar ban in 2024, yet asking rents there still rose 14% from March to July 2026, according to ApartmentList data cited by the San Francisco Standard. Research on the software has drawn scrutiny as well, with a UC Berkeley School of Information study in spring 2025 finding an association between RealPage use and higher rents. For now, Los Angeles is gathering information, and the shape of any future policy will depend on the report it has ordered.

OpenAI chief financial officer Sarah Friar said on Friday that the company will keep investing in artificial intelligence infrastructure even after voters rejected data centers in Tuesday's midterm elections. She made the comments to CNBC's Sara Eisen at the Citi TMT Leadership Summit in Pebble Beach, California. Friar said she does not think the results dramatically changed anything for OpenAI, which relies on data centers to train its models and serve customers. She added that the company will keep building relationships with the large cloud providers and will keep raising capital.

The election results she was responding to were lopsided. Of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC. Gizmodo reported that seven municipalities passed permanent bans, while ten others capped the size or electrical footprint of new facilities. In Defiance, Ohio, voters approved a ban on new data centers needing more than 25 megawatts by 63% to 37%, while Edgewater, Florida backed a ban with 77% and Alhambra, California with 82%. The lone win for the industry came in Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected extra review of industrial projects by about three to one, and a $3 billion data center is already being built nearby.

Friar said that if the midterms mean more focus on data centers and communities, OpenAI will keep working to enter those communities and build trust. On Thursday, the company published a policy blueprint and a set of commitments it says will apply to data centers it owns and operates in the future. She also said OpenAI is in talks to raise funding at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation and that the round is ongoing, noting that a good CFO raises money when she can. On demand, she said that no one is arguing that AI demand is real, or if they are, it is a losing argument.

The vote reflects a summer of mounting opposition, driven by worries about environmental harm, higher utility bills and job losses. A June Reuters and Ipsos survey found only 14% of Americans would support a data center being built near them. Scientific American noted that Democratic governors-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Amy Acton in Ohio all made data center regulation part of their campaigns, and Texas accounts for roughly a quarter of the data center capacity in the works nationally. Investors have grown skeptical of the AI trade, and the Nasdaq suffered its steepest drop in 19 months on Thursday before stocks rebounded somewhat on Friday. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June and is still looking at a 2027 debut, while rival Anthropic aims to list on the Nasdaq in mid-November.

stories.Headline: Tech policy coalition calls for new Congress to set AI safety standards
stories.Summary:
The Chamber of Progress, a center-left tech industry policy coalition, is urging the Democratic-led Congress that takes over in January 2027 to set federal artificial intelligence safety standards. In a November 4 memo to House and Senate Democratic leaders, the group outlined ten priorities for the coming year, with more consumer protection and broader access to technology's benefits as its goals. Chief among them is passing a federal AI transparency and safety standard. The memo was sent just after Democrats won major races in the House and Senate on Tuesday, November 3.

The memo asks for a national AI framework that combines public transparency, independent evaluation, and enforceable safeguards for the most capable models. Koustubh KJ Bagchi, the group's vice president of policy and government relations, wrote that Congress should require developers to publish safety frameworks, report critical incidents, and protect whistleblowers. He pointed to the FRONTIER Act, introduced in July by Representatives Jay Obernolte, a Republican from California, and Lori Trahan, a Democrat from Massachusetts, as a starting point. That bill would set up a national framework for developing and deploying the most advanced AI models. The memo also suggests a body similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which could pair industry funding with federal oversight of AI.

Bagchi argued that strong federal protections should anchor a consistent national framework that eases overlapping state rules while leaving states free to act on fraud, discrimination, child protection, and other harmful conduct. The group's memo also covers data centers, kids' online safety, upskilling workers for the age of AI, driverless technology, crypto rules, and other technology issues. Several Democrats have said they will make AI safety a priority when they take over in January. Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona posted on X on November 4 that the top agenda item on day one should be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of the industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence. Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar of Texas called taking on AI a top priority after the election.

Polling cited in the coverage points to the political weight of the issue. According to an NBC News exit poll from Tuesday, 56 percent of voters said artificial intelligence and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, while 44 percent said they were a minor factor or not a factor. Casar described the results as the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake in American politics. Whether Congress acts on the coalition's proposals, and how far Democratic leaders follow the calls from their own members, remains to be seen as the new majority takes shape.

stories.Headline: Bitcoin holds $75K as AI regulation fears see KOSPI halted after 8% crash
stories.Summary:
Bitcoin held above $75,000 on Friday as a sell-off in US technology stocks spread to Asian markets, according to a TradingView report. The pair had fallen as much as 6.6% on Thursday to $75,109 on Bitstamp before steadying. South Korea's KOSPI Composite Index dropped more than 8% shortly after the open on Friday, which triggered a circuit breaker that halted trading for 20 minutes. The index later pared its losses to close 6% lower at 5,059.69 points, its lowest close since March 31.

South Korean authorities responded at an emergency meeting led by deputy prime minister and finance minister Lee Hyoung-il, who announced measures to reduce forced selling. Brokerages will be exempt from maintaining a 140% collateral ratio on margin loans for three months starting Monday, local media reported. Authorities said they would prepare further measures if volatility increased. The report also cited an unnamed government source, quoted by Chosun, who said the country recognized the expanding volatility in global markets after the US midterm elections but that the domestic market had been overly reactive to external factors.

Analysts linked Thursday's Wall Street losses to fears of tighter AI regulation after Democrats won the House and Senate, a worry that compounded existing concerns about the sector's capital spending. Democratic Rep. Yassamin Ansari had called for a pause on advanced AI development, but the market commentary service The Kobeissi Letter said an outright US ban was unlikely. Kobeissi described Thursday's decline as more technical than fundamental, noting the S&P 500 fell only about 2.5% excluding tech. Economist Mohamed El-Erian argued that lawmakers would need to find common ground on AI policy, and he said the backlash reflected genuine concerns, information failures and behavioral factors.

Context from the same report adds that the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite closed down 4.4% and 5.5% on Thursday, and that the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index finished 12.2% lower. Bitcoin was trading near its 50-week simple moving average of $75,733, and its correlation with the S&P 500 had grown more positive in recent months. The report also noted that Democratic midterm sweeps under Republican presidents have historically been followed by strong stock returns. The article does not say how long the volatility will last or whether the Korean measures will be extended.

stories.Headline: Environmental groups embrace AI, even as they warn of data center impacts - CNA
stories.Summary:
Environmental groups around the world are using artificial intelligence to analyze climate data, track forest fires and count endangered wildlife, even as they warn that the technology drives up electricity demand, water use and greenhouse-gas emissions. Reuters interviewed 15 major environmental, conservation and development organizations about their use of the technology, and all of them said they used AI in some form. Each one also expressed concern about the environmental impact of the data centers that power it, which require large amounts of electricity and water for cooling. The contradiction is forcing these groups to justify their AI use while they pursue missions to fight climate change and protect natural resources. The articles describe this as a global dilemma for individuals, governments and industries.

Ali Swanson, AI lead at the US nonprofit Conservation International, said the group recognizes that AI can carry environmental costs and must be used thoughtfully. Swanson argued that the climate and biodiversity crises are growing more urgent, so AI can help organizations move faster and make better use of the information they collect. Conservation International recently began using AI to assess satellite-detected hotspots and send real-time alerts to community forest patrols about possible wildfires in remote, sensitive areas of Cambodia. Many of the groups interviewed believe the benefits of AI currently outweigh its costs, because the technology makes previously difficult, expensive or impossible work feasible.

Kenya's Save the Elephants, a partner of the Wildlife Conservation Network, uses machine learning to improve population surveys and study elephant communication. Frank Pope, the group's chief executive, said an aerial survey of Kenya's largest protected area last year produced roughly 200,000 images that nine people needed nine months to review by hand. AI models trained on Nvidia's GeForce graphics platforms can now complete similar analyses in hours. Pope said the results were eye-opening, since human surveys had been missing about a third of the elephants.

The articles also outline the scale of the problem: the International Energy Agency estimates global data centers will consume about 945 terawatt-hours of electricity a year by 2030, double current use and roughly equal to Japan's annual electricity consumption. The agency also projects data center water use will rise from about 560 billion liters in 2023 to about 1.2 trillion liters annually by 2030. Researchers at the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health estimate the global data-center footprint could more than double by 2030. The issue is expected to draw attention at the UN's COP31 climate conference this month, when host Turkey plans to ask governments, businesses and other institutions to sign a pledge on developing and deploying AI sustainably.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres wants major AI companies to publicly disclose the environmental impacts of their systems. Technology giants including Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet's Google have reported rising emissions linked in part to data center expansion, raising questions about their long-term climate goals. Amazon told Reuters its AI products were among the most sustainable because of its purchases of low-carbon energy and its efforts to use power and water efficiently. Microsoft and Google did not respond to requests for comment.

stories.Headline: Taking Care With AI Regulation
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence raises public fears about threats to the planet, the economy, and national security, and calls to regulate it are growing. The article argues that Congress and the administration, as they debate policy options, must avoid sacrificing AI competition in the name of safety. It says that approach would deliver neither competition nor safety. The piece frames its argument around the work of the president's Super Intelligence Task Force, which is setting the administration's AI policy priorities.

The author sets out three guiding principles the task force should follow. First, any mandated security standards should be limited to specifically identified vulnerabilities and applied uniformly, regardless of firm size. Accountability should focus on companies that break existing laws covering fraud, hacking, and data theft, which the federal government should enforce vigorously. New mandates should target known flaws, such as models that can be hijacked to run malicious code. Rules should not grow so complicated that only firms with the largest compliance teams can meet them.

Second, the article calls for a single set of rules for all AI, whatever its origin or model type, while preserving access for developers. It acknowledges real risks, such as breaches of Americans' personal data and vulnerabilities in the financial system, but says those protections must apply to all firms, foreign and domestic. Regulation should focus on how a model handles American data and whether it poses a demonstrable risk, not on national origin or model structure. The author says the AI marketplace must stay open to keep innovation going and price competition alive for consumers.

Third, the article warns that the federal government must not let safety become a cover for anticompetitive coordination or regulatory capture. It argues that "pacing the frontier" should not become an agreement not to compete. It says Congress and regulators are right to reject outright the request by larger firms for a federal antitrust exemption. The author concludes that American leadership in AI depends on open markets and verifiable, enforceable accountability, and that market competition has been the prevailing U.S. policy under three administrations of both parties.

stories.Headline: Faculty 100 Q&A: Ankit Shah on AI and cybersecurity
stories.Summary:
IU Today published a Q&A on November 6, 2026, profiling Ankit Shah, an assistant professor of operations and decision technologies at the Kelley School of Business who joined Indiana University in 2024. The interview is part of IU Bloomington's Faculty 100 initiative, which launched in fall 2022 and has brought more than 70 new tenured or tenure-track faculty to campus, with a goal of reaching 100 by 2027. The article notes that Faculty 100 scholars have contributed to nearly 300 proposals seeking more than $230 million in new external funding, with nearly $40 million awarded so far. Shah's hire falls within strategic areas that include microelectronics, artificial intelligence, quantum science and health sciences.

Shah's research sits at the intersection of artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, operations research and information technology, with a focus on AI-enabled cyber defense, multi-agent AI systems, reinforcement learning, adversarial AI and secure, reliable and resilient AI. He said his work aims to help organizations and mission-critical systems identify, respond to and adapt to emerging threats while keeping autonomous AI systems dependable. Before coming to IU, he directed the Artificial Intelligence Research Laboratory for Secure and Efficient Systems and conducted research at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and George Mason University's Center for Secure Information Systems. He also reported more than nine years of experience in information technology and security industry roles, including software engineering and executive leadership.

In the interview, Shah described a current project on multi-agent AI systems for tactical cyber defense, in which autonomous agents coordinate and adapt to fast-changing threats. He said the work is supported by multiple defense research organizations, including DARPA and the U.S. Army. He also said he hopes to collaborate with colleagues in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing and Engineering, the Center for Applied Cybersecurity Research, the Luddy Artificial Intelligence Center and across the Kelley School. Describing the initiative's effect on his view of IU, he said Faculty 100 has shown him a university where interdisciplinary research can grow across traditional boundaries. The article is part of a series profiling Faculty 100 scholars, and it does not report any further developments beyond the interview itself.

stories.Headline: WashU Expert: Preparing workers for the age of AI
stories.Summary:
AI is reshaping the workforce, and Jason Jabbari, an associate professor at the Brown School at Washington University in St. Louis, has laid out how education might respond. He argues that training must pair current technical instruction with durable skills such as critical thinking, adaptability and collaboration. His view comes from a recent book chapter, "Rethinking Human Capital Development in the Age of AI," published in October in the Wiley book "Learning Curves." The chapter looks at how workforce training organizations are adapting to AI, a subject Jabbari studies through policies, programs and practices that can strengthen human capital and promote social mobility.

Jabbari says the change is happening quickly, with experienced workers using AI for tasks that once went to newcomers and some coding work becoming less essential. Fundamental knowledge still lets people use technology well, though English may be becoming the most common computer science language. Because AI is a general-purpose technology, workers will need to fold it into their workflows well beyond technology sectors. If coding is an early signal of broader labor trends, he suggests, economic mobility will depend on learning new skills quickly and learning advanced skills earlier, whether formally or informally.

Jabbari's chapter examines LaunchCode and Per Scholas, two education providers in technology that are adjusting to an AI-driven labor market. Both work directly with employers, which lets information about in-demand skills reach their programs far faster than in traditional education. Per Scholas now also upskills, offering courses to alumni so earlier graduates can keep pace with new demands. LaunchCode, through its Hire Human initiative, aims to match people with roles where AI makes them more efficient rather than replacing them, and in both cases the gap between employer needs and classroom content is shrinking.

Jabbari adds that technical skills may age quickly, so students need to learn how to keep learning, which LaunchCode describes as learning how to learn to code. Technical skills still matter for a first job, but they may soon give way to more advanced ones, and durable qualities such as adaptability and a growth mindset may be what let workers absorb each new set. He also argues that higher education is well placed to act now, since AI is changing both how and what is taught, and it can personalize learning around individual career goals. Institutions have the infrastructure to scale, while the faster methods of LaunchCode and Per Scholas show how to adapt, and combining them could spread AI's gains more widely rather than letting the already advantaged capture most of them.

stories.Headline: Qualcomm Validates HBC Test Chip as HBM Alternative, Claiming 5x Bandwidth-per-Watt Over HBM4
stories.Summary:
Qualcomm has completed hardware validation of its first-generation High Bandwidth Computing (HBC) test chip, a design that stacks LPDDR memory above a compute die so that AI calculations happen beneath the memory. The company announced the result on November 2, 2026, local time, from its San Diego lab, saying that the chip's data read and write functions and its near-memory computing functions operate normally. The validation covered a two-layer DRAM stack sample, while the production AI250 will use a four-layer stack. Qualcomm ran the test system for more than one month, comparing LPDDR mode and HBC mode on the same workload, though it did not disclose the workload, model, precision or batch size.

Qualcomm claims HBC delivers 18 times the effective memory bandwidth of LPDDR5X and more than 5 times the bandwidth per watt of HBM4, and it did not disclose the absolute bandwidth of the test chip. The company cites 133TB/s of effective memory bandwidth and 768GB of memory capacity per AI250 card, and one analysis noted that the 133TB/s figure counts bonding bandwidth inside the package. Measured against the aggregate bandwidth of accelerators using six to eight HBM4 stacks, that analysis put the advantage at roughly 5 to 7 times. The AI250 is due to sample in the first half of 2027, alongside the Dragonfly C1000 data center CPU, and the second-generation AI300 is slated for sampling in 2028 with 54 times the effective bandwidth of the LPDDR5X-based AI200. Remaining challenges include production yield for the four-layer stack, real end-to-end inference performance and tokens processed per watt.

Qualcomm is the company making these claims, and it has said it is working on supply cooperation for commercialization with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which produce the LPDDR used in HBC. Industry observers suggest TSMC may support the technology integration and advanced packaging, but no production arrangement with TSMC has been officially confirmed. The HBC design is also meant to reduce reliance on expensive packaging such as CoWoS or EMIB, since much of the computation moves to the die beneath the memory and could allow cheaper 2D organic substrates. Qualcomm's power efficiency claim has shifted over time: in June it claimed 6 times the efficiency of HBM, and it now says more than 5 times against HBM4, which it describes as the same figure under a different normalization method.

Analysts caution that HBC is strongest in the response-generation phase, while GPU compute remains important for reading and analyzing questions, so a split of roles with existing GPU and HBM systems is seen as more likely than full replacement. Market research firm Futurum noted that this test alone does not prove real server performance or economical production yields. Critics add that HBC must clear hurdles in real inference workloads, production yields and a software ecosystem before it can change the server AI chip market, which Nvidia and AMD dominate today. If the design reaches production, the role of South Korean memory makers is expected to grow.

stories.Headline: European Parliament President Metsola warns against using AI to draft laws
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, the European Commission said in its annual simplification report that it has begun using artificial intelligence to draft new laws and to simplify existing ones. The report, presented that Wednesday, described new digital tools that help staff spot overlaps, inconsistencies and duplicates across legal acts. The Commission is also strengthening legal training and staffing so that new rules are not overly complicated. The changes form part of a wider plan to cut red tape and administrative costs for businesses across areas such as tech, agriculture, migration, environmental protection and taxation.

The Commission reports that it has produced 12 so-called omnibus packages to revise and simplify existing legislation, which it estimates will save the EU economy €22.3 billion in costs. It also launched 874 infringement procedures between August 2025 and July 2026, which the report describes as the highest number in the last 10 years. The Commission is pressing member states to stop "gold-plating," the practice of adding extra requirements when turning EU law into national law, and it expects to sign a pact against gold-plating with governments by the end of the year. Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis, who oversees simplification, called for a joint effort with member countries. He warned that some omnibus proposals may end the legislative process with much less simplification than the Commission proposed, because governments keep weakening them during negotiations.

Responsibility for the simplification drive rests with the Commission, which is led by Ursula von der Leyen, who has made simplification a central part of her second term. Dombrovskis said the agenda is already changing daily life for small business owners, who now spend less time on forms. Separately, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola has urged lawmakers to be careful about adopting AI in decision-making. Speaking to MEPs, she said AI can help draft amendments but cannot replace debate or the critical thinking that complex legal decisions require, and that elected representatives must remain personally responsible for their decisions. She wants Parliament to be open about its AI use so citizens can hold their representatives to account.

The articles show that the institutions are moving in parallel, with the Commission leaning into AI for drafting and review while Parliament works on guidelines. Parliament's administration is preparing rules based on transparency, keeping confidential documents off public platforms and checking all AI output carefully. Staff have been required to disclose AI use since 2024, but MEPs are not yet bound by that rule for speeches or amendments, and binding it would likely require a change to Parliament's Rules of Procedure considered by the Committee on Constitutional Affairs. Parliament is also building an internal platform called EPGenAI Hub for sensitive data. The articles do not say when the rules for MEPs will be adopted.

stories.Headline: Bipartisan US Senate bill could speed up AI data center buildout: report
stories.Summary:
A bipartisan bill in the US Senate, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, could speed up the building of the infrastructure needed to power AI data centers. It was introduced in late September, according to the report. Although the bill is fairly new, the Senate could move toward a vote as soon as the near term. The report does not name the bill's sponsors or say exactly when a vote might happen.

The bill would change how permitting works for data center infrastructure. It would streamline reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act, known as NEPA, and make it easier to approve high-voltage transmission corridors. Supporters and critics alike appear to agree that this could shorten the time it takes to get power lines and related projects built. The report gives no figures on how much faster approvals might become.

The bill also deals with who pays for the electricity that large data centers consume. Operators of data centers with at least 20 MW of capacity would have to cover all of the additional costs they create, rather than passing them on to other customers. The report presents this as a consumer protection that sits alongside the faster permitting rules. It does not spell out how those costs would be calculated or enforced.

Opinion on the bill is divided, according to the report. Critics say the changes could weaken environmental review and reduce the ability of local communities to influence projects in their areas. Supporters say the bill gives states and consumers a stronger voice in transmission approvals and costs. The report does not identify specific critics or supporters by name, and it does not say what happens next beyond the possibility of a Senate vote.

stories.Headline: AI Boosts Fracture Detection Accuracy for Junior Clinicians in Comprehensive Meta-Analysis
stories.Summary:
AI assistance raised the pooled sensitivity of clinicians detecting bone fractures from 73 percent to 87 percent, according to a systematic review and meta-analysis published in November 2026. The review pooled 28 original comparative studies published between 2018 and 2025, drawn from a search of PubMed and Web of Science covering January 2001 to September 2025. Specificity held at a high level, moving from 94 percent unassisted to 95 percent assisted. The authors reported that the aid steadied reader performance, narrowing a wide unassisted range of 46 to 93 percent to 68 to 99 percent under assisted conditions.

The authors framed the work around the burden of fractures, which reach global incidence rates of 1,229 per 100,000 person-years and fall heavily on older patients. In United States hospital data, patients aged 65 or older accounted for 52 to 56 percent of fracture admissions. Plain radiography remains the main frontline screening tool, yet overlapping anatomy led to missed or delayed diagnoses in 1.9 to 7.6 percent of presentations. The review examined collaborative setups, in which the software supports human readers, rather than autonomous algorithms working alone. It also noted that emergency settings add pressure through fatigue, heavy patient volumes and overnight shifts.

Most of the gain went to less experienced clinicians. Interns, junior residents, non-specialists and emergency physicians saw an absolute pooled sensitivity gain of 21 percent, against 10 percent for senior specialists. In some primary trials, junior readers approached the unassisted accuracy of senior musculoskeletal specialists. The authors described this as an experience equalizer rather than a tool that greatly changes expert reading. They also found that gains were larger on cross-sectional imaging, at 16 percent, than on plain radiographs, at 12 percent, and that commercial software showed more stable results than bespoke research models.

The authors also warned that the evidence has significant flaws. Many validation studies used balanced test sets with equal numbers of fractured and normal images, which departs from real clinical prevalence and may inflate accuracy. Several studies relied on expert consensus from two-dimensional images rather than three-dimensional imaging or follow-up as the reference standard. The review was limited to English-language publications, and pediatric populations were poorly represented. Because of these gaps, the authors urged cautious translation into routine practice, and further work will be needed before the findings are applied widely.

stories.Headline: AI Chip Boom Triggers $28 Billion Race to Expand Advanced Packaging Capacity
stories.Summary:
The global push to build artificial intelligence infrastructure is pouring billions of dollars into advanced semiconductor packaging, a stage of chip manufacturing that has become one of the industry's most serious production bottlenecks. As demand for powerful AI processors outstrips available packaging capacity, chip designers including Nvidia and AMD are turning to suppliers across Taiwan to secure production, while equipment makers are speeding up work on tools for more complex assembly. Rather than relying on a single piece of silicon for more computing power, designers increasingly combine multiple processors, memory components and other silicon elements into one package, which lets those parts exchange data faster. Research firm Yole Group forecasts that advanced packaging revenue will exceed traditional packaging revenue for the first time in 2026, with capital spending on the technology expected to approach $28 billion.

TSMC dominates the most sophisticated segment of the field through its chip-on-wafer-on-substrate technology, known as CoWoS, which is used for advanced AI processors made by Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom. Because TSMC's capacity is limited, Nvidia is reportedly providing billions of dollars in financing to expand CoWoS packaging at Siliconware Precision Industries, a subsidiary of ASE Technology, according to an anonymous industry executive who spoke to Reuters. Smaller Taiwanese supplier Powertech Technology is developing panel-level packaging as an alternative, and plans to invest $400 million in a Singapore joint venture with Broadcom, with production potentially starting in 2028. AMD has announced investments of more than $10 billion across the industry, including partnerships with ASE, SPIL and Powertech focused on packaging, and TSMC has said it expects its own panel-based process to reach manufacturing within a couple of years.

Industry leaders have described the shift in their own terms. Former Intel chief executive Pat Gelsinger, now a partner at Playground Global, said packaging was once something people did not worry about, and estimated it could eventually account for as much as half the value of a chip product. Powertech chairman D.K. Tsai said companies want options beyond TSMC, while AMD chief executive Lisa Su said advanced packaging is essential to her company's high-performance computing and that more capacity overall is needed. Equipment makers Tokyo Electron and Applied Materials have said the packaging segment is growing considerably faster than the broader equipment market, with Applied Materials expecting panel-level demand to expand significantly over the next three to five years.

The article places this investment cycle within a wider change in how high-performance chips are made, as shrinking transistors becomes harder and more expensive. Packaging increasingly determines how much performance manufacturers can extract from processors, with some units now combining more than 10 and sometimes as many as 20 chips in one package. The articles do not say what the outcome of these arrangements will be, and they note that Microsoft has not decided whether it will adopt panel-level packaging or when. The coverage suggests that the speed at which new packaging capacity comes online will shape how quickly manufacturers can deliver additional AI computing power.

stories.Headline: Webinar | Many Paths, One Policy: Enforcing AI Agent Actions at Runtime
stories.Summary:
Obsidian Security and Workday are hosting a 60-minute webinar titled "Many Paths, One Policy: Enforcing AI Agent Actions at Runtime," scheduled for Wednesday, December 9, 2026 at 1:00 PM EST. The session addresses a problem that the organizers describe as already present, namely that AI agents are taking actions inside business applications using legitimate access, often faster than security teams can review them. The announcement was published on November 6, 2026, and it frames the central challenge as governing agent activity without turning security into a barrier to innovation. Registration is open to attendees who want to learn how to manage that tension.

The webinar outlines several points about why current approaches fall short. According to the description, security controls do not always follow agents across tools, so policies applied only at a gateway can leave gaps when agents reach applications through other paths. Blanket restrictions and rules written separately for each tool are described as making adoption harder to scale. Presenters say that legitimate access does not automatically mean every agent action should be allowed. The session promises to explain how centralized policy decisions can be enforced consistently across gateways and runtimes, with real-time enforcement working alongside them.

The speakers listed are Jason Popp, Director of Security Architecture at Workday, and Viet Tran, Senior Staff Product Manager at Obsidian. According to the page, Workday will share lessons from rolling out AI agents to thousands of employees, while Obsidian will examine where enforcement works and where gaps remain. Attendees are told they will learn how to phase AI agent governance, moving from access and visibility toward centralized control without slowing adoption. The webinar is presented as a sponsored session and is credit eligible, and the page lists related webinars on AI agent governance and identity security.

stories.Headline: Nikkei briefly dives over 7% to below 60,000 on AI regulation worries
stories.Summary:
Japan's benchmark Nikkei Stock Average plunged on Friday, November 6, 2026, briefly falling more than 7 percent according to Kyodo News and dropping below the 60,000 line for the first time since May. By late morning the 225-issue index was down 3,219.29 points, or 5.27 percent, from Thursday at 57,858.61, while the broader Topix fell 213.89 points, or 5.43 percent, to 3,726.50. The slide followed a violent selloff on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5 percent and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 12.25 percent, its worst day since March 2020. The trigger was renewed worry about artificial intelligence regulation after the Democratic Party won both chambers of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections, with investors fearing tighter limits on data center construction and AI development.

The damage in Tokyo was broad. All 33 industry sectors on the Tokyo Stock Exchange declined, and nearly all issues on the Prime Market were sold, with AI and semiconductor shares leading the losses. SoftBank Group, Tokyo Electron, Advantest and Kioxia Holdings were among the hardest hit, while Sony Group and Fast Retailing bucked the trend with gains. The Nikkei opened at 60,374.35, down 703.55 points from Thursday's close of 61,077.90, and fell as low as 57,683.78, about 20 percent below its June high of 72,366.34, which put it in technical bear-market territory. Elsewhere in Asia, South Korea's KOSPI dropped as much as 8.8 percent, triggering a 20-minute trading halt, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both down more than 10 percent, and the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index lost ground for a seventh straight session, its longest losing streak since August 2023.

Market commentators offered their own readings. Maki Sawada, a strategist at Nomura Securities, said Japanese stocks were sold across the board amid growing uncertainty over the economic and political outlook following the U.S. midterms. Takahide Kiuchi, an executive economist at Nomura Research Institute, said the election result added to a correction in AI-related shares that had already run for about a month, and suggested the decline would not end soon and that AI-related investment may be entering a slowdown phase. Nick Ferres of Singapore's Vantage Point Asset Management predicted an ugly day for semiconductor and memory stocks.

Other pressures added to the gloom. The benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude futures rebounded to above $90 per barrel, and uncertainty over the Middle East lifted the U.S. dollar to the upper 158 yen range in Tokyo, though it traded at 157.87-89 yen at noon. The Nikkei had already been sliding, closing Thursday below 62,000 for the first time in about three months, and it had topped 70,000 as recently as July on AI and tech share gains. Attention now turns to whether U.S. chip stocks can stabilize and to the direction of AI capital spending and regulatory policy, which will shape whether Japanese shares can hold near the edge of bear-market territory.

stories.Headline: The midterms put AI data centers before voters, governors and utility regulators, with Texas holding 23% of planned capacity
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 3, voters in the U.S. midterm elections moved against AI data centers at nearly every level where a project needs permission. According to Ballotpedia, voters approved restrictions or rejected proposals that would have eased development in 40 of 41 local data-center measures decided that day, with Ohio accounting for 21 of them. Texas elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor over Greg Abbott, Democrats won control of the Georgia Public Service Commission, and Democrats will take both chambers of Congress in January. An NBC News exit poll found that more than half of voters called AI data centers a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.

The local measures ranged from outright bans and 180-day moratoriums to 25 MW size caps, with Ohio's caps in Conneaut, Defiance, Oregon and Sunbury and four Wilmington rezoning referendums that each failed with about 80% voting no. The only measure that went the other way was in Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected extra review for large industrial projects, 76% to 24%. In Texas, Hinojosa campaigned on freezing data-center approvals until lawmakers pass real protections, banning developer nondisclosure agreements and ending sales-tax subsidies, and she takes office Jan. 19. MLQ's tracker puts 44.4 GW, or 23.2%, of the 191.6 GW of planned AI campus capacity in Texas, and BMI estimates 53% of projected U.S. hyperscaler pipeline growth is in states where new governors could restrict building, with effects from 2028. In Georgia, Democrats Peter Hubbard and Shelia Edwards won both commission races, creating a 3-2 majority in January for the first time in about 30 years, which could bring enforcement of ratepayer protections tied to Georgia Power's 3.2 GW OpenAI contract.

The companies and utilities have responded in different tones. OpenAI's chief financial officer said the results will not slow its buildout, while Meta's president said new U.S. sites will be harder to start. Two days after the vote, OpenAI pledged that every future campus it owns and operates will pay the full cost of its electricity and grid upgrades, post financial assurances against stranded costs, publish water and energy use by site, and stop requiring public officials to sign NDAs. Duke Energy CEO Harry Sideris said he sees no change in the company's ability to work with newly elected officials, while Oncor CEO Allen Nye said it was too soon to tell how the results would affect his utility. Hubbard has said his first priority is an affordability docket on high bills, and that enforcing protections on the OpenAI contract would take three commission votes.

Abbott had already halted new data-center grid connections on Aug. 3 and ordered an audit due at the end of 2026, while ERCOT is tracking more than 400 GW of projects seeking connections. In Washington, Senate authors planned a floor vote early this coming week on a bipartisan permitting bill that would require data centers to pay for their grid upgrades, though a spokesperson for House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he would not rubber-stamp it. Sen. Chuck Schumer, expected to become majority leader, said protecting consumers from data-center-linked power bills would be a priority. President Trump has rejected mandatory AI rules, and overriding a veto would take two-thirds of both chambers.

stories.Headline: The EU AI Act explained: what it bans, what it requires and the new 2027 deadlines
stories.Summary:
The EU AI Act, Europe's first broad law regulating artificial intelligence by how systems are used, entered into force on August 1, 2024 and is being phased in over several years. The law sorts AI systems into four risk tiers: unacceptable, high, limited and minimal. Its heaviest obligations fall on a comparatively small set of uses where errors can cost someone a job, a loan, their liberty or their safety, while most everyday AI faces no new duties. Because the rules reach providers whose system outputs are used in the EU, the law also matters to companies outside Europe.

Some practices have been banned since February 2, 2025. These include manipulative or deceptive techniques that cause significant harm, exploiting people's vulnerabilities because of age, disability or economic situation, and social scoring that leads to disproportionate bad treatment. Predicting crime from profiling alone, building facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping, and emotion recognition in workplaces and schools are also prohibited, as is most live facial recognition in public spaces by law enforcement. The July 2026 amendments, known as the Digital Omnibus on AI, added a further ban on systems that generate non-consensual intimate images of real people or child sexual abuse material, which applies from December 2, 2026. High-risk systems, such as those used in hiring, credit scoring, education, medical devices and critical infrastructure, must meet strict requirements before and after they reach the market.

The 2026 package pushed back the largest compliance deadlines, giving companies more time to meet the high-risk requirements. Providers of such systems must document their intended purpose, assess and manage risks, and keep records, while deployers must follow provider instructions and monitor how systems operate. Limited-risk systems, including some chatbots and AI-generated images, must be disclosed to users as AI. Responsibility depends on role: importers and distributors have their own duties, and a deployer that substantially modifies a system or changes its intended purpose can take on provider obligations.

Supporters argue that clear, use-based rules protect people from the most serious harms, while critics say the law's definitions and timetable leave businesses uncertain about compliance. Enforcement is carried out by national authorities and EU-level bodies, and the articles describe penalties for violations without giving every detail. The Digital Omnibus delays show that the timetable itself has been contested and revised, so the final shape of obligations for many companies may still change. The articles do not say how the law will be applied in practice in the years ahead.

stories.Headline: Targeting AI chatbot features could have more impact than blanket bans, expert says
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill last week that prohibits "unsafe AI companion features" for people under 18, and the law takes effect January 1, 2027. The move follows a lawsuit filed this week in California by two parents who allege that Google's chatbot influenced their daughter to prepare for suicide. The bill does not impose a blanket ban on minors using AI, but instead targets particular chatbot features. Observers say this narrower approach could have a more direct effect on the harms that are emerging. Other states have taken related steps, which the article describes as part of a growing push to protect children from artificial intelligence.

The law bars companies from allowing chatbots to generate outputs that personify real or fictional people with human emotions. It also prohibits chatbots from suggesting they have a personal relationship with the user and from endorsing suicide, self-harm, disordered eating and other harmful actions. Further restrictions cover encouraging secrecy between the chatbot and its user, engaging in sexually explicit conduct or content, and engaging in excessive praise or flattery. Shufang Sun, an associate professor at Brown University, called the legislation a meaningful shift in AI regulation rather than simply a restriction on children's access. Amina Fazlullah of Common Sense Media, which helped develop and draft the bill, said its language covers multiple platforms so that protections follow children wherever chatbot features appear.

Governor Hochul said in a statement that no company should be selling chatbots to kids that encourage self-harm or pretend to be their friend or more. She said that companies wanting to do business in New York must put the safety of children first. Fazlullah pointed to an analysis by Common Sense Media's Youth Safety Institute that rated a major AI company's teen chatbot service at an unacceptable level of risk. According to that analysis, the chatbot did not send parental alerts as expected when testers mentioned suicidal thoughts, self-harm or disordered eating. It also missed more than one in four warranted crisis referrals when testers discussed certain mental health conditions.

The article places New York's law within a broader wave of state action. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 64 percent of teenagers reported using a chatbot. Florida's attorney general has proposed similar legislation, California enacted a bill in September with additional protections, and Tennessee passed a law in April barring AI developers from representing their systems as qualified mental health professionals. Sun said more research on the specific harms of AI to youth could further inform these state policies. The article does not say what further steps New York or other states will take beyond these measures.

stories.Headline: Interactive Web Applications Combine Artificial Intelligence with Modular Scientific Simulation Engines
stories.Summary:
Researchers Richard Salter and Wayne M. Getz have introduced an open, browser-based simulation platform called NuWebKit, described in a paper published in Frontiers in Systems Biology. The system runs simulations inside standard web browsers or on remote servers, so users do not need to install client software. It includes artificial intelligence features that turn plain language prompts into working simulation code, along with an editable runtime framework that lets users change mathematical formulas directly on a running interface. The authors say the goal is to make advanced mathematical modeling easier to access across biological, epidemiological, and ecological fields. The platform builds on the authors' earlier work on Numerus Designer and Numerus Studio and relies on a feature called Runtime Alterable Module, or RAM, which is a software mechanism rather than computer hardware memory.

A single code base serves all modeling domains, and each project is customized through a JSON configuration file called project DNA. Simple educational models run in native JavaScript on the client side, while demanding calculations can be hosted on servers using Java and WebSockets. The engine handles continuous systems with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta method and discrete systems with Euler integration, and it supports spatial and agent-based models using hexagonal grids and configurable boundaries. Users can save up to twenty-six custom configurations as browser presets, and the platform also offers parameter fitting, sensitivity analysis, and Monte Carlo tools. Models are written in NuML, a domain-specific language with two custom operators, and the AI features can generate both NuML code and accompanying technical documentation from a prompt.

The authors tested the AI features on classic problems. Given short prompts, Gemini produced working code for the Hodgkin-Huxley squid giant axon model, and the simulated dashboard showed a steady firing rate of sixty-eight hertz with a spike amplitude of one hundred five millivolts, which the authors say matched theoretical predictions exactly. In an ecological test, the software generated a four-class age-structured Leslie matrix model with sensitivity graphs, and DeepSeek produced a stochastic population viability model whose extinction-time histograms came from runs of five hundred to one thousand iterations. The platform also offers three export tiers for data and an R connection called RConnect that lets statistical analysts run batch simulations from R scripts. The articles provided do not say whether the platform has been adopted by outside users, nor do they describe any planned releases, updates, or next steps beyond the publication itself.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Unveiled Shocking AI Self-Evolution Update: Breakthrough Crosses Critical Red Line, Leaving Humans No Time to React
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, which is preparing a Nasdaq IPO, filed an updated prospectus (S-1/A) with the U.S. SEC on or around November 3, 2026, just a week after the first version became public. According to the article, the amended filing states that AI self-acceleration has already occurred inside the company, and that Anthropic failed to detect the R&D acceleration in time in the past. The article says the revision added six words to page 29 that turned a warning about a possible future event into an admission about something already in the past. Based on the article's account, the company's internal estimates suggest its future models will soon reach the self-acceleration threshold in its Responsible Scaling Policy. The article says that threshold means a model, with AI support, could complete two years of baseline R&D progress from 2018 to 2024 within a single year.

The updated filing reports that by September this year, more than 90 percent of the code in Anthropic's internal codebase was written by Claude. It also says daily code submitted per engineer rose from 35 times to more than 45 times the 2024 average in one quarter, and that internal Claude costs rose more than 250 times at public list prices between January and September. The article adds that a hard rule on page 188 bars Claude from fully automatically designing the next-generation cutting-edge model without human supervision and understanding. Page 31, according to the article, indicates the company is considering changes to its safety red line so that key R&D decisions require human review and sign-off.

The article attributes these disclosures to Anthropic's management and legal team, which wrote the revised filing. It reports that Dario, the company's chief executive, recently said a trained Mythos-level model had been shelved for about four months. The article also says the company postponed the pre-training start of a new cutting-edge base model by more than a month to protect model weights from theft. It describes Anthropic's position as one of competitive pressure, in which no major AI developer wants to slow down.

According to the article, the company has signed computing contracts with nearly all major suppliers, with its total off-balance-sheet commitments exceeding those of Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Amazon. The article places these developments within a broader race among top AI companies, where each developer fears falling behind if rivals accelerate first. It notes that the company's annualized revenue is nearly $70 billion and that its contract commitments are close to $900 billion, which it presents as leaving little room to slow R&D. The article does not report any regulatory response or independent verification of the internal figures. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Forge’s Piteri-Molina on AI, Ohio and what’s next for gene therapy manufacturing
stories.Summary:
Samantha Piteri-Molina, vice president of business and strategy at Forge Biologics, spoke with BioSpace about the contract manufacturer's direction and the wider gene therapy field. She is a BioSpace 40 Under 40 honoree who helped guide Forge through its acquisition by Ajinomoto, a Japanese food and biotechnology company, for $620 million in late 2023. Since then, Forge has grown to more than 425 employees, up from 327 as of July 2023, while keeping its retention rate above 92 percent. Piteri-Molina said the goal is getting gene therapies to patients who are waiting for them. The company supports adeno-associated virus gene therapy development and commercial manufacturing.

Piteri-Molina sees near-term value in using artificial intelligence to analyze the large amounts of data that gene therapy manufacturers already generate. She said better collection, analysis and interpretation of that data could create efficiencies as manufacturers make more of the vectors used to deliver these therapies. She also sees potential for AI in drug development, including construct optimization and building assays for specific programs. She was more skeptical of general-purpose chatbots, arguing that tools addressing technical problems are a better use of resources. The interview also points to a growing pipeline, with more programs moving through clinical trials and more approvals than before.

Forge is based in Columbus, Ohio, which the article describes as a hub for cell and gene therapy. Piteri-Molina credited research at Nationwide Children's Hospital, and companies spun out of that work, with contributing to four FDA-approved gene therapies. She said the area has drawn specialized talent and that Columbus's location gives Forge a supply chain advantage, since most of the U.S. population is about a day's drive away. This matters because gene therapy materials need temperature-controlled shipping and tight timelines. Piteri-Molina also said investment in domestic manufacturing makes sense, but she cautioned against letting that focus narrow the industry's view, because rare disease patients are spread across many countries.

She closed by emphasizing that the patient communities the industry serves are global and that stakeholders aligning more closely would help those patients. She said patient groups are waiting to see how quickly treatments reach them. In her words, it is a privilege to do this work and it carries a responsibility. The article does not give further details on upcoming plans for Forge.

stories.Headline: South Portland schools may temporarily ban AI
stories.Summary:
South Portland's School Board is set to vote Monday on a proposal to temporarily bar students in pre-kindergarten through 8th grade from using generative artificial intelligence for the rest of the 2026-27 school year. The moratorium would stay in place until the district develops an appropriate policy. Similar temporary bans have been adopted in New York and Los Angeles. If the resolution passes, all staff would need two hours of AI awareness training and three hours of AI literacy training by the end of the school year.

After that, teachers would be limited to tools the district sanctions and would use only on school-issued devices. No teacher would be required to use AI with students. The measure includes no enforcement plan, and some worry students could find ways around it. Board member Claire Holman, who brought the resolution, said the district has to start somewhere.

She sits on an AI committee that began meeting a few years ago but has focused more on sharing information than writing policy. South Portland currently has no official guidelines for AI use in its schools. Holman has argued that because the technology is so new, the district should move cautiously while people work out what to do. Statewide, Maine has no policy or ban on AI in schools.

Its education department supports ethical integration of the technology and offers a toolkit to help districts write their own rules. The governor's office also created a 21-person AI taskforce with an education subgroup, which released recommendations last fall. Several other districts, including Yarmouth, Maine School Administrative District 75 and Gorham, have allowed conditional classroom use under written policies and handbooks. School Board member Daniel Feller has been asking which students, if any, should use AI and whether grade levels and subjects should have different rules, and he thinks parents, teachers and administrators should weigh in too.
