stories.Headline: Opinion | US and China must join hands to measure rising AI tide
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is advancing so quickly that Washington and Beijing may not have a shared sense of how fast its capabilities are growing, according to an opinion piece by Marshall Li and Zhengfei Zhang published by the South China Morning Post on November 7, 2026. The authors argue that the next US-China talks on AI should start by asking whether both governments really understand this pace. They say the two sides need a common method for measuring progress before deciding how to respond. The piece notes that Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet in Shenzhen soon, with AI likely to stay high on their agenda.

The authors describe their ongoing exchanges on the technology as a positive sign, though they warn that governments may have less time to prepare for its consequences than they assume. They point to changes in creative and professional work, where AI is reshaping fields once thought hard to disrupt. In China, according to the article, more than 90 per cent of new microdramas released in the first eight months of the year were AI-generated, produced without cameras or live actors. A production that once needed as many as 100 people can now be finished in one week by a team of two to five. The authors add that AI has eliminated much of the well-paid work that actors once relied on.

The article frames the call for shared measurement as a responsibility of both governments rather than of any single party. It presents Li and Zhang as arguing that Beijing and Washington should work together to track how quickly the technology is progressing. The authors' central request is that the two governments first agree on a basis for judging AI's development and only then decide on policy. The piece does not describe any formal commitment or agreement reached by either government on this point. It instead positions the proposal as a step toward closing the gap between the speed of AI's advance and the speed of official responses.

Because the figures are drawn from people familiar with the matter rather than from an official filing, the final size and price could differ from the range reported. The Financial Times report attributes the plans to unnamed sources rather than to a public statement from the company. Responsibility for the plans therefore rests with Anthropic's leadership and the advisers handling the listing, though the articles do not name them. The sources described the company as continuing with its existing course, which suggests the plans were already in place before this report. The articles do not say what happens if the listing slips past Thanksgiving or whether regulators have signed off on the offering. The pages retrieved also carry only the headline and standard site content, so the broader context of the company's finances and the wider market is not described here. stories.Headline: AI Could Make Filmmaking Costlier Than the 35mm Era, Korean Pioneers Warn at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
stories.Summary:
AI could make feature filmmaking more expensive than the 35mm era, according to two Korean AI production pioneers who spoke at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. Kim Kwang-jib, founder and CEO of Studio Meta-K, warned that token fees on the most expensive commercial tools could top KRW500 million ($366,000) for a 100-minute film. He said AI companies are currently losing money and keeping prices low as a marketing move. If those costs rose roughly tenfold, he argued, they could exceed what Korean, Taiwanese and other Asian features now spend on live action and VFX.

Kim explained that every re-render is paid for again, so the total budget depends on how few rounds of revisions a project requires. He said that if a client sends 10 changes at once, the studio can re-render a single time, but if the same changes arrive one a day over 10 days, the studio must re-render 10 times. Lee Sang-wook, head of the AI Content Lab at MBC C&I, said budgeting is also hard because tools change weekly. His lab's 139-minute feature "Raphael" took about one year and four months to make, and it opens in Korean cinemas on Nov. 25.

Both speakers described the financial trade-offs of using AI in production. Kim said a Pizza Hut commercial that took about eight months and roughly KRW2 billion ($1.4 million) could be made in-house in about two weeks for around KRW30 million ($22,000). He said he does not think audiences will yet pay for fully AI films, so he favors a hybrid model in which AI generates large crowd scenes while leads are shot live. Lee said the lab's earlier AI shorts drew a cold market response, so it chose a cinema release because theatrical releases can move to streaming later.

The speakers also discussed jobs and the tools themselves. Kim said crews of hundreds on a single scene will become rarer, and that workers who learn AI will replace those who do not. Lee compared the shift to the arrival of sound and predicted new roles such as previsualization artists and continuity supervisors. The two companies also differ on open-source models, with Studio Meta-K using them for simpler shots and MBC C&I avoiding them because it cannot verify training data transparency. The session was moderated by Archin Yen, director and VFX supervisor at WWWIND Studio.

stories.Headline: 3 deliberate moves for businesses to maintain trust in AI decisions
stories.Summary:
Gartner's 2026 CEO and Senior Business Executive Survey found that 76% of leaders expect AI to be the technology most likely to disrupt their industry within three years. The same survey found that 59% of AI pilots never reach production, mostly because of problems inside organizations rather than the technology itself. Incorta, a company that provides a governed data and AI platform, has published guidance on how businesses can keep trust in their AI systems. Its advice centers on three deliberate steps that address why so many pilots stall and why AI outputs can be unreliable. The article appeared on November 6, 2026, and was produced by Incorta and distributed by Stacker.

Gartner notes that AI only pays off when the organization around it changes as well, which means redesigning processes, clarifying who makes which decisions, and aligning incentives. Without those changes, AI simply speeds up and amplifies whatever inputs already exist, whether they are good or bad. The article also says that AI can only give trusted answers when a business can say who has access to its data, how fresh that data is, where it came from, and what agents may do with it. Gartner predicts that through 2026, organizations will drop 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. A separate IBM study from 2025 reportedly found that only 16% of AI programs have scaled across companies.

Incorta's first recommendation is to centralize AI models, tooling, and infrastructure so that spending is controlled and visible, letting a chief financial officer see the full cost in one place. Its second is to govern data so that teams can build what they need without creating security risks. The article cites IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report, which found that one in five organizations had a breach tied to shadow AI, adding an average of $670,000 to breach costs. Of organizations that suffered an AI-related breach, 97% lacked AI access controls. Incorta's third recommendation is to build systems flexible enough to swap AI models, using adaptable interfaces and portable data so that businesses do not have to rebuild when better models arrive.

The article argues that once these foundations are in place, a business can rely on its AI responses and draw on a competitive edge that others cannot easily copy. Because competitors can access the same public models, the company's own governed data becomes the differentiator, including years of customer conversations, support tickets, contracts, and product and financial records. Incorta says that clear data governance, visible spending, and defined lines of ownership together let businesses trust the AI outcomes they generate. The piece is presented as sponsored content and was reviewed and distributed by Stacker.

stories.Headline: Scaling Up Metasurfaces: Accuracy, Computational Cost, and Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Hanyang University and Korea University Sejong Campus published a review article examining how to design large metasurfaces without excessive computing costs. The paper, titled "Scaling Metasurface Design: From Reusable Unit Cells to Full-Metasurface Inverse Design," was made available online on October 25, 2026, and appears in Volume 5, Issue 10 of the journal Opto-Electronic Science. Metasurfaces are thin optical layers of subwavelength structures that control the phase, amplitude, and polarization of light. The authors, Prof. Haejun Chung and Prof. Sunae So, reviewed strategies for scaling these devices to large apertures. The review was based on the research teams' analysis of existing methods rather than a new experiment.

The review organizes design approaches by how much of the device is treated jointly during calculation. Unit-cell methods reuse a library of meta-atom responses computed under periodic boundary conditions, which avoids repeated full-wave optimization of the whole device. Supercell methods treat several interacting elements as one composite unit, while full-metasurface inverse design treats the entire aperture as a coupled system. The authors note that the full-aperture approach improves physical accuracy but demands far more computing resources. Neural-network methods are examined across all these scales as surrogates, candidate generators, and learned components within solvers.

The authors cite a hardware-aware FDTD analysis that estimates a one-centimeter square aperture would require approximately 3.1 petabytes of resident memory under the stated assumptions. They also report that, in an ideal axisymmetric metalens, the reuse ratio of reduced radial phase patterns falls from 71.4% to 3.0% as segment width grows from one to six wavelengths. The paper does not claim these figures describe electromagnetic equivalence, optical performance, or computational savings. The authors stress that the choice of design method depends on required accuracy, interaction range, reuse potential, and available computing resources. They also recommend full-wave verification of final structures and assessment of experimental results under the relevant fabrication and operating conditions.

The article identifies several directions for further work, including coupling-aware local models, adaptive overlapping domains, and distributed full-wave solvers with lower memory requirements. It also suggests that neural operators could assist repeated field calculations, provided their predictions are validated against reference simulations. The authors call for consistent reporting of simulation dimensionality, numerical accuracy, memory, runtime, fabrication constraints, and experimental performance so that methods can be compared under defined conditions. The funding statement lists support from the National Research Foundation of Korea, the Ministry of Education, and other Korean agencies, and the authors declare no competing financial interests.

stories.Headline: Dollar climbs on safe haven demand as AI rout saps Asian markets - CNA
stories.Summary:
The US dollar index climbed 0.77 per cent to 102.26 on Friday, November 6, 2026, as a stronger-than-expected US jobs report pushed it toward its biggest daily gain in nearly five months. The Labor Department said nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000 in October, well above the 65,000 that economists polled by Reuters had expected, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1 per cent. The euro fell 0.67 per cent to $1.11437, and the Japanese yen weakened 0.47 per cent to 158.430 against the greenback. The move came as safe-haven demand lifted the dollar earlier in the day, after a selloff in AI-linked stocks spread across global markets.

The jobs data strengthened expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its December meeting. Market odds of a rise of at least 25 basis points rebounded toward 80 per cent after the report, according to the CME FedWatch Tool, up from about 67 per cent on Thursday. Treasury yields also rose, with the 10-year yield up 1.6 basis points to 4.85 per cent and the 2-year yield up 4.1 basis points to 4.52 per cent. Sterling dropped 0.71 per cent to $1.3355, on pace for its biggest daily fall since September 23, after the Bank of England raised rates for the first time in more than three years.

Fed officials speaking on Friday backed the case for tightening. New York Fed President John Williams said US growth has held up remarkably well through successive shocks, but that inflation is too high and must return to 2 per cent. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said inflation remains a top concern in his talks with businesses, and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said the central bank will likely still need to raise rates further despite what she called a "painful" tech stock selloff. Earlier in the week, US equities had slumped, with the S&P 500 losing about $3 trillion in market value and the Nasdaq suffering its worst one-day percentage drop in 19 months, amid fears that tougher AI regulation after the US midterm elections would slow economic growth.

Those regulatory fears centre on Democrats, who plan to introduce a wave of new legislation on artificial intelligence systems and data-center development when they take control of Congress in January, according to lawmakers, congressional aides and advocates. In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi proposed using proceeds from the Bank of Japan's sales of exchange-traded funds to finance her flagship investment projects, as the AI-driven rout threatened tax revenue. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said underlying inflation should stay near the 2 per cent target but acknowledged "some upside risks." The articles do not say when the Fed's December decision will be announced.

stories.Headline: ‘Pokemon’ Anime Studio OLM Trains AI Coloring Tool on Just Three Frames in Japan Government-Backed Project
stories.Summary:
OLM, the Japanese animation group behind the Pokemon anime, has built an AI coloring tool that learns a show's look from just three hand-painted frames, according to OLM Digital board director Yotsukura Tatsuo. He presented the tool at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest in Taipei. The tool came out of ANIMINS, a 15-month research project Yotsukura led under GENIAC, a generative AI program overseen by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, which wrapped up in February. Because such systems usually need large training sets, OLM instead has an artist color three frames, after which the system learns the show's line shapes and palette in about 90 seconds and colors each remaining frame in roughly 15 seconds.

Yotsukura said the tool is not generative AI in the strict sense, and that training only on a production's own frames avoids using other people's work. It can adapt when a new creature such as a dragon appears, and OLM stresses that it fits into existing anime workflows. At proof-of-concept stage, he estimated it has cut painting workload by around 30%, although the people who check each colored frame have somewhat more to do. Toon Boom Animation, the Canadian maker of Harmony and Storyboard Pro, is working on the same problem, with its coloring tool in beta inside its Ember AI suite and in-betweening expected to follow within a couple of weeks. One Manila studio that tested the coloring tool reportedly cut the painting time on a 90-second scene from 15 hours to two or three.

OLM employs around 600 staff across Japan, Malaysia, Thailand and the U.S., and produces the Pokemon anime, Beyblade, Hanakappa and The Apothecary Diaries. Yotsukura, who also serves as CTO for the group's Malaysian and Thai arms, said the group is also testing AI for in-betweening and for anime-specific agents that could help with directing and license management. Toon Boom's product marketing director, Harry Ravelomanantsoa, said the creative work stays with the artist while mechanical tasks go to AI. Yotsukura agreed with that split and said AI can only do what it has learned. Charles Beirnaert, chief creative officer of Blue Spirit, said his studio uses no AI on its Netflix projects, which the streamer's guidelines restrict, and that AI is not meant to replace animators.

Yotsukura compared the arrival of AI to that of 3DCG, which took around 20 years to gain acceptance in anime, but said AI will move faster because its quality is already high. He said he thinks "not using AI" is probably no longer an option. Beirnaert's team used AI to recreate a pilot that took a team of about 20 roughly three months, with one person finishing the work within days. The article presents these accounts as the views of the speakers at the event, and it does not report any outcome beyond what they described.

stories.Headline: Kansas Board of Education set to vote on artificial intelligence policy, discuss elementary recess policies
stories.Summary:
The Kansas State Board of Education is preparing to vote on a new policy covering artificial intelligence and student technology use, according to a report from KSNT. The board will meet Monday and Tuesday, November 9 and 10, 2026, in its November session. The vote concerns instructional technology policy for school districts and nonpublic accredited schools across the state. The board will also take up guidance on elementary recess during that same meeting.

The draft policy, which Kansas Education Commissioner Jake Steel will present, covers several areas of student technology use. Among the topics listed are the purpose and intended use of technology in elementary and secondary settings, student technology access, digital citizenship and student well-being, and artificial intelligence. It also addresses privacy and security, along with expectations for technology use and the consequences of violations. Board members will receive and discuss the recess guidance, but the recess policy itself is expected to come up for a vote at the December meeting.

The announcement came from the Kansas State Department of Education, which issued a press release about the meeting. Commissioner Steel is responsible for presenting the draft to the board. The report does not include any direct statements from the commissioner or board members about their positions on the proposals. It also notes that the board's decision on the technology policy will follow the discussion scheduled for the coming meeting.

The schedule suggests the state is moving on two fronts at once, with technology rules voted on in November and recess rules expected to follow in December. The articles do not say what the board will do if it fails to approve either measure at these sessions. They also do not indicate how the policies would take effect in local classrooms once adopted. Readers who want to follow the outcome can watch for the board's decisions after the November meeting and the December recess vote.

stories.Headline: Amazon’s AI Spending is Pressuring Free Cash Flow. Is the Stock Still a Buy?
stories.Summary:
In early November 2026, The Motley Fool published an analysis by Adria Cimino asking whether Amazon's stock remains a buy despite heavy spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure. The piece was carried on Yahoo Finance on November 7, 2026, and on Fool.com the same day. It notes that Amazon Web Services is the world's largest cloud provider and that the company's core retail business and its AI businesses are both pushing revenue to record levels. In the third quarter, AWS reached an annual revenue run rate of $184 billion, with quarterly revenue up 39% to $46 billion, the fastest growth in almost five years.

The article explains that Amazon must make large investments to meet current demand and prepare for future demand. The company forecasts $220 billion in capital spending for the full year, which has put pressure on free cash flow. In the third quarter, Amazon reported negative free cash flow of more than $42 billion over the trailing twelve months, driven by purchases of property and equipment. The company also lifted its capex forecast by $20 billion during the second quarter, while keeping the full-year forecast unchanged in the third quarter. Amazon's chief executive, Andy Jassy, said on the second-quarter earnings call that the free cash flow headwinds would continue until the new data centers are running, and that spending occurs about two years before monetization begins.

The author argues that the spending is necessary if Amazon wants to keep its lead in AI, and points to AWS growth as evidence the investment has paid off. The article describes Amazon's e-commerce moat, including its fulfillment network and Prime subscription, and says AWS now makes up more than 60% of total operating income. It also cites Amazon Bedrock as the company's fastest-growing multi-billion-dollar service and says the stock trades at 23 times forward earnings estimates. Based on these points, the author concludes that Amazon is a stock to buy and hold for the long term. The article is an opinion piece, and the page also carries a note that the author holds a position in Amazon.

stories.Headline: XCMG Highlights International Innovation at "AI + Construction Machinery" Competition
stories.Summary:
The 15th China Innovation and Entrepreneurship Competition, "AI + Construction Machinery" Division, co-organized by XCMG, concluded in Xuzhou on October 30, 2026. The competition drew participants from more than 20 countries and regions, with international companies and universities among the winners. Its projects focused on smarter and more sustainable construction machinery and operations. The event was hosted by the Torch High Technology Industry Development Center of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology along with other government and industry organizations. More than 2,750 teams registered, and the competition received over 1,600 project submissions.

After preliminary and semifinal rounds, 106 projects advanced to the finals, and international teams earned awards in both the Customer Co-Creation and Professional Contest tracks. Austria's VA Erzberg GmbH won first prize in the Customer Co-Creation track for an electric mining truck project. Fortescue Trading Shanghai took second prize in the same track for work optimizing the full lifecycle of zero-emission mining equipment. Urgench State University in Uzbekistan earned third prize for SmartFleet UZ, an AI platform meant to predict equipment failures for UzXCMG machinery. Indonesia's Manado State Polytechnic won third prize for TerraSight AI, a system that automatically monitors earthwork progress and volumes.

Germany's RWTH Aachen University received an Excellence Award for a solution that adapts autonomous mining trucks to multiple operating scenarios. XCMG Group and XCMG Machinery chairman Yang Dongsheng said the competition is meant to turn real industry needs into innovation challenges and bring partners together to solve technical problems in construction machinery. He named embodied intelligence as a key area for development and said XCMG would use its innovation platforms, testing resources and industry funds to bring AI innovations to worksites and serve customers worldwide. At the closing event, agreements were signed covering six projects selected through the Open Challenge track and four commercialization projects. XCMG said it will continue connecting competition teams with funding sources, industry and research partners, talent and suppliers to help bring these innovations to market.

stories.Headline: iQIYI Revives 90-Year-Old Lost Film with NadouPro, Shortlisted for the AI Unit at the Golden Rooster Awards
stories.Summary:
Chinese streaming platform iQIYI has used its NadouPro AI platform to recreate "Visiting Shanghai after Sixty Years," a short film from 1938 that has been lost for nearly 90 years. Because no physical prints, reels or scripts survived, an eight-person team built the film from scratch in just two months at the iQIYI-XMU Joint Laboratory of Film Restoration. The team relied only on production still photos, posters and newspaper clippings as guides. The project has been shortlisted for the "2026 Future Images AI Unit" at the 39th Golden Rooster Awards, one of China's most prestigious film honors.

The film, one of China's earliest science-fiction works, used comedy to imagine life sixty years into the future. Recreating it required solving two difficult problems in generative video: keeping characters looking the same from shot to shot and controlling the camera precisely. NadouPro addressed the first by locking in permanent digital assets for each character's face, proportions and costumes before shooting. The team used the platform's 3D Director Studio to control positioning, composition and movement. The 1938 sequences follow the look of early black-and-white cinema, while the 1998 scenes use a documentary style with natural light and handheld camera work.

Enji YANG, the film's director, said NadouPro helped the team move from random image generation toward shots with clear directorial intent. He said the team still followed traditional methods, including script analysis, character design and storyboarding, before deciding how AI would realize the audiovisual design. Aigong ZHANG, the film's chief planner and director of the joint laboratory, said the project shows how AI can fit into a professional filmmaking workflow. Zidong JIANG, iQIYI's director of AI restoration technology, said the platform let the team move beyond the conventional restoration mindset and reconstruct the film creatively from historical materials.

The project builds on iQIYI's AI restoration work, which began in 2017 and includes its proprietary ZoomAI tools for scratch repair, super-resolution, noise reduction and frame interpolation. Through its joint lab with Xiamen University, the company has already returned several 4K classics to screens. The article presents the reconstruction as an extension of that work into recreating lost films rather than only repairing surviving ones. No further release dates or screening plans for the restored film are given in the article.

stories.Headline: How differences in economics, public policy, and cultural patterns could explain greater pessimism about AI in the West than in Asia and emerging economies (Gillian Tett/Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times columnist Gillian Tett published a piece on November 7, 2026, asking why Americans appear more pessimistic about artificial intelligence than people in parts of Asia and in emerging economies. The article's headline poses the question directly, but the text available to me is only the paywall page, so I cannot see its full argument. Accompanying coverage on Techmeme that same morning focused on a separate matter, a report that a Chinese executive linked to Megaspeed had been recruited by China's top spy agency. Taken together, these items show a moment when AI is drawing close attention from business, government, and the public. The Tett piece itself is framed as an explanation of a gap in attitudes rather than a single event.

The available sources do not spell out the economic, policy, or cultural factors that Tett identifies as explanations for the difference in attitudes. They also do not give any figures on public opinion in the West or in Asia that would show the size of the gap. What the sources do contain is reporting on the money flowing into the sector, including a roughly $11 billion funding round for OpenAI at a $1.25 trillion valuation and expectations that Anthropic would seek $80 billion to $100 billion in a public listing before Thanksgiving. Reports also said that some investors viewed the lower valuation of that listing as a possibility. These figures show the scale of commercial expectations, though they do not establish how ordinary people feel about the technology.

Responsibility for the espionage allegations rests with U.S. intelligence officials, who reportedly concluded that Alice Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. The New York Times and the Financial Times both reported that the officials believed she had sought to influence Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, and that Congressional committee leaders asked him for a closed-door briefing about his ties to her. Huang has not been quoted in these reports as responding to the claims. Commentators quoted on social media disputed how much weight to place on the reports, and the sources do not settle those disagreements. Whether the briefing takes place, and what follows from it, is not something the articles can predict.

stories.Headline: Trump official who wants data centers on public lands has tens of millions invested in AI industry
stories.Summary:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the Trump administration's push for AI infrastructure, has substantial personal investments in the AI industry, according to a November 2026 investigation by ProPublica that was republished by the North Dakota Monitor. The reporting found that Burgum's 2026 financial disclosure shows much of his wealth sits in Arthur Ventures, an investment firm he co-founded, and that between $18.1 million and $64.4 million of those holdings are in AI companies, based on an analysis by the public lands group Save Our Parks. The articles say that in the year before he joined the administration, while he was North Dakota's governor, he realized between $2.1 million and $11 million in capital gains from AI-related investments, and in 2025 he sold AI stocks and equity that produced between $2.5 million and $15.1 million. Under his Senate confirmation ethics agreement, he resigned from positions at Arthur but kept his financial interests there.

The administration has also offered federally managed public lands for data centers, which the articles say could be built on as much as 91.3 million acres, an area comparable to Montana, according to a U.S. Geological Survey report released earlier in the year. Public opposition to data centers has grown, and the articles note that local and state processes have slowed projects in ways federal property may not allow. The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing permit applications for about 15 data centers and 17 associated infrastructure projects across six Western states, and the articles say the rent charged for data centers on public land, described by an Interior spokesperson as an annual fair-market-value rent, may be low enough that the public's economic benefit is unclear until projects are permitted. A federal land law from 1976 that predates data centers is being used to permit them, according to the reporting. The Boulder City, Nevada, project was paused by an Interior appeals board and sent back for further review after the BLM approved a change in plans in June without studying its environmental implications.

The Interior Department says Burgum has met his federal ethics and financial disclosure obligations and that claims his decisions are driven by personal investments are false and unsupported. The department added that his work requires engaging industry leaders and international partners. Ethics experts quoted in the articles said his investments appear to be legal under a criminal statute with a high burden of proof, but Cynthia Brown of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington said non-criminal ethics rules bar officials from acting in ways that create the appearance of a conflict, and Richard Painter, a former Bush administration ethics lawyer, said Burgum should stay away from decisions benefiting an industry in which he is heavily invested. Democratic senators wrote to Burgum in October demanding he stop efforts to use public lands for data centers and disclose his role. The articles also report that Steve Pearce, the BLM director, and Michael Boren, a Forest Service overseer, hold AI investments of their own, and that hundreds of Trump appointees have financial ties to major AI-linked companies, though the articles do not say what action, if any, will follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia’s $20bn AI chip pile-up - Asian Tech Roundup
stories.Summary:
Reuters has reported that around 600,000 Nvidia H200 AI chips are stranded in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China. The high-end processors typically sell for $32,000 to $40,000 each, putting the total value near $20 billion. Because Beijing has not approved large-scale imports, the chips remain in the territory, even though Chinese AI companies are eager to buy them. The stockpile would be enough to supply three xAI Colossus-sized hyperscale datacentres.

Grey-market prices have reportedly tripled, with eight-GPU H200 servers offered in mainland China for more than $900,000 in October. At that valuation, the 600,000 chips installed across 75,000 eight-GPU servers would be worth more than $67 billion. The standoff is a test of Beijing's push for domestic firms to depend less on US technology while still matching its AI capability. Small shipments have been approved, but the authorities have not yet allowed large imports of the US-made processors.

The report does not name a single party taking responsibility for the holdup, but it places the decision with the Chinese government, which has been reinforcing a self-sufficiency strategy. The reporting describes the Chinese authorities as refusing entry to the chips while the country's AI companies press for them. Beijing has also urged the US and EU to reconsider tariffs on Chinese goods, linking larger purchases of American farm products to lower trade barriers. The articles do not say when or whether the impasse will be resolved.

stories.Headline: West Virginia sues Snap over children's safety, AI chatbot
stories.Summary:
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey has filed a consumer protection lawsuit against Snap, the maker of Snapchat, according to an MLex report dated November 6, 2026. The suit alleges that Snap deceived West Virginia parents and children about how safe its platform is, even though the company allegedly knew young users were being exposed to sexual exploitation, harmful content and compulsive-use design. It also claims Snap rushed the launch of its "My AI" chatbot to children without adequate safety testing. The state further alleges that Snap misled families about what the chatbot does with children's private conversations and location data.

The lawsuit centers on the claim that Snap's public statements did not match what the company knew about risks to minors. According to the report, the complaint describes harms ranging from sexual exploitation to content that is harmful to young people, along with features that encourage compulsive use. The chatbot allegations focus on timing and disclosure, since the state says the product reached children before adequate safety checks were done. The articles do not say what remedies or penalties the state is seeking, nor do they give a dollar figure. Snap's response is not described in the coverage.

According to the MLex summary, the attorney general brought the case in his official role, and the allegations are framed as a violation of state consumer protection rules. The report describes the claims as the state's allegations and does not present them as findings. It also links to the complaint itself, which is the primary source for the specific claims. The reporting does not include any statement from Snap in reply to the suit.

The articles provide only limited context beyond the complaint itself. They do not say whether other states have taken similar action against Snap or whether the chatbot is subject to any separate regulatory review. The coverage also does not indicate when the court will schedule its next steps or what the company is expected to do next. Any further developments would have to come from later court filings or reporting.

stories.Headline: ‘Shock absorbers’: Korn Ferry says managers are carrying AI change that executives aren’t ready to lead
stories.Summary:
Korn Ferry published its Talent Trends 2027 report on October 22, based on a survey of more than 1,300 talent and senior leaders, from CHROs to CEOs and board members, in more than 75 countries. The findings show that just 6% of those leaders believe their organizations' top executives are fully prepared to lead AI-driven transformation. Two-thirds of respondents, or 66%, expect middle managers to spend more time helping their teams through change than overseeing day-to-day work. The firm also found that 77% of respondents see capability gaps as a bigger challenge than talent shortages, and 78% believe too few people are ready for how work will be done in the future. Together, these results suggest that managers are being asked to absorb a large share of the pressure created by AI adoption.

The added burden is sitting on managers who already have little spare capacity, and many now oversee larger teams after years of cuts to management layers. Cathi Rittelmann, a senior client partner at Korn Ferry, described managers as the shock absorbers of the organization, whose job is to keep teams moving even when they cannot say exactly where things are heading. Susan De La Vega, senior vice president of global tech market and client experience at Korn Ferry, told Fortune that AI transformation requires redesigning the workforce, not just rolling out new technology. She said managers often must defend and communicate AI mandates they had no say in and little context to explain. She also warned that when leadership later changes course, employees end up redoing work, and that poor communication can erode trust and drive away valuable people.

De La Vega placed much of the responsibility for getting this right on senior leaders, arguing that they should learn the tools themselves so they can speak credibly about what AI changes and what it does not. She recommended job-specific training, since a finance analyst and a data scientist have different needs, and time and room for employees to experiment. She also said managers should be briefed on the reasoning behind leadership decisions before those decisions reach their teams. Rather than waiting for a flawless master plan, she urged leaders to share what they know, acknowledge what remains uncertain, and lay out the broader roadmap. Her view is that middle managers need a system behind them to do this work effectively.

The communication gap is not unique to Korn Ferry's research, according to Gallup data cited in the article. As of May, only 25% of U.S. employees said their organizations had communicated a clear plan for integrating AI, even though 47% said their employers had begun using AI tools. A July Gallup analysis found that 43% of employees whose employers had communicated a clear integration plan were engaged at work, compared with 28% of those whose employers had not or who were unaware of one. Employees whose manager actively supported their team's use of AI were engaged at 48%, compared with 30% among those without that support. The article does not describe specific steps companies have announced beyond these recommendations.

stories.Headline: AI meme era hits K-pop — and even tycoons are dancing to 'Neon'
stories.Summary:
A2O Lite, a newly debuted K-pop girl group, saw its hit "Neon" spark a wave of AI-generated parody videos after the song's release in October. Users swapped the faces of the members in the song's opening choreography for those of public figures, including SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won and Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Lee Jae-yong. The parodies took off after listeners noticed that the chorus lyric "Neon and Beyond" sounds like Korean words for "unmarried" and "divorce." Some versions also featured characters from the Netflix drama "The Glory" and even animals. The trend has drawn attention to how easily such content can now be made.

Making one of these clips requires little time, skill or money, according to the reporting. A reporter tested an AI video platform that offered a ready-made template from the music video, and it took less than three minutes to produce a 15-second face-swapped clip. Users only needed to upload photos, with two images needed for each face swap, and the first clip was free for new users. Longer videos or additional clips required paid credits. Experts quoted in the article said this accessibility is the main reason the trend spread so quickly.

The article raises legal concerns because most of the videos were made without the consent of the people whose faces were used. Kim Hern-sik, a popular culture commentator, said copyright questions grow more complicated when users pay AI platforms to create content using K-pop artists' work. Attorney Hwang Jin-seop of Lawfirm Taeryun said that calling something parody does not protect it from legal claims, and that courts weigh the purpose of the expression, its necessity and the harm caused to portrait rights and reputation. The article notes that sexually explicit deepfakes are a far more serious matter under Korean law.

Under a 2024 revision of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Sexual Crimes, creating such videos can bring up to seven years in prison or a fine of up to 50 million won, about $37,300. Viewing or possessing them, even if they are never published, can be punished with up to three years in prison or a fine of up to 30 million won. The agencies for Jennie of Blackpink and Yoona of Girls' Generation have said they will take legal action after deepfake videos of those artists circulated online. The article does not say what outcome those cases will have, and it does not report any new legal action tied to the "Neon" parodies.

Articles.Title: AI meme era hits K-pop — and even tycoons are dancing to 'Neon'

stories.Headline: Texas Data Center Restrictions Threaten Timelines, but Not Necessarily AI Demand
stories.Summary:
Texas data center restrictions are threatening construction timelines, but the article argues they do not necessarily reduce overall AI demand. Published by Investing.com on November 7, 2026, the analysis by Ivana Delevska followed a sharp sell-off in data center and AI hardware stocks after Democrats won both chambers of Congress and the governorships of Texas, Georgia and Ohio. Investors had priced in a risk that a quarter to half of planned data centers would never be built. The writer contends that the more likely outcome is that economics and timelines shift for projects not yet approved, with capacity elsewhere filling the gap.

The article describes the Texas situation in detail. Requests to connect new data centers to ERCOT, the grid operator serving most of Texas, climbed from more than 230 GW in February to over 438 GW by June, nearly 90% of it from data centers. In August, Governor Greg Abbott ordered ERCOT to review large data centers awaiting connection, and in September he told the state environmental regulator, TCEQ, to stop issuing data center permits until that review is completed, expected in mid-December. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who won the governor's race in November, takes office January 19 and has promised a moratorium on new data centers until lawmakers set rules on power, water and local input. The article notes that only about 19.5 GW of Texas's roughly 93 GW pipeline is under construction, and that Galaxy's Helios campus and Oracle's Stargate campus at Shackelford are expected to keep moving.

The article attributes the pushback mainly to local communities concerned about electricity prices, grid strain, air and water, and it presents the Texas moves as efforts to clear an unrealistic connection queue rather than to halt construction. The writer's view is that the Texas risk is one of timing rather than cancellation, and that projects that no longer make sense in Texas will likely move to states such as Virginia, Pennsylvania and Indiana or to countries including Malaysia, where Google committed $15 billion for 2027 to 2028. The analysis also argues that capital, not regulation, sets the buildout's pace, estimating roughly $1.0 to $1.2 trillion of investment for 25 to 30 GW expected in 2027. It adds that a slower buildout could mean higher GPU prices and a longer hardware cycle. The article lists upcoming events to watch, including the Texas grid review in mid-December, CoreWeave's results on November 10 and NVIDIA's on November 17.

stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: University of Nebraska sets new rules for artificial intelligence use across campuses
stories.Summary:
The University of Nebraska system announced new expectations for artificial intelligence use on Thursday, when President Jeff Gold issued a directive covering all campuses. The directive is meant to guide how students, faculty and staff use AI tools across their studies, teaching, research and daily work. Rules for the system's campuses are set to take effect at the same time as the new policy. Under the directive, approved AI tools may be used for university business, and that use is limited to tools that have been approved by the university. The system has also introduced a ChatGPT Edu enterprise platform, which Nebraska says gives students, faculty and staff access to a secure version of the tool that does not use their data to train outside models.

Nebraska signed a memorandum of understanding with OpenAI to provide the platform, with a reported cost of about $800,000 for the system's campuses. Users who have an account on the platform will be able to access it through their university credentials. President Gold is responsible for the directive and said in a statement that the university must use AI in ways that protect privacy, promote academic integrity and support students. He added that the policy would give students and employees clear guidance on how to use the technology responsibly.

A university spokesperson said the system would share further details on training and enforcement in the coming weeks, though the articles do not specify the dates. The move comes as universities across the country work out how to handle generative AI in classrooms and offices, and it follows months of debate among faculty about the technology's role in teaching and assessment. The articles do not say how violations will be handled or whether any campus has already reported problems with the new rules. Nebraska's campuses are expected to begin applying the policy this academic year, and further guidance from the system is expected in the weeks ahead.
