stories.Headline: What AI benchmarks can teach accounting firms
stories.Summary:
A recent Accounting Today opinion piece, written by Yunita Anwar, an assistant professor of accounting at Shenandoah University, reviews two studies of AI performance on accounting work published by Mercor and Digits. The author argues that firms should treat benchmark results as a starting point for their own questions rather than as proof that a system is ready for use. Mercor's study involved 12 licensed CPAs and four month-end tasks, comparing AI-assisted work with unassisted work. The tested agent earned perfect rubric scores across 20 runs, while unassisted accountants averaged about 37 percent. The Digits study, which looked at transaction categorization, found a much smaller gap, with its best one-shot model scoring 79.5 percent against a human baseline of 79.1 percent, a difference inside the paper's stated sampling error.

The article suggests that firms structure a small pilot around three questions: what task is being measured, what information each participant has, and how success is defined. For example, a firm could ask a system to draft an expense-coding schedule from approved invoices and account definitions, requiring a source reference for every entry and a separate list of unresolved items, without posting anything live. The author recommends running one comparison with matched materials and another with the firm's intended access to prior records and follow-up questions, so the two results stay distinct. Success should be defined in advance across separate dimensions, such as category, amount, source reference and appropriate flagging of missing evidence, and the test cases should include deliberate exceptions like unfamiliar vendors and conflicting receipts. The piece also urges firms to record every reviewer change along with its reason, to agree on a stopping rule if an error cannot be explained, and to write down the specific decision the trial supports.

Anwar's position is that strong AI results should be welcomed but examined in context. Her stated aim is for firms to learn which combination of technology, information and professional review produces dependable work before expanding any use. The article is an opinion and practical guidance rather than a report of a new regulatory requirement, and it does not describe any firm adopting these steps. The same Accounting Today page carries unrelated news on IRS payment features, PCAOB registration revocations and other profession updates.

Articles.Title: What AI benchmarks can teach accounting firms - Accounting Today

stories.Headline: This was the week the AI trade cracked. So what's next?
stories.Summary:
A sharp sell-off hit AI and tech stocks this week, wiping out more than $2 trillion in value in a single session before shares bounced back the following day. Investors reacted to a wave of Democratic election wins that raised concerns about the future of AI, a technology that tech companies are spending heavily to develop. NPR's Rafael Nam and John Ruwitch discussed the moves on air. Analysts and reporters have not settled whether the sector is in a bubble that is about to burst.

Nam described the scale of the losses as staggering and said investors had already been uneasy about the AI trade all year. Data centers are central to AI companies, so proposals to create moratoriums or slow their development unsettled traders. Ruwitch said there has been a construction boom in AI data centers, with trillions of dollars committed to more of them. Local residents have raised worries about water and electricity costs and about jobs. In San Jose, California, Ruwitch reported that plans call for as many as 13 new data centers, and a resident there said things were moving too fast.

Data centers were also on the ballot nationwide on Tuesday, and Ruwitch said candidates who spoke against them won races in Texas, Ohio and South Carolina. He also reported that dozens of local measures in 13 states blocked or restricted future data center development. Ruwitch said the election results suggest it will be harder going forward for AI companies to build out their infrastructure. The articles do not name a single party or company as directly responsible for the sell-off, and they do not say what policy changes will follow. The reporting leaves open how far the local measures will spread and whether the pullback will last.

Articles.Title: This was the week the AI trade cracked. So what's next?

stories.Headline: Cashfree Launches ‘Checkout For Agents’ To Enable AI-Led Payments
stories.Summary:
Cashfree Payments, a fintech soonicorn, has launched a tool called Checkout for Agents that lets AI agents process customer payments. The article dated November 6, 2026 reports the launch and says the feature is built on WebMCP, an open-source model context protocol. Merchants already using Cashfree's checkout page can use the service without code changes or technical updates, according to the startup. The company frames it as a fix for a friction point in agentic commerce, where AI agents must decode web pages built for humans.

The article says global purchases initiated by AI agents are projected to reach $1.5 trillion by 2030, yet traditional web interfaces remain built for human navigation. Cashfree says agents now use about 2 million tokens on average to decode a page before executing a transaction. With WebMCP, the checkout tool tells agents the available actions directly, including reading the order total and selecting a payment mode. Cashfree claims this cuts token consumption by over 40 percent and lets personal AI assistants such as Instinct, Meta's Muse and Grok Bot reach the final payment step with fewer errors.

The final transaction authorisation stays with the user. Cashfree co-founder Reeju Datta told Inc42 that dropping off at the payment layer would stop, conversion speed would rise, and success rates for agent payments would be near 100 percent. He expects agents to drive a significant share of traffic to Cashfree's customers, noting that agent traffic has grown around four to five times annually and converts five times better than his SEO traffic. On the risk of agents taking unauthorised actions, Datta said the offering preserves existing authorisation mechanisms and creates no heightened vulnerabilities.

If the final step requires an OTP, the user still has to enter it to approve a payment. Cashfree was founded in 2015 by Datta and Akash Sinha and offers payment gateway, cross-border payment, payout and banking API services. The company says it processes over $80 billion in annual transaction volume for more than one million businesses, including MakeMyTrip, Zomato, CRED and Delhivery. The article notes that rivals are also pursuing agentic commerce, including IPO-bound Razorpay, which is repositioning itself as an AI-powered business operating system with its Agent Studio, Bengaluru-based Nudge, and Swiggy, which lets users interact with its app through external AI agents to order food and book tables.

Articles.Title: Cashfree Launches ‘Checkout For Agents’ To Enable AI-Led Payments - Inc42

stories.Headline: Arkansas transportation officials explore AI’s potential for infrastructure, roadway safety
stories.Summary:
Arkansas transportation officials gathered in Rogers for the final day of the Arkansas Transportation Summit, hosted by the Arkansas Department of Transportation, to discuss how artificial intelligence could shape engineering, infrastructure and roadway safety. The three-day event brought together roughly 600 transportation officials and professionals to talk about emerging technology, infrastructure needs and future planning. Industry leaders said the next challenge is moving AI from experiments into everyday operations. The discussions took place Friday, November 6, 2026, according to the reporting. Chris Bosco, AI strategic initiative leader for the engineering firm Freese and Nichols, said the industry has spent the past two years learning how AI can support existing work.

He demonstrated an AI agent that analyzed engineering plans for an older Arkansas bridge and used them to build a 3D model of the structure. His company has also built a quality-control tool that checks project plans against design guidelines and flags inconsistencies. Bosco said the goal is continuous quality checks as engineers work, rather than waiting for a review milestone. He also pointed to uses in cost estimating, construction management and training future engineers through simulations.

Shashank Shekhar, a managing director and partner with Boston Consulting Group, said AI is meant to help professionals process more information and make better-informed decisions, not replace human judgment. He said the difference between agencies that have scaled AI and those that have not comes down to discipline in moving from pilot projects to proven value across the organization. University of Arkansas engineering professor Ngan Le described research on computer vision and video analytics that can interpret complex scenes involving people, vehicles and changing conditions. She noted that transportation agencies already run extensive camera networks that could feed such systems.

Eric Simpson, IT infrastructure services manager at the department, said the agency must decide how to use decades of data responsibly, and he said AI could help break down silos between divisions. Simpson also described using AI to anticipate roadway safety problems and target maintenance resources, but he stressed that policies, modernized data systems, employee preparation and accountability must come first. The department's AI guidelines list five principles: human oversight, data protection, transparency, accountability and security. Gayle Combs, a cybersecurity and infrastructure security adviser, warned that transportation systems are tied to energy, water and communications, so a disruption in one area can spread to others.

She urged organizations to identify critical assets and build relationships with partners, and she cautioned that AI could make cyberattacks more sophisticated. Panelists also raised the risk of employees relying on AI answers without checking them. Simpson summed up the tension by saying speed without governance is a serious risk. The next summit is scheduled for Sept. 21-23 at the Statehouse Convention Center in Little Rock.

Articles.Title: Arkansas transportation officials explore AI’s potential for infrastructure, roadway safety

stories.Headline: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails
stories.Summary:
Wired's Steven Levy, writing in his Backchannel newsletter on November 6, 2026, reports on a fast-growing market in which AI developers buy companies' internal work records, including documents, emails, Slack messages, tickets and call transcripts, to train their models. Levy says he received cold pitches offering media companies such as Wired between $350,000 and $1.8 million for a one-time copy of their old work records, with one pitch raising the figure to as much as $2 million. A freelance writer was offered $1,000 for a single story by a company called Handshake, which said it licenses professional documents across many fields so labs can test how models handle real knowledge work. Anthropic told Wired it acknowledges a big market for such data but does not buy workflow from live companies like Wired, and OpenAI did not respond before publication.

The market is led by a few young firms, including Handshake, Micro1 and Mercor, which Levy says are buying databases "as if it were a modern gold rush." Mercor, founded in 2023, has cofounders who became billionaires at 22 last year, and its CEO, Brendan Foody, told Levy that AI labs were frustrated by the quality of simulated data and need real messy business records. Foody said his company strips personal identifying information before data is transferred and that this can be verified. Micro1's CEO, Ali Ansari, estimated that labs, enterprises and robotics companies pay about $40 to $50 billion a year for data, a figure Levy could not verify, and predicted the spending would exceed a trillion dollars a year within two to four years. Levy also notes that a bankrupt Spirit Airlines put digital assets up for sale, including 80,000 email accounts, 500 million internal messages, 20.6 million SharePoint files and a million time-card records, and that the sale is now on hold after the flight attendants' union said it involved their private information.

Critics raise concerns that the anonymization may not fully remove personal details. Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, general counsel of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said unstructured emails and Teams messages are harder to scrub and may contain personal matters, and the union's president said the data became valuable so that models could replace jobs. Venture capitalist Gordon Ritter said the industry has not set norms for data acquisition and that the AI industry is moving faster than standards can be set. Ansari acknowledged that objections from workers are a fair point but said they would be manageable, arguing that workers will accept the trade-off for the abundance AI can bring, a claim Levy says he finds a convenient justification for compromises. Levy also describes a meeting with Tenkara, a two-year-old company whose head of commercialization confirmed that much of his job is buying data, and Levy says he declined to offer Wired's own editorial documents.

Articles.Title: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails

stories.Headline: Dr. Dre Has Zero Issues With AI in Music, Says He's 'Extremely Excited' About It
stories.Summary:
Dr. Dre said he is "extremely excited" about artificial intelligence in music and film, speaking on the debut episode of Listen & Laugh, the new podcast hosted by Ice Cube and Mike Epps. The episode was published on November 6, 2026, and Complex reported on it the following day. Dre said he did not see a problem with the technology and argued that people who object to it are not creative enough. Dre described AI as offering a new level of creativity and imagined a future where an actor could approve an AI-generated version of their own image and voice in a film. When Ice Cube asked whether Dre would mind if a producer used AI to copy his mixing style, Dre said he would not be upset and would respect it.

He compared AI use to sampling, saying he would welcome a remake of "Nuthin' but a 'G' Thang" that outdid the original, and he warned that people who do not adapt may be left behind. Ice Cube, who has been vocal against AI tools, said he supports creators who use them but objects to shortcuts that let people skip the years of work needed to make a great record. He also said his concern is with computers taking "total control" of the creative process. Dre pushed back, asking why the older generation should resist new tools simply because they are unfamiliar with them.

The two continued debating before agreeing to disagree. The exchange follows Ice Cube's 2023 comment, made on the Full Send Podcast, that AI-generated music was "demonic." The articles do not say whether the two will revisit the topic on future episodes. The full episode featuring Dre is available on Complex.

Articles.Title: Dr. Dre Has Zero Issues With AI in Music, Says He's 'Extremely Excited' About It

stories.Headline: Foxconn posts highest-ever monthly revenue in October, up 45.73 pc YoY on AI demand - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Taiwanese electronics manufacturer Hon Hai Precision Industry, known as Foxconn, reported record revenue for October 2026. The company said its consolidated revenue rose 45.73 per cent year on year to NT$1.305 trillion, or about USD 39.61 billion, its highest monthly figure ever. The figures came in an unaudited monthly revenue report released on a Thursday and reported by ANI on November 6, 2026. Foxconn credited the growth mainly to strong demand for artificial intelligence products, consumer electronics and computing products.

The October total was up 12.66 per cent from NT$1.159 trillion in September 2026, and it compared with NT$895.7 billion in October 2025. In US dollar terms, October revenue rose 39.7 per cent year on year and 11.4 per cent month on month. Cumulative revenue for the first ten months of 2026 reached NT$8.98 trillion, a 40.40 per cent increase from NT$6.39 trillion a year earlier, which the company described as its highest-ever figure for that period. Growth was broad across segments, with cloud and networking products, smart consumer electronics, computing products and components all cited.

Cloud and networking products dipped slightly from September, which Foxconn linked to changes in the consignment model, tight supply and the early production ramp of new models. Foxconn itself attributed the results to strong AI-related demand and higher shipment prices in several segments. It said AI-related operations are expected to keep growing in the fourth quarter of 2026, supported by the traditional peak season for information and communications technology products. The company also said it would keep monitoring the volatile global political and economic environment.

It stated that the figures had been submitted to the Taiwan Stock Exchange and had not been reviewed or audited by a certified public accountant. The company will hold its investor conference call for third-quarter financial results on November 12, and its November monthly revenue report is expected on December 5. Those dates are the next scheduled points at which investors can expect fuller financial detail. The articles do not provide further forecasts beyond the fourth-quarter outlook described above.

Articles.Title: Foxconn posts highest-ever monthly revenue in October, up 45.73 pc YoY on AI demand - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking
stories.Summary:
Open-weight AI models from China are now nearly as capable as the best closed models at carrying out network hacking, according to new research from Vals, a company that measures AI capabilities. The findings, reported by WIRED on November 6, 2026, were based on tests of how well different models could complete multi-step instructions on simulated corporate networks. Vals ran two scenarios, one involving a mock network reached through a public-facing website and another requiring a model to compromise one company network to reach a second. The results point to a turning point the cybersecurity field has long anticipated.

In the tests, OpenAI's most advanced cyber model, Daybreak, completed 81 percent of its assigned tasks on average across two runs, and it is available only to trusted partners. DeepSeek, an open-weight model from China, completed 73 percent on average and scored equally with Daybreak on some tasks. The research also found a large cost gap, with Vals estimating that an attack using GPT-6-Sol cost $17 to $46 in tokens while the same kind of attack with DeepSeek cost $2 to $3. Rayan Krishnan, CEO of Vals, said the lower cost gives defenders a strong reason to use open models rather than proprietary ones. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The findings matter because US frontier labs, particularly Anthropic, had justified limited releases of new models on the idea that gated access would only buy time before advanced hacking abilities became widely available. Anthropic's frontier red team lead, Logan Graham, told WIRED in April that the company's Project Glasswing gave trusted access to new models so defenders could get a head start. He said at the time that the world should prepare for these capabilities to be broadly available within 6, 12, or 24 months. The Vals results suggest closed models no longer hold a clear edge in cyber skills, which could make efforts to slow the spread of such capabilities largely pointless. Seven months after Graham's remarks, the article says, that transition seems to have arrived roughly on schedule.

The article also notes that experts still disagree about whether AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity or mainly amplified problems that already existed. Real-world observations of criminal and state-backed hacking, it says, show attackers generally conserve resources and rely on older, less capable models for most activity. Alex Zenla, cofounder and chief technology officer of the cloud security firm Edera, agreed that open-weight models can already produce advanced attacks, especially modified versions that have had safety training removed. He added that closed labs have likely trained unreleased models that go further, describing the situation as a cat-and-mouse game. Zenla warned that this may be the start of a dangerous security landscape.

Articles.Title: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking

stories.Headline: Thornton hardware store uses AI system to fight shoplifting
stories.Summary:
A Thornton hardware store is using an artificial intelligence camera system to combat shoplifting that has become a recurring problem. Richard McLamb, the store's manager, says employees deal with shoplifting attempts several times a week, and some thieves have targeted larger items, including a snowblower that he believes walked out the door. The store has installed the system, which watches live video feeds from cameras throughout the store. When it spots activity it considers suspicious, it sends employees a video clip of the incident so they can respond quickly.

The technology comes from Veesion, which provides AI-powered video surveillance for retailers. According to the company, almost 7,000 stores use its software, and nearly 1,000 of them are in the United States. Hiren Mowji, Veesion's director of sales, says the AI identifies suspicious activity in live video and sends retailers alerts with footage attached, giving them proof. McLamb says the alerts let employees step in before merchandise leaves the building. He recalled one case in which a person was caught on camera hiding screwdrivers and hammers in his pants before heading toward the exit.

McLamb said he stopped that person, recovered the merchandise and called police. Mowji described retail theft as a problem worth more than $100 billion that is getting worse every year, and said Veesion wanted to offer a practical solution for business owners. McLamb said the system also acts as an extra set of eyes, freeing employees to spend more time helping customers while staying aware of what is happening in the store. He believes that attentive customer service can also discourage theft, since thieves are less likely to steal when staff are close by.

Articles.Title: Thornton hardware store uses AI system to fight shoplifting

stories.Headline: SIU School of Medicine developing AI medical training
stories.Summary:
The Springfield Memorial Foundation and the SIU School of Medicine are investing $2 million to develop medical training programs that use artificial intelligence, according to a report published November 6, 2026. The work is underway at the Ed Curtis Laboratory for Innovation in Medical Education in Springfield, Illinois. The program turns real people into AI avatars, which medical professionals then train to respond to common patient interactions and questions. Medical students can engage with these avatars using a camera and microphone.

The main platform is a difficult conversations simulator that focuses less on diagnosis and more on relationships and on delivering bad news with empathy. The training covers situations such as referring a patient to hospice care, explaining a new allergy, and delivering a cancer diagnosis. The cases come from doctors, and the lab has recently begun working with correctional medicine on questions arising within institutions run by the Illinois Department of Corrections. The platform also lets doctors create their own cases by typing a description, such as a patient with lung cancer, and having the system generate the scenario.

Pinckney Benedict, the lab's program director and chief architect, is the main voice on the project. He said the technology reflects a new era of simulation because conversations can now happen without another person present. He argued that the training means a doctor is not facing a family's worst news for the first time with no preparation. Benedict also said the lab wants to be a leader in digital medical simulation and hopes to share the program with medical schools across the country.

Articles.Title: SIU School of Medicine developing AI medical training

stories.Headline: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web
stories.Summary:
Security researchers have found hundreds of copies of Artex, a Chinese-made AI hacking tool, publicly exposed on the internet where anyone can reach them. Artex is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses. It has been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. Because it is free to download and run, it has become a popular choice for people who cannot access the most advanced cybersecurity AI models from Anthropic or OpenAI.

Censys, a firm that scans the internet for exposed systems, reported in a blog post that it found more than 800 distinct Artex deployments accessible from the web without a password. Its principal security researcher, Silas Cutler, said that not every instance is used maliciously and that many belong to authorized testers. The software does not require these systems to be reachable from the internet, so their exposure is unexplained. Exposed instances can also reveal attack tools, including implants, which are hidden programs used to keep access to a victim's network.

Security companies have tied Artex to several large attacks. In September, it was used against the South Korean finance industry, and CrowdStrike attributed those attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who left an open directory hosting the system. Censys said the exposed instance had been online for months and appeared to hold data from attacks reaching beyond South Korean banks, including payment and gaming companies. Earlier in October, Artex was also used in an attack on IT support provider ConnectWise, which let Chinese-linked hackers spy on thousands of organizations whose data sits in Microsoft's cloud. Microsoft said the hackers moved so quickly that defenders had little time to respond.

Many of these attacks relied on simple weaknesses, such as guessing weak or known passwords and the lack of multi-factor authentication. Artex has since announced that it will become closed source, limiting further releases to paying customers, but dozens of copies of its code remain on code-sharing sites and can still be used in active attacks. The reporting shows that basic misconfigurations can expose both attackers and their targets. The articles do not say whether the exposed deployments will be taken offline or what steps regulators or vendors will take.

Articles.Title: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web

stories.Headline: IREN (IREN) Stock Price Rallies As Q1 Results Spotlight AI Margins
stories.Summary:
IREN jumped roughly 20% in a single session after releasing its first quarter 2027 results, a sharp turnaround for a stock that had fallen more than 40% over the prior month. Investors responded most strongly to the company's artificial intelligence cloud business, which generated about US$200 million of the US$228 million in total revenue. Adjusted EBITDA margin came in near 29%, a notable step up from roughly 14% in the prior quarter. The results point to a shift away from legacy bitcoin mining toward AI infrastructure services.

Total revenue fell from US$240 million a year earlier, but the mix moved decisively toward AI cloud. The company still reported a net loss of US$263 million, compared with net income of US$385 million a year earlier, and a loss of US$0.66 per share. Management described its AI capacity for 2026 as largely sold out and said discussions for 2027 and 2028 were advanced. Its Horizon 1 facility is live with Microsoft, and operating annual recurring revenue reached US$1.0 billion.

The company, however, pushed its US$4 billion ARR target into early 2027 rather than late 2026, and it still plans a fiscal 2027 capital spending program of US$25 billion to US$30 billion funded largely with debt and customer prepayments. Bulls see the quarter as evidence that IREN is becoming a contracted AI utility, while bears worry that rising overhead, interest costs and the decommissioning of mining hardware will run ahead of recognized AI revenue. The timing of new capacity coming online late in the quarter is central to that concern. The articles indicate that the coming quarters will show whether the company can convert its contracted backlog into revenue while financing a very large build-out.

Articles.Title: IREN (IREN) Stock Price Rallies As Q1 Results Spotlight AI Margins

stories.Headline: AI’s Hidden Footprint, From Quartz Mines to Kenyan Click-Workers, Bared in Taiwan Creative Content Fest Doc ‘The Technological Sublime’
stories.Summary:
A documentary titled "The Technological Sublime," directed by Jannes Callens, is heading to the Taiwan Creative Content Fest in Taipei, where it will be shown as a work in progress. The film follows the physical supply chain that keeps artificial intelligence running, beginning at quartz mines in the Appalachians and moving on to chip plants in Taiwan, lithium fields in Chile, undersea cables and click-workers in Kenya. Its aim is to show what the technology costs people and the planet. The festival runs from November 6 to 9 at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, organized by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency. Callens says that AI is often discussed as something abstract and invisible, but his research showed a tangible ecosystem behind the idea of "green" AI.

He noted that an online image search for AI mostly returns humanlike robots, with almost nothing showing the hardware and labor underneath, which pushed him toward the subject. He describes the film as a work of art meant to bring nuance to the AI debate by showing the achievements of the technology without ignoring its material, ecological and human costs. His earlier documentary, "Dor (Longing)," won the Best Belgian Film award at the Brussels Independent Film Festival and was selected for Visions du Réel. The first scenes of the new film have already been shot, and the team is waiting to secure the rest of its financing.

Delegate producer Steven Dhoedt, who has long followed new technology, said many people still find AI abstract despite the hype around it. He praised Callens for choosing a grounded, less sensational approach, which he believes suits the moment. Because filming spans four continents, the producers are still seeking more investors and partners. Belgian broadcaster VRT has come on board, and talks are underway with other European broadcasters.

The team is also working with James Chia-Hao Hsu of Reel Asia Pictures, its Taiwan partner, to start conversations with distributors and sales agents at the festival. The film is a co-production between Brussels-based Visualantics, Paris-based Tag Film, Cobra Films and Taipei-based Reel Asia Pictures. Dhoedt said TCCF gives the project a real chance to reach audiences in Asia. The article does not say when the finished film will be released or whether it has secured a distributor.

Articles.Title: AI’s Hidden Footprint, From Quartz Mines to Kenyan Click-Workers, Bared in Taiwan Creative Content Fest Doc ‘The Technological Sublime’

stories.Headline: Sashem Brey: Building a holiday budget with AI - Watching Your Wallet
stories.Summary:
The only article that bears on the headline is a short 13abc.com feature, published November 6, 2026, titled "Sashem Brey: Building a holiday budget with AI - Watching Your Wallet." The piece says the station is exploring how to use artificial intelligence to put together a simple holiday budget, so that viewers can celebrate the season without taking on new debt. The rest of the page is a list of unrelated local headlines, including a Toledo traffic safety story, a dance fundraiser, and a report on the Lucas County Board of Elections. The feature itself offers no specifics beyond that stated goal. It does not name the AI tools used, give sample budget figures, or describe any steps or recommendations.

It also does not say how the segment was produced or who is behind the analysis. Because the article is only a brief teaser, the substance of the budgeting approach cannot be confirmed from this material alone. Nothing in the provided articles identifies a person responsible for the budgeting content beyond the on-air reporter whose name appears in the headline, Sashem Brey. The page offers no quotes from Brey or any other source on the subject.

The surrounding items concern separate matters, such as the Ohio Secretary of State placing the Lucas County Board of Elections under heightened oversight after delayed election night reporting. No follow-up coverage of the budgeting segment appears in the material provided, so whether further installments or results will be published is not stated. Readers looking for more detail would need to check the station's site or broadcast directly. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Sashem Brey: Building a holiday budget with AI - Watching Your Wallet

stories.Headline: SK Hynix (KOSE:A000660) Unveils Cooler AI Memory As Data Center Scrutiny Grows
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, listed in Seoul as KOSE:A000660, introduced an iHBM low-heat memory design that it says is meant to reduce cooling demands in AI data centers. The company presented the new iHBM architecture as offering lower power use and less heat output than conventional high bandwidth memory used in AI servers. The announcement was reported on November 6, 2026, with the article published that day. Management framed the product as a response to growing scrutiny of the water and electricity consumed by data centers running AI workloads.

According to the report, the launch is also part of a broader effort to attract and retain chip engineers as Chinese competitors expand their hiring. The article describes SK hynix as a global memory and semiconductor supplier that makes chips for data centers, consumer devices and enterprise hardware. Any shift in its product mix toward lower power iHBM would therefore affect how AI infrastructure is built and cooled. The report does not give pricing, shipment dates or specific figures on power or heat savings.

The article is an AI-assisted analysis produced by Simply Wall St. and carried by Yahoo Finance, and it does not name a company official as a direct speaker. It states that management positioned iHBM as a response to scrutiny of data center water and electricity use, and that SK hynix highlighted the launch in connection with talent retention. The piece also says the company's long-term success depends on continued heavy capacity expansion, including new fabs and advanced packaging, while keeping its balance sheet disciplined. It stresses that it is general commentary and not investment advice.

The article presents the iHBM launch as a test of the bull case for SK hynix's heavy AI memory investment, since it targets power and cooling pressures in AI servers. It also notes the bear case that a custom low-heat design adds technical complexity and capital needs at a time when Chinese DRAM rivals are raising pay to recruit engineers. The report says nothing firm about what happens next beyond these competing considerations. It is also unclear from the article whether the iHBM design has begun commercial shipments.

Articles.Title: SK Hynix (KOSE:A000660) Unveils Cooler AI Memory As Data Center Scrutiny Grows

stories.Headline: The AI advantage isn’t access, it’s adoption - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has moved past the question of access, and the tools are now embedded in software that employees already use. At an Economic Times Business Verticals Workplace 2035 fireside chat, Anurag Bansal of Accenture LearnVantage and Vaibhav Kumar Srivastava of Google Cloud discussed this shift with Muqbil Ahmar of ETCIO. The panel focused on what separates organisations that merely have AI from those gaining real value from it. The published account, dated November 6, 2026, frames the competitive divide as one of skills, confidence and operating capability rather than technology.

Bansal argued that because everyone has access to similar tools, the difference lies in how well people use them. He compared AI to a blank canvas and a pencil, where everyone holds the same tool but produces different results depending on understanding. He said organisations are at very different stages, with some still assessing possibilities, others running pilots, and a smaller group integrating AI into workflows at scale. He pointed to Accenture's workforce of over 810,000 people as an example of why adoption must reach the whole organisation rather than a small group of early adopters. The article suggests that a successful pilot shows a technology works but does not show that an organisation can change how work gets done.

Bansal also warned that rapid innovation can hold organisations back, because constant evaluation of the next model or platform can replace actual implementation. He argued that companies should start adopting AI now and allow their capability to evolve alongside the technology, comparing this to how people adapt to operating system upgrades. Srivastava described the move from classical to generative AI over the past three years, noting that AI can now generate text, audio and video and is increasingly taking over tasks once requiring human intellect. He said AI is becoming accessible beyond specialist teams, which he described as a potential leveller, though he added that results still depend on a user's ability to frame problems and judge outputs.

The panel also addressed learning, with Srivastava expecting curricula that now update every six months or a year to become far more dynamic and interactive over time. The article concludes that the next advantage will belong to organisations that turn access into adoption and adoption into continuous learning. Bansal said collaboration between companies such as Accenture and Google Cloud would help organisations adopt faster. The article does not report any specific outcomes or timelines beyond these comments.

Articles.Title: The AI advantage isn’t access, it’s adoption - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Australian firms warned on narrow AI view by executive
stories.Summary:
Whitewater Reinventions has warned that many Australian organisations take too narrow a view of artificial intelligence, and that responsibility for AI is moving beyond IT and into the executive suite. The comments, reported by IT Brief Australia on 6 November 2026, feed into a wider debate over whether companies use AI mainly to automate existing tasks or to redesign how they operate. Adam Salzer, Executive Chair of Whitewater Reinventions, argued that this limited view is holding back local businesses. He said many leaders still see the technology as an efficiency tool or a source of risk rather than a route to broader organisational change. Salzer contrasted this with overseas firms, which he said are more likely to tie AI to strategy, operating models and commercial opportunity.

Salzer pointed to several surveys to show the gap. He cited BCG research finding that roughly three-quarters of managers in India and Greater China expect AI to deliver major benefits. Deloitte research found that only 65 per cent of Australian respondents planned to increase AI investment in the next financial year, nearly 20 percentage points below the global average. A Thoughtworks study, he said, found Australian management teams tend to focus AI on cost reduction, and about one in six reported having no AI strategy at all. He argued that this caution could leave companies exposed as AI spreads through core business functions, and that the strongest performers redesign processes, products and systems around the technology rather than adding tools to existing workflows.

Salzer also said AI governance is moving away from specialist technology teams and into operations, human resources and chief executive-led programs. That shift pushes leaders to make decisions on workforce design, customer service, product development and accountability. He said some executives use AI tools daily but still need to judge which questions to ask, which outcomes to seek and how to measure returns. He illustrated the point with a recent discussion in which a chief executive questioned whether a manager's points came from Microsoft Copilot or from the individual's own thinking, and he argued that management responsibility cannot be handed to software.

Salzer cited IKEA as an example of AI changing jobs rather than simply removing them. The retailer introduced its Billie chatbot to handle routine customer queries, affecting more than 8,500 call centre staff, and those employees were retrained as remote design advisers. He said this created a new sales channel worth about €1.3 billion, or more than A$2 billion. He added that organisations measuring AI against financial and operational outcomes while embedding agentic systems are increasingly outperforming those that do not, and that smaller Australian firms may move faster because they have fewer established processes to protect. The article does not describe specific next steps beyond Salzer's call for AI to be treated as a transformation opportunity rather than a technology issue.

Articles.Title: Australian firms warned on narrow AI view by executive - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: McDonald's will expand AI ordering to save 50 hours of labor weekly. Franchisees question the costs
stories.Summary:
McDonald's plans to expand its AI ordering system, Archy, to additional drive-thrus in the United States and Australia, according to Restaurant Dive. The company hopes the technology will save about 50 labor hours a week at its restaurants. CEO Chris Kempczinski announced the expansion during an earnings call, where he also said more overseas trials are scheduled for 2027. Most U.S. McDonald's restaurants are expected to receive the system, which takes voice orders in both Spanish and English.

The labor savings form part of a wider technology initiative that the company says is meant to raise restaurant margins by 2.5 percentage points. Archy sits alongside automated inventory tracking and connected equipment within the ArchIQ AI platform, which the chain announced in September as part of its Next initiative. During that September investor day, McDonald's reported that Archy's accuracy exceeded 90 percent and that customer satisfaction was high in early tests. Kempczinski said the technology would let staff focus on customer service and food quality, and he promised updates on Next throughout 2027.

Franchisees have raised doubts about whether the benefits will outweigh the costs. According to Peter Saleh, an analyst who covers restaurants and food distributors, operators said in October that the margin target seemed highly theoretical and that few details had been given about how productivity would improve. Saleh wrote that franchisees were most enthusiastic about the inventory management tools, which some believe could cut manager hours and food waste. Operators also questioned whether the consumer actually wants AI taking orders, and whether voice ordering fits with the company's renewed focus on service and hospitality.

The article places the expansion within a broader debate in the fast-food industry about automation and human service. Chick-fil-A has said its drive-thru orders will stay human-to-human even as rivals test AI, and McDonald's is retraining two million workers as chains reconsider kiosks and apps. The articles also note that AI systems depend on energy-hungry computing infrastructure that can strain resources and raise power bills. The articles do not say when the U.S. rollout will be complete, and they leave open how the costs will be split between the company and its franchisees.

Articles.Title: McDonald's will expand AI ordering to save 50 hours of labor weekly. Franchisees question the costs

stories.Headline: Edera's Object Capability Bounded Authority Promises to Isolate Credentials From AI Agent Workloads
stories.Summary:
Edera, a company whose co-founder and distinguished engineer is Ariadne Conill, has launched a security model called Object Capability Bounded Authority to isolate autonomous AI workloads and Model Context Protocol servers from sensitive credentials. The launch was reported by InfoQ on November 6, 2026. The model addresses a common risk in which organisations give coding agents and external tool integrations API tokens, cloud keys, and administrative credentials that can be exposed to prompt injection or supply chain manipulation. Edera says the technology enforces granular object capabilities at the hypervisor level so that agents can act without holding standard access credentials. Under this approach, an agent could be authorised to modify one GitHub repository without a personal access token, so any compromise stays within that narrow scope.

The architecture separates the authority needed to perform a task from the credentials needed to carry it out. Several runtime components support this. The capcurl tool routes authorised API requests through an isolated broker while hiding the authentication material, and capsudo allows specific privileged commands to run without standing administrative privileges or root access. Workload identity is verified cryptographically through SPIFFE and SPIRE integrations, which establish mutual TLS connections without relying on long-lived static secrets.

The same capabilities can be applied to Model Context Protocol servers, restricting them to particular resources and commands even if the host model behaves unexpectedly. According to the article, initial functionality covering scoped command execution and workload identity has been released, while credential-brokered API access and deeper orchestrator integrations are to follow as part of the broader Project Lunchbox initiative. The article attributes the launch to Edera and identifies Ariadne Conill as its co-founder and distinguished engineer, known for contributions to low-level open-source security. It does not include any statement from the company beyond the description of the product.

The article's author is Olimpiu Pop. The reporting places the model within a wider industry concern about how enterprises provision authority to non-deterministic software, and it notes that engineering teams often build custom credential-handling middleware to fill this gap. The article presents the approach as a promise to standardise that enforcement in the hypervisor and runtime layers. The remaining features are scheduled for later release, and the article does not give dates for them.

Articles.Title: Edera's Object Capability Bounded Authority Promises to Isolate Credentials From AI Agent Workloads - infoq.com

stories.Headline: AI physics startup PSI says a system running a non-public Anthropic model proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a quantum computing question open since 2008 (PSI)
stories.Summary:
Physical Superintelligence (PSI), an AI physics startup, announced on November 6, 2026 that a research system developed in-house had proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a question in quantum computing open since 2008. The system ran on PSI's own infrastructure and used instances of a non-public Anthropic model. According to the company, the system produced a complete proof on the third day of the run, and the Lean proof assistant, which checks each step by computer, accepted it. The system then worked on related open problems and improved the result twice, with Lean accepting the final version.

The conjecture concerns whether quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones on random inputs, which lack the structure that powers speedups like Shor's algorithm from 1994. The articles describe the proof as showing that, if the conjecture holds, an ordinary computer can predict a quantum computer's answer to a yes-or-no question about a random string while reading far fewer bits than the quantum machine would need, so no exponential advantage exists unless the string has a rare pattern. The proof rests on a plan by Shachar Lovett and Jiapeng Zhang, in which one inequality had been left as a conjecture. The PSI team replaced that inequality with a new one proved in the manuscript, drawing on earlier work by David Reimer and several other researchers.

David Turturean, a Member of Technical Staff at PSI, led the work, developing the research system, scoping the problem and running it, and he is responsible for the correctness of the paper. Jim Halverson, an Advisor at PSI, audited the proof, and Phiala Shanahan, also an Advisor, commented on the Lean formalization. Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle and Li-Yang Tan of Stanford University had earlier, in August 2026, settled a special case of the conjecture, and they have since read the full proof, sent comments and are writing a shorter exposition for experts. They called the result a huge advance that resolves a decades-old conjecture. Earlier work had established weaker bounds or special cases only, and the articles say PSI's proof completes the full conjecture.

Articles.Title: AI physics startup PSI says a system running a non-public Anthropic model proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a quantum computing question open since 2008 (PSI)

stories.Headline: New Jersey is gambling on AI: Will taxpayers roll snake eyes on CoreWeave?
stories.Summary:
New Jersey has committed $250 million in tax credits to CoreWeave, an AI data center company, for a $1.8 billion facility at the former Merck campus in Kenilworth. The credits are $50 million a year for five years, and the facility is expected to create 143 permanent jobs, which works out to roughly $1.75 million in subsidies per job. The article, written by environmental activist Jeff Tittel and published by the Jersey Vindicator on November 3, 2026, argues that the state is taking a costly gamble with public money. It contends that the money could instead go toward schools, renewable energy, flood protection, and other community needs.

The article points to CoreWeave's heavy debt, which it says has reached tens of billions of dollars, along with borrowing costs that have climbed to yields reportedly above 15 percent. In the second quarter of 2026, the company reported about $2.58 billion in revenue and $640 million in net interest expenses, and the author notes that nearly 25 cents of each revenue dollar went to interest. The piece also cites Elon Musk, who responded to CoreWeave's rising borrowing costs with "Yikes" and later warned on October 25 that more than 200 AI cloud companies could face failures and consolidation. The author argues that these warnings make the subsidy look especially risky for taxpayers.

The article says the Legislature has passed legislation to end data center tax credits, but CoreWeave's existing award was grandfathered in, so the commitment remains in place. It states that the facility will require about 40 megawatts of electricity, though the larger campus has been associated with potential needs of up to 250 megawatts, and it says CoreWeave plans a $150 million electrical substation and closed-loop cooling. The author asks CoreWeave to prove that its claim of 100 percent clean energy will be met, and warns of added emissions, noise, and neighborhood disruption. The article raises a further concern: whether the state could recover the credits if CoreWeave went bankrupt after they were issued or sold, a question the author says taxpayers deserve answered.

Articles.Title: New Jersey is gambling on AI: Will taxpayers roll snake eyes on CoreWeave? - The Jersey Vindicator

stories.Headline: AI Tool of the Week: this Gemini feature brings textbooks into AI learning
stories.Summary:
Google has added a feature to its Gemini Notebook, formerly known as NotebookLM, that lets students ask questions based on textbooks drawn from a built-in catalogue. The feature was described in a Mint article published on November 7, 2026, and Google's October 29 post says students can now access hundreds of textbooks from providers in the US and India. Answers come with inline citations and direct links to the original passages, so a student can check where the information comes from. The textbooks are free to use through the Add sources and Textbooks options within a notebook.

The feature addresses a problem the article describes: students who ask a general chatbot about a chapter may get confident answers that do not match the book their teacher follows, and they cannot easily verify them. Instead of downloading PDFs of the right edition, a student can select a book from the catalogue and ask questions grounded in it. Gemini Notebook can also turn a chapter into study guides, practice quizzes and flashcards. The article notes that the catalogue includes S Chand Publishing alongside OpenStax and the Open Textbook Library. It also says eligible ebooks bought on Google Play Books can already be added as sources.

The article was written by Jaspreet Bindra and Anuj Magazine, co-founders of AI&Beyond, as part of Mint's weekly "AI Tool of the Week" feature. It was excerpted from Leslie D'Monte's weekly TechTalk newsletter. The authors state that their tool recommendations are independent and based on their internal testing, and that the creators did not influence them. The article does not describe any response from Google beyond its October 29 post. It also does not say whether the catalogue will expand beyond the current set of providers or how schools and teachers are expected to adopt the tool.

Articles.Title: AI Tool of the Week: this Gemini feature brings textbooks into AI learning

stories.Headline: AI advising the White House? Why the task requires people—especially young folks
stories.Summary:
Jason Furman, a former chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under President Barack Obama and now a Harvard professor, recently said that if he were running the CEA today he would, somewhat regretfully, use current AI systems instead of hiring 20 human economists. He said the chair's job would be safe. After pushback, including from former staff, he softened his position and called for an AI-intensive CEA with only a skeleton staff. Under that version, he would still largely replace junior staff, recent college graduates and graduate students, with AI.

Furman based his argument on what AI can already do, pointing to a website he built called Econvitals that offers data dashboards, blog posts, memos, briefings and research papers. The author argues he is focusing on tasks rather than the organization's mission. The CEA, created in 1946, is meant to give the president objective economic advice on domestic and international policy. The author says its most important role is to stop bad ideas, and that AI models tend not to challenge them the way people do. Staff economists, many on leave from universities or detailed from the Federal Reserve or cabinet agencies, have less to lose by dissenting than political appointees.

The author, a Bloomberg Opinion columnist and former Federal Reserve economist, recalls working with junior staff who were often the first to notice when something did not add up. He describes a project his CEA year began with a magazine article about Americans unable to cover a $400 emergency expense, a finding that came from a Fed survey. Economists could not initially answer the president's question, and the work was creative rather than mechanical. The author says AI could speed data work and provide extra checks, and could help revisit researchers' views or tailor the Economic Report of the President to new audiences.

The author concludes that the CEA will change with AI, and that it should. He agrees with Furman that juniors spending their days overseeing bots would be a poor use of taxpayer money and talent, but argues that this reflects a choice about job design rather than a fact about AI. The same tools could free junior staff from monotonous data pulls and formatting so they can make quality improvements and pursue questions no one can yet answer. In the author's words, the president deserves a better CEA, not a smaller one.

Articles.Title: AI advising the White House? Why the task requires people—especially young folks

stories.Headline: Nvidia is driving the AI boom. Good
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, the American chipmaker whose graphics-processing units power artificial intelligence, has become the world's most valuable company, worth $5.4trn, according to an Economist analysis published by Mint on November 5, 2026. Its demand is described as insatiable, and the firm is projected to generate $370bn in net income next year and possibly reach $1trn in sales by 2029. The company's share price is said to be 14 times what it was when ChatGPT was released in late 2022. Nvidia alone accounts for 8% of the S&P 500, and the article notes that it has produced about 15 cents of every dollar the American stock market has returned since 2023.

The article describes a web of financing that has drawn comparisons to the dotcom era. Through $1trn-worth of deals, Nvidia provides cash or guarantees so that data-centre landlords and AI labs can buy its chips, and some critics call it the "bank of AI." Morgan Stanley estimates its overall credit exposure at $200bn by the start of 2029, which could later reach $300bn or more. The article also notes that Nvidia's share of research and development spending has fallen from over a fifth of sales to less than a tenth, while non-Nvidia AI chips now hold 38% of the market, up from 26% in 2023. Nvidia still keeps about $99bn in cash and expects to generate roughly $200bn this year.

The article's author argues that the worries are mostly unjustified and that the risks would fall largely on Nvidia's shareholders. It presents Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive, as a leader who believes the main obstacle to AI is insufficient infrastructure rather than weak demand, and who has concluded that the markets will not supply capital at the necessary scale. The article also reports that Goldman Sachs, BlackRock and Blackstone joined Nvidia last month in a $500bn data-centre initiative. It adds that AI revenue, from Anthropic and other firms and the hyperscalers, may now be around $150bn a year, far short of the $2.5trn needed for AI capital spending. The article concludes that if the bets fail, the costs will be borne mainly by investors, and if they succeed, the AI era may arrive sooner.

Articles.Title: Nvidia is driving the AI boom. Good

stories.Headline: AI-driven attacks put telecom security on govt radar
stories.Summary:
The Department of Telecommunications has stepped up efforts to protect India's telecom infrastructure from increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, including those powered by artificial intelligence. According to officials who spoke on condition of anonymity, the department has held several rounds of meetings with Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Reliance Jio and state-owned BSNL to strengthen network firewalls and other protective measures. The talks follow a series of advisories from the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warning about AI-enabled intrusions. The reporting, published on 6 November 2026, does not give a single date for the start of the meetings.

The department has mandated annual network security audits for telecom service providers, including vulnerability assessments and penetration testing. External network audits are required once every three years. DoT has also set up a telecom security operations centre to improve monitoring, situational awareness and coordination on cybersecurity. Separately, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India has proposed draft guidelines for the responsible use of AI in telecom networks, which call for risk-based classification of AI systems, human oversight, safety assessments and reporting of serious AI-related incidents to the regulator. Under the proposal, operators would remain accountable for AI systems they deploy, including those built or supplied by third parties.

A senior DoT official said the department is working with the operators and that the telcos are independently building security mechanisms, which the official described as robust. The official said the department has not seen any untoward incidents involving private operators or BSNL. The Cellular Operators Association of India had not responded to queries at the time of publication. CERT-In, in an advisory dated 15 October, flagged AI agents that gained unauthorised access to ICT assets of Indian organisations, and in a 4 November advisory it reported escalating AI-driven attacks on banking, financial services and insurance entities by a threat actor it calls Crafty Falcon.

The article places the Indian effort against wider global activity. It notes that Singapore disclosed in the previous year that all four of its major telecom operators had been targeted by a Chinese-linked group, and that Singapore announced further cybersecurity steps in March 2026. It also recalls the Salt Typhoon campaign that affected AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile in the United States, which came to light in 2024. The article does not say when the DoT's further talks with operators will conclude or when TRAI's draft framework will be finalised.

Articles.Title: AI-driven attacks put telecom security on govt radar

stories.Headline: Delhi HC orders takedown of AI-generated videos targeting CM Rekha Gupta
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 6, 2026, the Delhi High Court ordered the removal of several social media posts and videos published by the Aam Aadmi Party that allegedly depicted Chief Minister Rekha Gupta in a defamatory and demeaning way through AI-generated images and deepfake videos. The order came from Justice Manoj Jain in a defamation suit Gupta filed against the party. The posts were reported to have appeared on AAP's official and verified social media accounts. Gupta's plea asked the court to restrain the party from publishing or circulating such content.

According to the plea, the material portrayed her as a liquor vendor, hawker and delivery agent and as head of a fictitious scheme called "Har Har Rekha or Ghar Ghar Theka Yojana." One video allegedly showed her serving drinks to men at night, while another showed AI-generated figures of her and the Deputy Chief Minister pouring liquor and ice cubes. Gupta's plea said the videos looked so real that they created a misleading impression of her involvement in selling and serving liquor. The court noted that one video posted on X on November 4 had reportedly drawn about 75,000 views, 1,600 likes and 470 reposts when its screenshot was taken.

Justice Jain said that the offensive portrayal of the Chief Minister through AI-generated videos could not be treated as permissible political satire. He distinguished healthy criticism and humour from content that attacks personal dignity, and said the posts in question crossed that line by being defamatory and offensive to a woman holding constitutional office. He added that satire may hurt an individual but cannot be allowed to cause irreparable harm to dignity or reduce a person to an object of ridicule. The court also observed that holding public office invites greater scrutiny, yet does not permit the compromise of an individual's dignity.

Referring to earlier decisions, including the Raghav Chadha case, it said that until legislation regulates AI-generated content, courts must examine whether such use infringes the right to dignity. The court issued notices to all defendants, including AAP, and listed the matter for further hearing on December 4, 2026. The articles do not report any response from AAP to the order or to the allegations. They also do not say whether the content has already been removed from the platforms.

Articles.Title: Delhi HC orders takedown of AI-generated videos targeting CM Rekha Gupta

stories.Headline: NCS programme doubles reach, bringing AI and coding skills to more lower-income pupils
stories.Summary:
NCS gave more than 130 primary pupils from lower-income families hands-on lessons in artificial intelligence, coding and robotics on Oct 31 at its NCS Hub in Ang Mo Kio. The event was the largest edition yet of N-Able Me!, the company's flagship corporate social responsibility initiative, and it marked a doubling of the programme's reach in its fourth year. The pupils, all in Primary 3 to 6, took part in practical sessions rather than traditional lectures. The programme aims to narrow the digital divide by giving children from lower-income families early exposure to technology.

The curriculum included a three-hour Micro:bit workshop in which pupils learned coding basics and worked in teams to build simple games. Each participant took home a Micro:bit device to support learning beyond the event. At a Superhero AI and Robotics Booth, children used an app developed by NCS employees to create AI-generated images of themselves as superheroes pursuing their dream jobs. A 1½-hour AI masterclass introduced foundational machine learning and prompt engineering, and robotics activities let pupils see hardware engineering up close.

NCS said the programme was run by a team of company tech volunteers and supported by strategic partners including the Ministry of Social and Family Development, ComLink+, Yayasan MENDAKI and The Straits Times School Pocket Money Fund. Senior Minister of State for Social and Family Development and Home Affairs Goh Pei Ming, the guest of honour, encouraged the participants and presented them with completion certificates. Goh said that when government, community and corporate partners work together, children can be given a better start. NCS chief executive Sam Liew said technology should be an inclusive enabler whose benefits reach everyone.

The pocket money fund, started in 2000 by The Straits Times, provides financial relief to children and youth from lower-income families and has helped more than 230,000 cases to date. Under the scheme, primary pupils receive $65 a month, secondary students receive $100 a month, and those in ITEs, junior colleges and polytechnics receive $125 a month. Liew said the aim is to equip young people with foundational tools so they can see themselves as builders in the AI era. The articles do not say whether the programme will expand further or when the next edition will take place.

Articles.Title: NCS programme doubles reach, bringing AI and coding skills to more lower-income pupils

stories.Headline: Home-based patient care among AI applications being tested at next-gen 5G, 6G research centre
stories.Summary:
On November 3, 2026, the National University Health System (NUHS), telco Singtel and telecommunications equipment maker Ericsson signed a memorandum of understanding to open a research centre testing AI healthcare on 5G-Advanced and 6G networks. The centre is exploring a future in which hospital patients recovering at home are watched by wearable medical devices that detect dangerous changes, such as a sudden spike in blood pressure or an abnormal heart rate. If the readings point to an emergency, hospital staff and emergency services are alerted in real time. NUHS chief executive Yeoh Khay Guan said the partners hope to turn future telecommunications technology into practical healthcare applications. NUHS runs hospitals including National University Hospital, Ng Teng Fong General Hospital and Alexandra Hospital.

The partners say current 5G may not cope with the larger data loads expected as more patients recover at home, patient data becomes more complex and AI tools generate more data. The newer networks are expected to handle those volumes, with 5G-Advanced launched in 2025 and 6G slated for commercial launch in 2030. According to Singtel, the newer networks will be faster than current 5G and have much lower latency, meaning they respond more quickly. Chau Yuen, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University, said 6G is predicted to support a much larger number of connected devices. Because more processing can move to the cloud, devices such as augmented reality headsets could be made smaller and less bulky.

Yeoh said the planned uses include autonomous mobile robots for logistics and patient care, internet-connected devices for home care and support for surgeons during operations. NUHS plans to replace its Microsoft HoloLens headsets, which surgeons use to view a holographic image of a patient's heart from CT scans, with slimmer augmented reality glasses. Gao Yujia, director of the new National University XG AI Centre, said better networks and AI could place the hologram on a patient more accurately than is possible by hand now. Gao also said that no AI deployed on 5G so far can give hospital-wide recommendations, and that such systems have worked only at small scale, such as on a single ward. NUH is already testing nursing robots, which are meant to help nurses handle an expected rise in patient numbers rather than replace them.

Articles.Title: Home-based patient care among AI applications being tested at next-gen 5G, 6G research centre

stories.Headline: Redefining Investment Advisory in the Age of AI
stories.Summary:
On 2 November 2026, Forthright Securities, a Hong Kong brokerage under JF SmartInvest Holdings, took part in the Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK event at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre as a first-time exhibitor and Gold Sponsor. The company's pitch was that as its AI tools grow more capable, its human advisers matter more. The article is a paid post produced by the advertising partner, published on 5 November 2026, and the event opened on 2 November with more than 45,000 participants from over 120 economies. Regulators used the week to announce new measures on artificial intelligence applications and governance, tokenisation and payment connectivity.

The company's main product is the Forthright Smart Investment Terminal, a tablet aimed at experienced individual investors. It combines AI-powered analysis, real-time market support monitoring and analytical tools with the firm's investment research, while the human adviser handles questions the models cannot settle. The firm says its three most-used AI features, AI Assistant, Market Monitoring and Portfolio Analysis, have each been used by more than 80 per cent of clients. On the opening day, the Securities and Futures Commission set out plans for principles-based guidance on AI applications with greater autonomy, focused on safety and preserving human accountability and oversight.

Richard Zhengwei He, chief executive of Forthright Financial and Forthright Securities, spoke at a session titled "Agentic Alpha: The Future of Dynamic Wealth." He said agentic AI is goal-based and expects it to change how financial institutions work with clients in the short term. In the longer term, he said he sees no inherent conflict between financial institutions and agentic AI, which he described as bringing reliable, understandable and suitable guidance to people previously excluded from the financial system. Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee, speaking at the opening session, said the city has become the world's largest cross-boundary wealth hub, with net inflows to its asset and wealth management industry up roughly 200 per cent last year.

The article describes the wider context as a shift in how Hong Kong investors trade, with 95 per cent of the city's stock investors now trading online, according to the Investor and Financial Education Council's latest study. The company describes itself as a licensed brokerage that opened a four-floor flagship investor experience hub in Sheung Wan in July 2026 and gained virtual asset business qualifications in May 2026. The article does not say what the firm plans next beyond continuing to pair its AI tools with advisers. The text is promotional and carries a risk warning stating that AI analyses are for reference only and do not constitute investment advice.

Articles.Title: Redefining Investment Advisory in the Age of AI

stories.Headline: Cloudflare Soars 20%, IREN Surges 15% as Earnings Beats Spark AI Cloud Rebound; CoreWeave Jumps 10%
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, Cloudflare reported third-quarter results after the market close, and its shares rose about 20% to $293.43 in morning trading on November 6. The same day, IREN, a GPU cloud provider, reported its first-quarter fiscal 2027 results and its stock climbed roughly 15% to $20.81 after a steep drop the prior session. Gains spread to CoreWeave, which was up about 10% at $48.07 even though its last earnings report dated to August 11. The article describes the moves as a relief rally in battered AI cloud stocks.

Cloudflare's revenue rose 39% from a year earlier to $782.5 million, above the $738.3 million consensus, and its adjusted earnings per share of $0.38 beat the $0.34 forecast. The company raised its full-year revenue outlook to between $2.963 billion and $2.964 billion and set adjusted EPS guidance at $1.35. For the fourth quarter, it expects sales of $845 million to $846 million. IREN's revenue climbed to $228 million from $137 million in the prior quarter, with its AI Cloud segment rising to $200 million from $71 million, and it reported a narrower net loss of $263 million. The company also cited a five-year contract at $22 million per megawatt, with the customer prepaying 90% of related GPU capital costs.

Cloudflare's GAAP net loss widened to $34.1 million from $1.3 million a year earlier, and the article attributes much of that to $174.1 million in stock-based compensation. CEO Matthew Prince called the quarter the company's best ever. IREN faces about $6 billion in planned capital spending that still needs funding, and management has targeted more than $4 billion in annualized revenue run rate by January 31, 2027, a goal that may slip to the end of February. The article notes that CoreWeave's stock had fallen about 48% over the prior month amid concerns about its debt load, and that broader risk appetite also improved after a strong October jobs report showing 165,000 added jobs.

Articles.Title: Cloudflare Soars 20%, IREN Surges 15% as Earnings Beats Spark AI Cloud Rebound; CoreWeave Jumps 10% - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: Lumai tests optical AI servers to cut data center power
stories.Summary:
Lumai, an optical compute company, is testing its Iris Nova optical AI inference servers in the UK's Scaling Inference Lab. The deployment is meant to show how optical compute performs in a commercial data center setting. The company is aiming to ease the power strain that rising AI inference demand is placing on data centers. Iris Nova is Lumai's first server and the first optical inference platform in the lab.

Phillip Burr, product director at Lumai, told Data Center Knowledge that power is the biggest challenge facing data centers. He said that demand for inference is growing faster than the power available to serve it. Lumai says optical compute uses light rather than transistors to carry out matrix multiplication, a core part of inference. The company describes its design as hybrid, with optics handling the multiplication while electronics manage memory, control and nonlinear functions. Lumai says the computation itself uses negligible energy.

Iris Nova is aimed at the prefill phase of inference, where the prompt and its context are processed. Burr explained that prefill is compute-bound, which makes it a good fit for optical compute. The decode phase, where output tokens are generated, is limited by memory bandwidth and is less suitable for the technology. Burr also said model training is not a strong fit today because of precision and weight update requirements. Taking prefill off GPUs lets them concentrate on decode in what is called disaggregated serving.

Iris Nova works with standard software frameworks, including PyTorch, vLLM and SGLang, according to Burr. It uses components made in high volume for data center communications and runs in standard air-cooled racks without liquid cooling. The UK's Advanced Research and Invention Agency supports the Scaling Inference Lab, which CommonAI CIC operates. The articles say the deployment will generate data to shape Lumai's next production product.

Articles.Title: Lumai tests optical AI servers to cut data center power - ET Datacenters

stories.Headline: Kyndryl Holdings (KD) Reaffirms Outlook And Expands AI Push, Is The Rebound Fully Priced In?

Kyndryl Holdings reaffirmed its full-year outlook after second-quarter results that beat earnings expectations, according to a Simply Wall St article published on November 7, 2026.
