A small business owner, Wang Daoxing, said his company spends more than 2,000 yuan a month on tokens for software development, presentations and promotional materials. The article also notes that generative AI users in China exceeded 700 million at the end of June 2026, about half the population, according to a September report from the China Internet Network Information Center.

Tian Feng, president of the Fast Think Institute and a former dean at SenseTime's Intelligence Industry Research Institute, told the Global Times that the trend shows AI reaching beyond developers and large enterprises. He said each token carries real costs for computing, electricity and equipment, and argued that pricing will need more transparency as tokens become consumer goods. He recommended disclosing prices per million tokens, model versions, validity periods and rules for unused allowances, because consumers have found it hard to compare offers across models and providers. He also said the true test of demand is whether buyers actually use their tokens and renew, and that over time AI computing could become a routine household or business expense, much like electricity or mobile data.

Articles.Title: Tokens hit China's shopping carts as ordinary Chinese consumers join the AI boom - Global Times

stories.Headline: Measuring how AI agents handle everyday wet-lab science
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published a report on November 6, 2026, introducing BioBasicsBench, a benchmark that measures how well AI agents interpret raw experimental data from routine wet-lab science. The benchmark was developed with Ligo, a biotech company focused on enzyme design. It contains 100 tasks across five areas of everyday lab work: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. The company said existing benchmarks, built around charts and images selected for scientific papers, may miss the ambiguity and troubleshooting found in day-to-day lab work.

The tasks use raw evidence such as gel and blot images, plate photographs, microscopy stacks, sequencing reads, instrument exports and bench videos, often with reference sheets like ladder charts and plasmid maps. Scientists wrote the tasks from their own experiments and paired each with an expert-written grading rubric. Each task went through an internal review by a Ligo scientist who had not written it, an external review by a PhD-level wet-lab scientist, and a final internal review. Agents return a structured answer, and credit is assigned against individual rubric criteria, so a partially correct analysis can earn partial credit.

OpenAI evaluated seven models, covering 37 model and reasoning-effort settings with five attempts on each of the 100 tasks, for 18,500 results in total. At the highest reasoning setting, xhigh, GPT-6 Astra averaged 66.7% of available credit, with a 95% confidence interval of 60.3% to 73.1%. GPT-6.1 Sol scored 62.0%, GPT-5.6 Sol 43.8%, and the lowest model at that setting, GPT-5.2, 31.2%. The company said the results show progress on routine lab analysis but leave room for improvement in interpreting images, checking controls and applying experimental context.

OpenAI credited Astra's gains to stronger native multimodal capabilities and gave examples where it avoided unwarranted conclusions. In one case, GPT-5.6 Sol labeled cells as dead from a dye signal that a second dye could also produce, while Astra called for better controls to separate the signals. In a DNA cloning example, Astra noticed a detail on a negative control plate that GPT-5.6 Sol missed. The article's account of what happens next is limited to the company's stated aim of helping scientists accelerate biological research.

Articles.Title: Measuring how AI agents handle everyday wet-lab science

stories.Headline: Microsoft plans to use fewer neoclouds as AI buildout shows signs of strain
stories.Summary:
Microsoft is reportedly moving to shrink the number of neoclouds it works with, according to people familiar with the matter, as it focuses on a few key suppliers and builds out its own data centers. The plan was first reported by Bloomberg and CNBC's sources say Microsoft is still in an evaluation stage and has not decided which neoclouds it will drop. Microsoft has worked with several of these providers in recent years, including CoreWeave, Nebius, Chronoscale, IREN, Lambda and Nscale, as well as Oracle. Two people said Microsoft opted not to renew a deal with Oracle. One source said the company wants to prioritize its own data center footprint.

Microsoft's spokesperson said in an emailed statement that its infrastructure strategy is built on flexibility and choice, combining company-owned data centers, leased facilities and partnerships with third-party providers. The company said it regularly reviews these investments against customer demand and adjusts plans as circumstances change. It described its approach to reviewing neocloud investments as a normal and responsible way to manage large, complex projects. The spokesperson added that the pace of new agreements reflects what the company needs today. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases in its latest quarter and said that spending will accelerate in the second half of its fiscal year.

The move comes as neoclouds face strain from rising interest rates, heavy debt loads and doubts about whether the AI buildout will continue at its current pace. Shares of CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have each fallen by roughly half over the past month, even after a rally on Friday. A recent industry review counted 323 neoclouds, and experts have predicted that many will not survive. Microsoft has already walked away from a site with Nscale in England and, according to the Financial Times, decided against renewing a contract with Nscale in Texas. Microsoft's spokesperson did not directly address the reported cuts in those contracts.

Several neocloud companies are set to report results soon, with CoreWeave and Nebius scheduled to report next week. IREN said its AI revenue more than doubled from the prior quarter to $200 million, and its co-CEO said capital markets have become more selective. Microsoft's reliance on neoclouds grew after the launch of ChatGPT in 2022 drove demand for GPUs. The articles do not say which neoclouds Microsoft will ultimately cut or when that decision will be made.

Articles.Title: Microsoft plans to use fewer neoclouds as AI buildout shows signs of strain

stories.Headline: Project EVE: Claude plays MMORPGs
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has published a research post, dated November 6, 2026, describing experiments in which its Claude models played two science-fiction multiplayer games from the EVE Universe, EVE Online and EVE Frontier. The work was part of the Anthropic Fellows Program, ran from April to July 2026, and was done in partnership with Fenris Creations, the studio behind the games. The aim was to test whether AI agents can handle long, complex, high-stakes-style tasks like organizing with others, managing scarce resources, and trading in a shared economy, using a low-stakes environment. In EVE Online, Claude did not trade in the live game, since automated trading there is against the rules. Instead, the team built a simulator that replayed the buy and sell orders players had actually posted on the game's largest trading hub, and gave four Claude models, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5, an initial capital of 3 billion ISK to maximize profit over two-week windows.

Over nine such windows, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 were profitable in every window, growing capital by about 16%, 22% and 43% on average, while Opus 4.6 gained about 4%. In longer six-month runs, average earnings rose from around 200% to 600% of initial capital between Opus 4.6 and Fable 5, which the authors describe as a tripling over roughly four months between their releases. The models mostly used a strategy called spread capture, buying where sellers were asking less than an item's typical value and reselling quickly. Opus 4.6 was the exception, hand-picking items with larger margins and making more calculation errors along the way. The authors note important caveats: the replay cannot react to the agents' own trades, and when synthetic orders undercutting the agents were added, profits fell by roughly 35%, though the agents stayed profitable.

When the models were instead told to make directional bets on prices based on news and patch notes, they performed much worse, and only about half of Fable 5's runs turned a profit. In EVE Frontier, teams of four Claude agents worked through long missions in the live game, using code to handle fast-moving parts of the game, and coordinated well as a team. However, when one agent was secretly told to undermine its team, its teammates almost never caught it. The authors say these results show what teams of agents do well and where they break down, and what safeguards might be needed before trusting them with more consequential work. The article also mentions that earlier Anthropic projects had Claude run a shop in the office, haggle for colleagues and write code to fly a drone, and that the team plans further study of multi-agent interaction.

Articles.Title: Project EVE: Claude plays MMORPGs

stories.Headline: Google Stock (GOOGL) Falls 2.2% as AI Stocks Slide (Nov 5)
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, the parent company of Google, closed at $282.57 on Thursday, November 5, 2026, down $6.36 or 2.20% from the previous close of $288.93. The decline came during a broad selloff in AI-linked stocks that swept Wall Street that day. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315.00, so Alphabet's drop was smaller than the index's. Volume reached 53.4 million shares, well above the 30-day average of 32.5 million. Financial media tied the selloff to concerns that the Democrats' midterm election wins could bring tougher AI regulation and a slower data center buildout.

Fox Business reported that rising electricity prices had made power-hungry data centers a political issue, with some Democrats calling for restrictions or pauses on new projects. An eToro market analyst said markets were pricing in the midterm results and expected the AI infrastructure buildout to become slower and more expensive. CNBC reported that Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft each fell between 2% and 4%, and that Qualcomm's weak earnings forecast also contributed to the selloff. CNBC noted that 41 local ballot measures in 10 states that would restrict data center construction went to a vote on Tuesday, November 3, according to Ballotpedia. Meta President Dina Powell McCormick said on Wednesday night that building data centers would be "going to be harder" after the elections.

The reports reviewed named no cause specific to Alphabet for Thursday's decline. Alphabet's shares remain 30.85% below their 52-week high of $408.61. Alphabet's third-quarter 2026 results showed consolidated revenue up 25% to $127.6 billion, with Google Cloud revenue more than doubling to $30.7 billion. Purchases of property and equipment rose to $51.4 billion in the quarter from $24.0 billion a year earlier, and free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion. The articles do not describe any further market developments after the close on November 5.

Articles.Title: Google Stock (GOOGL) Falls 2.2% as AI Stocks Slide (Nov 5)

stories.Headline: Antonino Emanuele Scurria: AI's next step is from the virtual world to the real world
stories.Summary:
Antonino Emanuele Scurria, a 2026 World Internet Conference (WIC) Global Youth Leader, spoke in an interview during the 2026 WIC Wuzhen Summit about how artificial intelligence might move from virtual settings into the physical world. The interview was published by China Daily on November 7, 2026. He pointed to robots and digital twins of cities as early examples of that shift. Scurria is a PhD student at Universite Libre de Bruxelles who studies AI and theoretical physics. Scurria said the speed of AI development over the past two years has surprised him.

He cited the range of tasks people now use AI for, including writing code, creating videos and solving mathematical problems. He described the pace as faster than he had expected. The articles do not give further figures or dates on this progress. Scurria said gatherings such as the WIC give people a place to discuss where these technologies are heading. He also said such meetings help participants consider what those developments mean for the future they share.

The articles do not name any regulator, company or policy linked to his remarks. The articles provide no further detail on what the next steps in this shift would involve or when they might arrive. The piece is a short interview summary, and the page also carries an unrelated exhibition item about Yunnan. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Antonino Emanuele Scurria: AI's next step is from the virtual world to the real world - China Daily

stories.Headline: How can APEC facilitate AI cooperation across Northeast Asia?
stories.Summary:
The Korea Institute for International Economic Policy's Beijing Office chief representative, Hyun Sang Baek, spoke at a symposium on AI cooperation across Northeast Asia, held on October 30 in Beijing. The event was co-organized by the International Business School of Beijing Foreign Studies University and the China Daily Opinion Channel. Baek's remarks, reported by China Daily, focused on how shared regional ambitions for artificial intelligence could become concrete results. The discussion placed the APEC AI Initiative at the center of that effort. Baek said the APEC AI Initiative has set a common direction for regional cooperation on artificial intelligence.

He expressed hope that this year's APEC meeting in Shenzhen will help move that vision into practical action. He called for deeper collaboration on AI applications in manufacturing, industrial robotics and smart manufacturing. He also argued that small and medium-sized enterprises and research institutions should take part, so the benefits are spread across the region. Baek's position, as reported, is that the APEC AI Initiative provides the framework and that the next step is implementation. His emphasis on bringing smaller firms and research bodies into the work reflects a concern that gains might otherwise concentrate among larger players.

The article does not describe any formal commitments, agreements or timelines beyond the hope expressed for the Shenzhen meeting. It also does not report responses from other officials or governments at the symposium. The article offers no further detail on what form the cooperation would take or how it would be funded and overseen. Whether the Shenzhen meeting produces concrete measures on these points remains unstated in the reporting. Readers should look for the outcomes of that APEC gathering to see whether the call for action is taken up.

Articles.Title: How can APEC facilitate AI cooperation across Northeast Asia? - China Daily

stories.Headline: Joe Tsai: Open source helps more people take part in AI development
stories.Summary:
Joe Tsai, co-founder and chairman of Alibaba Group, said at the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit on November 3 that open-source AI models can cut research and development costs for small and medium-sized enterprises. He argued they also let developers in emerging economies build AI applications suited to their own countries. His remarks were reported by China Daily, which published them on November 5, 2026. Tsai linked the push toward openness to rising demand for AI applications, which he said is outpacing the supply of computing power. Chinese technology companies, in his account, are stepping up efforts to release their models as open source and to open up their wider ecosystems.

He added that Alibaba has open-sourced more than 470 Qwen models. The move is presented as a way to widen who can take part in building AI rather than leaving development to a small group of firms. Tsai pointed to a nonprofit organization in Uganda as an example of how this works in practice. The group used open-source Qwen models to develop models for local languages, and those models now cover 68 African languages. According to the speech as reported, this helps more people overcome language barriers and make use of AI tools in their own tongues.

The example was offered as evidence that open models can reach communities that commercial products often overlook. The articles provided do not describe any policy changes, deadlines, or formal obligations arising from the speech. They also do not report reactions from other speakers or companies at the summit, or any plans for further releases beyond the figures Tsai cited. Beyond the summit remarks, the source material contains nothing on how the Uganda project was funded or how widely the African-language models have been adopted.

Articles.Title: Joe Tsai: Open source helps more people take part in AI development - China Daily

stories.Headline: AI medical innovations take center stage at 9th CIIE
stories.Summary:
At the ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai, a range of AI medical solutions were unveiled and became a main highlight of the expo's medical equipment and healthcare products exhibition area. The technology has moved beyond imaging assistance into surgical navigation, chronic disease management, and intelligent decision-making during medical interventions. The CIIE is described as a key platform for testing AI applications, connecting with hospitals, and speeding up their adoption. The reporting presents these developments as a sign of how quickly the technology is being put to use in clinical settings.

Roche is showing solutions built with ecosystem partners that combine AI and digital tools across the industrial chain, aimed at breaking down data barriers and improving precision in diagnosis and treatment. One tool is a one-stop AI research aid that helps doctors choose topics, review literature, and generate solutions, which the company says will raise research efficiency. Another is a digital remote patient management system that sends follow-up reminders and provides disease education so patients can manage their health at home. Haier's healthcare arm, Incaier, is presenting six AI-driven scenarios, including autonomous labs, autonomous drug management, and proactive health. Incaier also launched an AI strategy built around a central "Incaier brain," and it says its platform serves researchers, healthcare professionals, and patients and already has more than 450 AI-native applications.

Australian biopharmaceutical company CSL signed an agreement at the CIIE with Beijing's Peking Union Medical College Hospital to explore using AI to identify and help diagnose hereditary angioedema, a rare disorder that causes recurring swelling attacks. A hospital representative said the partnership hopes to use advanced AI algorithms to support traditional lab testing and move cutting-edge technology into clinical tools more quickly. The hospital expects this to improve early diagnosis and screening efficiency for clinicians. Philips, in its 2026 China edition of the Future Health Index report released at the CIIE, also highlighted the growing clinical value of AI and the rise of human-machine collaborative medical teams. Philips China's chief regional leader, Liu Ling, said China is actively bringing AI into medical practice and is becoming a leading force in global medical AI applications.

The Philips report found that 95 percent of Chinese clinical healthcare workers surveyed said their focus has shifted or will shift toward higher-value clinical work, compared with a global average of 82 percent. It also found that 81 percent of Chinese patients surveyed believe learning to use AI will become an essential skill for health management, against a global average of 59 percent. In addition, 69 percent of Chinese healthcare workers said they believe AI helps improve patient health outcomes. Taken together, the figures suggest that Chinese respondents are more optimistic than their global counterparts about the role of AI in both clinical work and personal health management.

Articles.Title: AI medical innovations take center stage at 9th CIIE - China Daily

stories.Headline: AMD debuts 6th Gen EPYC at CIIE, bets on Agentic AI
stories.Summary:
AMD is showing its 6th Gen AMD EPYC processors in China for the first time at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai, where the company has taken part for the sixth consecutive year. The display, which runs under the theme "Empowering the Agentic AI Era," is the centerpiece of its cloud computing showcase. The report, published by China Daily on November 7, 2026, describes the event as ongoing at the time of writing. The article does not give exact booth figures or dates beyond that. The new processors are built on the "Zen 6" architecture and use 2nm process technology, according to AMD.

The company says inference, the stage where trained AI models produce results, is becoming a larger share of AI workloads, and this shift is changing how data centers are designed. On the consumer and business side, AMD is highlighting its Agentic PC, which uses Ryzen AI Max Series processors to run large AI models locally. The company says this approach protects data privacy and reduces token costs. Spencer Pan, senior vice-president of AMD and president of AMD Greater China, is quoted as saying that growth in agentic AI is driving continued demand for computing power. He said AMD's full-stack product range, spanning cloud, edge and endpoint devices, along with its open software ecosystem, lets the company work closely with customers, partners and developers in China.

Pan also said AMD hopes to use the expo to combine leading computing technologies with China's varied industrial settings, so that AI can become a strong driver of industrial development. The article places the company's presence within its education efforts in China. Through a program called "Spring Rain," AMD is working with universities to set up AI training labs and innovation demonstration centers that bring its open-source ROCm software and Ryzen AI platforms into teaching and research. At this year's expo, the company is showing university projects, including protein structure research by East China Normal University using the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 processor and a smart home project from Beijing University of Technology. The article does not say what comes next for these products or programs beyond the expo.

Articles.Title: AMD debuts 6th Gen EPYC at CIIE, bets on Agentic AI - China Daily

stories.Headline: Open collaboration and AI bring new possibilities for entrepreneurship
stories.Summary:
Marko Mendieta, founder and director of Mision Ecuador Foundation, said at the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit that an inclusive internet and emerging technologies can create opportunities for entrepreneurship and economic growth. He pointed to artificial intelligence as a tool that could help people set up one-person ventures and grow their businesses. The remarks were reported by China Daily, with the article dated November 7, 2026. Mendieta stressed that technological development should generate jobs and improve people's lives. His comments formed part of the summit's discussion of openness and collaboration.

Mendieta praised the Wuzhen Summit for bringing together people with varied ideas and perspectives. He said the gathering had created room for dialogue and cooperation aimed at a better future. According to the report, he framed these exchanges as central to turning new technology into broader economic opportunity. The article does not detail specific programs, figures or commitments that resulted from the event. Its focus stays on his general views about inclusion, collaboration and the role of emerging tools in entrepreneurship.

The article identifies Mendieta as the source of the views it reports, and it attributes no contrary positions to anyone else. It does not describe any policy change, funding measure or deadline tied to these remarks. Beyond the summit itself, the piece contains only a brief unrelated item about an exhibition showcasing Yunnan's lifestyle and scenery. The report also notes that its summary was generated by AI and that China Daily takes no responsibility for that summary. No further developments are described in the article.

Articles.Title: Open collaboration and AI bring new possibilities for entrepreneurship - China Daily

stories.Headline: AI is getting smarter. What's next for human journalists? - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
The Xinhua article, published on November 7, 2026, asks whether artificial intelligence will make human journalists redundant as the technology grows more capable. It frames the question around the World Media Summit, where media professionals were invited to share their views on what the future holds for the industry. The piece opens with a light tone, noting that AI never needs a break and asking whether people will be able to leave work early or be laid off early. Beyond the question itself, the articles provided offer little detail on specific findings or changes.

The page around the story points to the wider setting in which the discussion took place. Several related items mention the World Media Summit in Beijing, where delegates explored how robots are entering everyday life in China and where AI's role was highlighted as global media leaders met. Other items on the same page cover the China International Import Expo, autumn scenery in Shaanxi and Beijing, and a festival in Guizhou, but these are not directly tied to the journalism question. The articles do not name the individual media professionals who spoke or report what they concluded.

The articles do not say who is responsible for any policy or decision about AI in newsrooms, and they contain no direct statements from officials or executives on the subject. Because the piece is framed as a question to summit participants, its main voice is the publication itself rather than any identified source. The articles also do not describe any concrete steps, timelines or outcomes that would follow from the discussion. Based on the material provided, the story is an open-ended feature rather than a report of a decision or event with defined consequences.

Articles.Title: AI is getting smarter. What's next for human journalists? - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Japan's Nikkei posts 3rd-largest point drop on record as AI-linked stocks tumble - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 6, 2026, Japan's benchmark Nikkei stock index plunged more than 3,600 points, marking its third-largest point drop on record. Artificial intelligence-linked stocks came under heavy selling pressure in Tokyo trading. The sell-off followed renewed worries about tighter regulation after the U.S. midterm elections. The 225-issue Nikkei Stock Average closed down 3,643.13 points, or 5.96 percent, from Thursday, ending at 57,434.77. During the session it fell more than 4,300 points at one point and briefly dropped more than 7 percent.

The broader Topix index shed 232.40 points, or 5.90 percent, to finish at 3,707.99. The Nikkei's close was its lowest since mid-April, and selling spread across nearly all stocks on the Prime Market. Tokyo stocks followed overnight losses on Wall Street, where technology shares fell. Investors there reportedly worried that Democratic gains in the midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data center construction and AI investment. Xinhua's report does not name any specific official or company as responsible for these moves.

It attributes the sell-off to market concern rather than to a formal government action. Analysts quoted by Xinhua said concerns about a possible economic slowdown also emerged as a new factor weighing on the market. That worry broadened the sell-off beyond technology stocks. The articles provided do not say what policy steps, if any, will follow or how markets are expected to move next.

Articles.Title: Japan's Nikkei posts 3rd-largest point drop on record as AI-linked stocks tumble - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Interview: China to play key role in advancing Global South media cooperation in AI era, says Bernama chairman - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China is well placed to play a key role in supporting the Global South's media sector through its advances in artificial intelligence, its wide range of international media partnerships and its stated commitment to cooperation, according to Wong Chun Wai, chairman of the Malaysian National News Agency, Bernama. Wong made these remarks in a recent interview with Xinhua in Kuala Lumpur. He said such cooperation could help media organizations adapt to technological change, build their capabilities and gain a better understanding of China through exchanges and firsthand reporting. Wong was in Beijing for the 7th World Media Summit, which runs from November 5 to 9 under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action."

Wong said the rapid growth of AI is transforming the media industry, opening new opportunities for news organizations while forcing them to rethink how they operate. He warned that buying a tool and installing it in a company is not enough, and that businesses must consider how AI could fundamentally reshape newsroom operations. He hoped the summit would give media organizations a platform for practical discussion of AI applications and newsroom change, so they could learn from one another. He also wanted greater attention at the summit to the practical needs of Global South media and to concrete cooperation on technology use and capacity building. Wong urged participants to move past general commitments toward cooperation that produces tangible results.

Wong recalled taking part in the 6th World Media Summit in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in 2024, and said his visit to Kashgar had stayed with him. Visiting the region let media practitioners see it firsthand and compare it with what they had read or heard before. He recalled that some participants, passing cotton fields and seeing machines used to cultivate the crop, described the scene as the real Xinjiang. Wong argued that such visits give international journalists a clearer picture of China, where development keeps bringing change even to places they have already seen. He also stressed the value of accessible, people-centered content on subjects such as tourism, food and how young people live in each country, since China remains a very important topic for Malaysia.

Wong added that China's fast growth in its creative and cultural industries offers lessons for Malaysia as it works to expand its own creative sector. He said he watches a lot of Chinese AI and short dramas to see how the sector is advancing and to learn how Malaysia might do the same. He expressed hope that the 7th World Media Summit would further strengthen cooperation between Bernama and Xinhua. He also encouraged media organizations across the Global South to turn shared ideas into concrete initiatives.

Articles.Title: Interview: China to play key role in advancing Global South media cooperation in AI era, says Bernama chairman - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Forget six fingers. AI’s bigger story is quantity
stories.Summary:
Ten thousand AI agents were set loose on an open problem in mathematics, whether the equations of fluid flow always behave, and within four days they produced a proof that specialists are still debating. The same lab then posted more than 700 manuscripts at once, each result costing only a few hours of machine thinking. The writer, Nilesh Jasani, founder and portfolio manager of GenInnov Asset Management in Singapore, argues that this flood of results, rather than the old complaints about errors, is now AI's most important story. The article describes a tool that rewrote a half-million-line programme into a new language in 11 days, a job its creator estimated would take three expert engineers a year. The same article says another model found thousands of unknown security flaws in major operating systems within weeks, one of which had hidden from human auditors for 27 years.

A genome atlas predicted the effects of all nine billion possible single-letter changes in human DNA. Jasani also cites an AI system that proposed about 380,000 stable crystal structures, compared with roughly 20,000 found in all of human experimentation. He notes that the maintainers of curl ended their bug bounty after a flood of poor AI submissions, though their later reports were largely accurate but overwhelming in volume. Jasani's central claim is that institutions built for a trickle, such as peer review and court dockets, cannot cope with this volume, and he says the quality debate offered remedies that quantity does not. He writes that human attention, trust and time do not grow exponentially the way machine output does.

He also argues that the physical world is the last brake, so whoever controls the final physical step holds a veto over the many intellectual steps before it. For businesses, he expects continuous and compounding disruption, with many gains arriving as ordinary costs quietly disappearing. He warns that organisations unable to sort, verify and act on abundance will fall behind. The article is an adaptation of a piece first published on GenInnov's blog, and it frames the present as the last comfortable moment before a tsunami becomes visible. Jasani concludes that quality was the question people knew how to argue about, while quantity is the one they will have to live with.

Articles.Title: Forget six fingers. AI’s bigger story is quantity - The Business Times

stories.Headline: AI can make art in seconds – how are artists in Singapore fighting to keep their craft alive?
stories.Summary:
Singapore's creative community is responding in several ways to generative AI, which can produce images, videos and other visual works from text prompts in seconds. Work that once took artists hours, days or months, such as restaurant menus, commercials, event posters, billboards, microdramas and book covers, can now be generated quickly. Reactions range from curiosity and frustration to disgust, with concerns centred on copyright, consent and the value of human creativity. CNA Lifestyle spoke with illustrators, animators, graphic designers, painters and arts educators about how the technology is changing their work.

Artists' objections begin with how generative AI is trained. Its models learn from vast amounts of existing material, and OpenAI says its training data includes publicly available online material as well as material provided or generated by users and researchers. Goh Wei Choon, co-founder and illustrator of The Woke Salaryman, argues that the technology scrapes the work of other creatives without permission. Illustrator Farihath Samsul said someone had used AI to transform her original work, which she called theft. Muralist Terence Tan, known as Ubin Artist, also questions how much individuality remains when new work is generated from existing material.

Artists are protecting their work in practical ways. Felicia Low-Jimenez, co-founder of comic publisher Difference Engine, said her team tracks AI features in software such as Adobe and Google Workspace, does not put creators' work into generative AI and does not accept AI-generated submissions. Farihath has written terms into her contracts that bar clients from running her commissioned work through AI. Some artists use Glaze and Nightshade, tools developed by researchers at the University of Chicago, though these do not remove art already used in training or guarantee protection. Graphic designer Pann Lim doubts such tools can keep pace with advancing AI, and Muhammad, the content producer behind Ihasamic!, argues that stronger safeguards should come from organised collective action rather than individuals alone.

Several artists are also stressing what makes their work human. Muhammad said the answer to AI's engineered dishonesty is honesty, extending to fair and prompt pay for freelancers. Jolene Tan, a freelance animator whose work appears on Singapore's MRT platforms, shares videos of her animation process, which can take weeks or months, to show how it differs from AI output. Terence Tan values the visible brushstrokes and imperfections in his hand-painted murals. Lim, who has worked in design for nearly three decades, put it simply: "You can use AI, but you don't need to give up your soul."

Preserving these principles is harder for artists who must earn a living. Lim distinguishes between artistic expression and artists' "rice bowls," and notes that some employers expect creatives to use AI. Goh said he finds it brutal to label artists who use AI as betrayers of the rest of the community. The tension between holding firm principles and keeping income remains unresolved for many in Singapore's creative community.

Articles.Title: AI can make art in seconds – how are artists in Singapore fighting to keep their craft alive? - CNA Lifestyle

stories.Headline: Debunked Episode 31: CVS Health Restructure, AI ROI Report Findings, FTC Warning Letters
stories.Summary:
CVS Health has announced that it will split into two companies in 2028, a move that dominated healthcare news in the week after the midterm elections. One business will keep the CVS Health name and include Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health and Signify Health, and it will be led by David Joyner, the current chairman and CEO. The second business, to be called CVS Pharmacy, will be a national retail pharmacy and community healthcare company that includes about 9,000 pharmacies, mail pharmacy, MinuteClinic and the Health100 technology services business. Prem Shah, the current group president of CVS Health, will lead that company. The articles describe the split as a national retail operation separated from the insurance and pharmacy benefit businesses.

The restructure was described as a response to concerns about vertical integration and conflicts of interest. Debunked co-hosts Arundhati Parmar and Samir Batra said the business plans still reward higher profits, which they argued would benefit shareholders more than customers. Mark Cuban, co-founder of Cost Plus Drugs, called the move "brilliant financial engineering." Batra also linked the split to the Break Up Big Medicine Act from Senators Elizabeth Warren and Josh Hawley.

The articles place the move within a wider trend, with some states seeking to bar pharmacy benefit managers from owning pharmacies and federal bills proposed to break up large healthcare companies. The podcast also covered artificial intelligence, citing the second edition of Bessemer Venture Partners' Healthcare AI ROI Scorecard, which surveyed healthcare executives. It found that returns are highest in areas such as revenue cycle management, that only 46% trust AI-generated tools to support clinical decision-making, and that 77% override AI suggestions more than half the time. The FDA is expected to publish a final rule on how generative AI-enabled medical devices will be regulated, following a discussion paper earlier this year that drew more than 300 comments.

Parmar cited remarks by Rick Abramson, director of the FDA's Digital Health Center of Excellence, who said generative AI tools may need to be evaluated similarly to a physician's periodic competency review. That would depart from the agency's traditional approach to software as a medical device. The Federal Trade Commission sent warning letters to 24 healthcare organizations last month over inadequate price transparency, which Batra compared to a referee issuing yellow cards to players. The articles do not say what follow-up action, if any, the agency will take against those organizations.

Articles.Title: Debunked Episode 31: CVS Health Restructure, AI ROI Report Findings, FTC Warning Letters

stories.Headline: AI data-center stocks slide, renewables rally after Democratic US midterm sweep - CNA
stories.Summary:
Data-center stocks fell on Wednesday and clean-energy shares rallied after Democrats took control of Congress in the US midterm elections, Reuters reported on November 4. The result includes wins in Republican strongholds and in the data-center hubs of Texas and Georgia, and it brings divided government to Washington. Investors responded by repositioning for tougher scrutiny of the AI boom and a change in policy priorities. A second report, from Tom's Hardware, described the vote as a comprehensive defeat for AI data centers, with 45 measures on the ballot and Americans overwhelmingly voting against developments.

Among data-center operators, Applied Digital fell 8.8%, CoreWeave dropped 9.5% and Cipher Digital slid 21%. Power and equipment suppliers tied to the buildout also came under pressure, with GE Vernova down 11.5%, Constellation Energy down 9.2% and Vistra down 15.4%. Large US cloud companies bucked the trend, as Amazon and Microsoft each jumped 6% and Alphabet rose 4.6%, because investors bet a slower construction pace would raise the value of existing assets and curb Big Tech's heavy AI spending. On the clean-energy side, First Solar gained 8.4%, Sunrun added 6.9%, Enphase Energy rose 8.8% and NextEra Energy climbed 4.6%, while in Europe Vestas rose 2.9%, Orsted 4.6% and EDP Renewables 2.8%.

Other sectors moved too. Trump Media & Technology Group dropped 13%, SpaceX fell 3.5% and Tesla lost 3.3%, and defense stocks declined as investors reassessed expectations for President Trump's proposed $1.5 trillion budget, with Northrop Grumman down 3.7% and RTX, Lockheed Martin and L3Harris losing between 3% and 6%. Hospital operators and insurers rose, with HCA Healthcare up 8.5%, Universal Health Services up 6.8%, Centene up 7.3% and Molina Healthcare up 6.3%. Private prison operators GEO Group and CoreCivic fell 3.8% and 2.1%.

Analysts offered several explanations. Mark Malek of Siebert Financial said the AI buildout would become more expensive rather than disappear, with fewer tax incentives and more responsibility for power and water costs squeezing returns, and he judged borrowers to be more vulnerable than the biggest spenders. Art Hogan of B. Riley Wealth argued that hyperscalers already have their data centers, so those assets are worth more if overbuilding is avoided, though slower construction would also mean slower capital spending. Kathleen Brooks of XTB said the result casts doubt on a possible SpaceX and Tesla merger, since Congress could slow it with extra scrutiny, and she noted Musk had given hundreds of millions to the Republican Party.

On context, the data-center boom sparked public backlash this year, and analysts doubt any legislation could meaningfully stall construction, though a Democratic Congress makes more hearings and investigations likely. Democrats could also use the Congressional Review Act to challenge rules that ease sales of gas-powered trucks and SUVs. Morgan Stanley analysts said Congress now has more room to pursue Democratic healthcare priorities, such as restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies or reversing parts of the GOP's Medicaid cuts, but they still see meaningful changes as unlikely before the next presidential election cycle. Lale Akoner of eToro warned that a difficult debt ceiling negotiation could delay defense spending increases.

Articles.Title: AI data-center stocks slide, renewables rally after Democratic US midterm sweep - CNA

stories.Headline: AI Effects on Fees Requires Transparency With Clients, Attorneys at Harvey Event Say
stories.Summary:
Law firm attorneys and in-house counsel say that legal artificial intelligence is already shaping how legal work is priced. stories.Headline: AI sell-off hits Singapore tech stocks, but analysts see correction rather than end of boom - CNA
stories.Summary:
Singapore-listed technology stocks fell sharply at the open on Friday, November 6, 2026, as fears of tighter AI regulation under a Democratic-led US Congress triggered a global sell-off. Semiconductor equipment supplier UMS Integration dropped 15.2 per cent at the open before rebounding about 12 per cent to close at S$1.69. AEM Holdings fell as much as 13 per cent in early trade and recovered about 9 per cent to close at S$6.20. Frencken Group sank over 8 per cent at the open and closed about 6 per cent lower, while Venture Corporation dipped 1.5 per cent at the open and closed 3 per cent down. The Straits Times Index was down by over 2 per cent as Asian markets followed the global rout.

Analysts described the sell-off as a correction in AI valuations rather than evidence that the AI investment cycle had ended. OCBC's head of wealth advisory, Chez Anbu, said Singapore tech stocks were being pulled along by the regional AI unwind, and that the strongest performers this year were likely most at risk of further pullbacks. He said any eventual US rules might differ in scope, implementation and timing from what investors now expect, and would need the signature of President Donald Trump, who holds veto power. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said the intraday reversal showed buyers were stepping in after the sharp correction. She warned that the biggest downside risk would come if investor concerns began to translate into reduced orders, capital expenditure or earnings guidance.

Mr Anbu said Singapore's technology sector has significant but concentrated exposure to the global AI investment cycle, mainly through the semiconductor and electronics supply chain. AEM and UMS are most directly linked to the cycle, while Frencken and Nanofilm have meaningful exposure and Venture is more diversified across several electronics and industrial segments. He pointed to substantial investments, including Micron's US$24 billion plan and Applied Materials' expansion of its Singapore operations, as a longer-term cushion. He also cited a forecast that global spending on data centres will grow by roughly 27 per cent annually through 2029, while noting that competition from neighbouring markets could erode Singapore's advantage over time.

Ms Chanana said AI should be viewed in three phases: chips, then infrastructure and data centres, and then adoption, when businesses begin generating measurable productivity gains and revenue. She said Singapore is moving from the infrastructure phase toward adoption, a transition likely to be uneven, and that its semiconductor firms remain more exposed to the first two phases. She expected volatility to persist as investors separate companies with strong earnings visibility from those whose growth depends on uninterrupted AI infrastructure spending. Mr Anbu said volatility would likely stay high until the US regulatory picture becomes clearer, and that no one could reliably call a near-term rebound.

Articles.Title: AI sell-off hits Singapore tech stocks, but analysts see correction rather than end of boom - CNA

stories.Headline: Copyright Suits Over AI Training Continue With Latest Surge Against Meta
stories.Summary:
Meta is facing a new wave of lawsuits accusing the company of using copyrighted works to train its artificial intelligence models without the authors' permission. The suits are the latest in a series of cases testing how intellectual property law applies to AI. Reporter Brendan Pierson wrote about the filings in a Law.com article published on November 6, 2026. The article's framing is that the litigation continues to build against the company. One of the plaintiffs' lawyers, Kyle Roche of Freedman Normand Friedland, explained his firm's approach.

He said the firm chose to sue on behalf of individual authors rather than bringing a class action. According to him, a class action can be difficult because it may be hard to prove that all members of the class were affected by the AI companies' conduct in the same way. The article attributes this reasoning to Roche and does not describe any ruling on the merits. The article does not give the number of new lawsuits, the courts where they were filed, or the specific works involved. It also does not say how Meta has responded to the allegations.

Much of the text on the page is subscription material and site navigation, so the available detail is limited. Related Law.com coverage on the same site includes a November 5, 2026 piece reporting that only 31% of in-house legal professionals surveyed in a Pinsent Masons report said junior colleagues were driving AI adoption. A separate November 4, 2026 article reported that at least two AI-native law firms had bid for Weil Gotshal & Manges' data. Neither piece addresses the Meta lawsuits directly.

Articles.Title: Copyright Suits Over AI Training Continue With Latest Surge Against Meta

stories.Headline: HK, mainland markets feel rumble of Dem AI jitters
stories.Summary:
Mainland and Hong Kong stocks tumbled in early trade on Friday, November 6, 2026, as a global tech sell-off spread across Asian markets. The Hang Seng Index fell 392 points, or 1.58 percent, to 24,404 in Hong Kong, while the artificial intelligence index was down about 7 percent. Investors were rattled by fears of tighter AI regulation and a slowdown in the sector. The sell-off followed a sharp move on Wall Street the previous day.

On the mainland, the Shanghai Composite Index opened down 77 points, or 2.11 percent, at 3,612, and the blue-chip CSI300 Index slipped 1.5 percent. The Shenzhen Component Index opened down 426 points, or 3.72 percent, at 11,044, and the ChiNext Index opened down 128 points, or 4.99 percent, at 2,438. Technology stocks led the decline, with the Star 50 Index and the AI Index both down more than five percent at the open before losses narrowed somewhat. In Hong Kong, the China enterprises index fell 120 points, or 1.44 percent, to 8,248, while the tech index dropped 129 points, or 3.11 percent, to 4,025.

The report ties the selling to the aftermath of the US midterm elections, in which Democrats won big. Overnight, the tech-led Nasdaq recorded its deepest one-day drop since "Liberation Day" in April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced sweeping tariffs. That drop wiped out trillions of dollars in market value on fears of more scrutiny of artificial intelligence. The article attributes these fears to the market's reaction to the election outcome rather than to any specific regulatory action.

The wider context is that investors across the region were reacting to the prospect of closer oversight of AI companies in the United States. The articles do not say whether any new AI rules have been proposed or passed, nor do they give a timeline for further action. They also do not report any official response from regulators or companies. The markets had partly recovered from their opening lows during Friday trading, but the articles provide no closing figures.

Articles.Title: HK, mainland markets feel rumble of Dem AI jitters - RTHK News

stories.Headline: OECD Digital Economy and Society Outlook 2026 | Spotlight on powering AI progress: The future of compute
stories.Summary:
The OECD has published its Digital Economy and Society Outlook 2026, and this edition includes a spotlight on the future of computing power that powers artificial intelligence, according to an OECD.AI page dated November 6, 2026. The Spotlight examines how compute capacity may change across the layers of the AI technology stack and what that means for how quickly AI can advance. The OECD framed the report around three themes: anticipated technological advances and challenges in compute, the economics of AI compute including investment and access, and the policy choices needed so that future compute supports shared AI progress. The page presents the publication as part of the organisation's wider work on trustworthy, human-centric AI, carried out through the OECD.AI platform. The articles describe the Spotlight as an analysis rather than a set of binding requirements, so it does not set new rules or deadlines for governments or companies.

Its stated purpose is to outline the dynamics shaping compute and to identify policy considerations that governments may weigh. The OECD.AI material around the report also points to related initiatives, including a voluntary process in which organisations developing advanced AI systems can submit reports to share information on risk mitigation measures. The same site describes an index that assesses countries' progress in implementing the OECD Recommendation on AI. The available text does not give specific figures on computing capacity, investment amounts, or energy use in the Spotlight itself, so those details cannot be reported from these sources. The OECD is the publisher of the report and the operator of the OECD.AI platform, which says it works with many partners and that its AI work joined forces with the Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) under a single brand.

Experts from around the world advise GPAI and contribute to its work, according to the page. The articles do not name individual authors or quote officials on the Spotlight's conclusions. The page also notes that governments are not only regulators and investors in AI but also developers and users, and that governments need to track AI incidents and hazards to manage risks. The Spotlight's full findings and recommendations would need to be read in the complete publication, which the page offers as a download. The articles do not say what follow-up steps the OECD plans beyond making the report available.

Articles.Title: OECD Digital Economy and Society Outlook 2026 | Spotlight on powering AI progress: The future of compute - OECD AI Policy Observatory

stories.Headline: One Engineer Commands AI Army for Chip Design
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is moving beyond answering questions and into the work of designing and verifying semiconductors. Next-generation chips such as high-bandwidth memory are so complex that signal, power, and thermal issues must be considered at the same time, and AI agents are now being introduced into that design process. On the 5th, TERA Lab, led by Professor Kim Jung-ho of the School of Electrical Engineering at KAIST, announced it will hold an online event called "TERA AI Agent Day" on the 11th to present the AI agent ecosystem currently applied to semiconductor design. The lab says the event will feature a keynote by Professor Kim on a blueprint for a "single engineer–multiple agents" model. In that model, one engineer directs many specialized AIs rather than relying on a single AI for every function.

Rather than giving every specialized task to one AI model, the approach links task-specific agents with design software to solve complex problems. Human judgment is brought in at the necessary stages of the process. Student researchers will present case studies drawn from actual research projects. These include an agent that analyzes the signal integrity of high-bandwidth memory and of next-generation high-bandwidth flash, along with a system in which multiple AIs work together to optimize the placement of electrodes that connect stacked chips. TERA Lab aims to have each student develop at least two agents.

The article does not give figures on the number of attendees, the cost of the program, or the timeline for commercial use. Professor Kim said that in the future, the competitiveness of engineers and developers will depend on their ability to design specialized AI agents directly and to make them cooperate effectively. He added that future researchers will evolve into "AI agent architects" who design and operate AI agent ecosystems. The statements come from the lab's announcement ahead of the event and describe the direction the lab is pursuing. The article does not indicate any further schedule beyond the event on the 11th.

Articles.Title: One Engineer Commands AI Army for Chip Design - 동아비즈니스리뷰

stories.Headline: ‘Father of HBM’ KAIST Professor Joungho Kim Unveils Semiconductor Design Cases Using AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Professor Joungho Kim of KAIST, widely known as the "father of HBM," has begun work to automate next-generation semiconductor design using artificial intelligence. KAIST's TERA Lab, which he leads, announced on November 5 that it will hold the online event "TERA AI Agent Day" on November 11. At the event, around 15 student researchers will unveil AI agents they developed, along with examples of how those agents are used in semiconductor design and research. The articles do not say how many agents will be presented or what specific results they have produced so far.

Semiconductor design brings together many specialized fields, including circuits, packaging, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal integrity, and electromagnetic interference. TERA Lab is researching a structure in which AI agents specialized in different fields divide up tasks and then share their results. The stated goal is to automate repetitive analysis and verification, shorten design time, and let engineers concentrate on key technical decisions. In his keynote, Professor Kim is scheduled to outline the direction of next-generation R&D under the topic of intelligent, autonomous AI agent architecture for next-generation HBM and High Bandwidth Flash design.

Researchers will also demonstrate technologies applied to actual design, such as printed circuit board design and automatic impedance matching using 3D electromagnetic field simulation software from Synopsys. TERA Lab was founded in 1996, the year Professor Kim joined KAIST, and this year marks its 30th anniversary. As of the end of October, the lab had produced 123 graduates in total, 71 doctoral and 52 master's graduates. The articles do not describe any commercial partnership or product timeline tied to the event.

Articles.Title: ‘Father of HBM’ KAIST Professor Joungho Kim Unveils Semiconductor Design Cases Using AI Agents - 매일경제

stories.Headline: The New York Times Doesn’t Understand AI’s Role in Suppressing Wages
stories.Summary:
A Gizmodo column published November 6, 2026, by Matt Novak argues that the New York Times missed the more important way artificial intelligence is affecting the American labor market. The Times article, written by Ben Casselman under the headline "A.I. Was Supposed to Come for Our Jobs. So Far, Evidence Is Mixed," asked whether AI has disrupted employment, and Novak says it never mentions wages. Novak notes that the piece was published on a Friday and came shortly after the midterm elections, which he says showed widespread public hostility toward AI and data centers. He also points to the Times's mention of Microsoft offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, while white-collar sectors such as accounting, legal services, and finance mostly added jobs in October.

Novak describes the broader labor numbers as mixed but not alarming. The U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, more than expected, and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent. He writes that wages rose just 3.1 percent over the past year according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, while the latest available annual inflation rate was 3.7 percent in September, which means real wages have fallen. He cites a Federal Reserve Bank of Boston study from September finding that workers who feared losing their jobs to AI were less likely to believe they could negotiate higher pay. He argues that low unemployment usually pushes wages up, and that AI has seemingly broken that pattern.

Novak attributes the argument largely to David Kelly, Chief Global Strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management, who said on CNBC in September that workers feel threatened by AI and lack the confidence to ask for raises. Kelly is paraphrased as saying that the wage growth figure, measured year over year, was the lowest since May 2021. Novak also quotes CNBC host Leslie Picker agreeing that workers may feel they had better keep their heads down. Novak himself says the Times piece is "mostly fine" as a snapshot of public confusion, but he contends that it overlooks the possibility that AI is weakening bargaining power before any effect appears in unemployment figures. He lays out several scenarios, including a slow hollowing out of the middle class and a decade of lower living standards, while acknowledging that no one can yet know which will occur.

Articles.Title: The New York Times Doesn’t Understand AI’s Role in Suppressing Wages

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Models Show Moderate Accuracy in Detecting Trigeminal Neuralgia Phenotypes
stories.Summary:
Researchers from The Fifth Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University published a systematic review and meta-analysis in Frontiers in Radiology finding that magnetic resonance imaging artificial intelligence models show moderate accuracy in identifying pain-related nerve phenotypes in patients with non-secondary trigeminal neuralgia. The team pooled eight eligible studies comprising 628 nerve-level observations. Using a bivariate random-effects model, they found a pooled sensitivity of 0.83, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.78 to 0.87, and a pooled specificity of 0.81, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.74 to 0.86. The summary area under the curve was 0.86, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.82 to 0.88. The authors describe these tools as potential adjunctive diagnostic instruments rather than replacements for clinical judgment.

Trigeminal neuralgia causes recurrent, brief, shock-like facial pain that is often triggered by light touch, eating, or speaking, and it can severely disrupt sleep and daily life. The authors used the term non-secondary trigeminal neuralgia to cover classical and idiopathic forms once structural causes such as tumors or multiple sclerosis plaques have been excluded. Distinguishing these forms matters because it shapes decisions about procedures such as microvascular decompression. Standard visual review of scans is limited, since vessel contact against the nerve also appears in people without symptoms. The review notes that the diagnostic criteria for classical disease require definite morphological changes, not contact alone.

Quantitative radiomic and machine-learning methods aim to detect subtle differences that the eye cannot reliably see. The reviewers searched the literature following the PRISMA 2020 statement and its diagnostic accuracy extension, and registered their protocol in PROSPERO under identifier CRD420261394456. The initial searches produced 164 citations, which became 103 unique publications after removing 61 duplicates. After screening, 38 full-text reports were assessed, and eight studies met all eligibility criteria. Six studies used 3.0-Tesla scanners, one used a 1.5-Tesla system, and one used both field strengths.

Model types ranged from logistic regression and support vector machines to neural networks and ensemble classifiers. The review found mild heterogeneity, with inconsistency values of 20.77 percent for sensitivity and 27.65 percent for specificity. Risk-of-bias assessments flagged concerns including small samples, limited external validation, and possible data leakage during feature selection. The authors caution that the evidence rests on only eight mostly single-center, retrospective studies without independent multicenter testing.

They also note that the analysis combined contralateral-nerve designs with healthy-control comparisons, two tasks they describe as biologically different. Exploratory subgroup analyses showed that radiomics-only models achieved a pooled sensitivity of 0.84 and specificity of 0.84, while models combining radiomics with morphological variables reached 0.86 and 0.78. Excluding one influential study shifted the pooled sensitivity to 0.82 and specificity to 0.78. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Models Show Moderate Accuracy in Detecting Trigeminal Neuralgia Phenotypes

stories.Headline: Global Study Maps Mounting Energy Water Material and Land Demands of Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
A systematic review of forty-six environmental studies has mapped the energy, water, material and land demands of artificial intelligence, finding that the physical infrastructure behind machine learning draws heavily on electricity, water, minerals and land. The work was carried out by researcher Sibongiseni Hlabisa and published in the journal Carbon Neutral Systems. The authors searched Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar for studies published from 2015 to 2025, starting from about 3,130,000 records and narrowing them through successive screenings until forty-six sources met all inclusion criteria. The corpus combined twenty-two peer-reviewed articles and proceedings, seventeen technical and government reports, four preprints and three reference volumes.

The review's central finding is that artificial intelligence cannot be judged through carbon figures or narrow efficiency measures alone, because its footprint grows as computing workloads expand. Training a single large model such as PaLM-2 or GPT-3 is reported to consume between 1.3 and 1.5 gigawatt-hours of electricity. The International Energy Agency projects that data center electricity demand will rise from 415 terawatt-hours in 2024 to 945 terawatt-hours by 2030 under its base case, approaching 1,200 terawatt-hours by 2035, with the United States accounting for nearly half of global growth. Water is needed both to cool servers and to make chips, with evaporative cooling using roughly 7,000 to 12,000 liters per megawatt-hour and each silicon wafer requiring 1.8 to 2.5 cubic meters. Hyperscale data centers typically occupy 30 to 100 hectares, and the review notes that some regulators, including authorities in Ireland and Singapore, have already moved to limit or condition new facilities.

The authors argue that policymakers should move beyond voluntary corporate efficiency metrics toward binding regional limits on cumulative electricity, water withdrawal and land conversion tied to local ecological capacity. They point to practical measures such as capturing waste heat for district heating, recycling ultrapure water in chip plants, recovering metals from retired hardware, and shifting non-urgent computing to times and places with surplus wind or solar power. The review also warns that the benefits of computing are concentrated in the Global North while extraction and e-waste burdens fall on the Global South, and it acknowledges significant empirical gaps in the underlying evidence. The articles supplied do not say how these recommendations will be taken up by governments or industry, so the outcome remains open.

Articles.Title: Global Study Maps Mounting Energy Water Material and Land Demands of Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: AI For People And Not For Profit – OpEd
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion piece rather than a news report, and it draws on a specific event: a 2026 pilot run by the Utah Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy with the AI health-tech company Doctronic. The pilot began in January 2026 and used an automated AI system to process renewals of refill or repeat medications for 190 chronic conditions, based on earlier prescriptions written by licensed physicians. The state office said the system would work within strict parameters and under physician oversight, and it was meant to ease the workload of doctors and widen patients' access to care. Within three months, in April 2026, the Utah Medical Licensing Board called for the immediate suspension of the pilot, which ended the first legally AI-led system to renew prescriptions for chronic non-controlled medications.

The board said the pilot compromised patient safety and put patients at risk. It also said that AI or other financial motives should not be allowed to override the duty to protect patients, and that this was what had happened in this case. The author, Bhabani Shankar Nayak, a professor of business management at London Metropolitan University, uses the episode to argue that AI companies are pressing governments worldwide to deploy AI in healthcare for profit. He argues that medical professionals and researchers are calling instead for a "human loop" covering every stage of an AI system's life, from problem formulation and data collection through model development, validation, and final decisions on how the tools are used. He also contends that the same principle applies in every sector, since people's welfare should not be sacrificed for productivity or profit.

The author's broader claim is that AI and its language models carry demographic, racial, gender, social, cultural, and class biases from the way problems are framed, data is collected, and models are built and tested. In his view, these biases can produce wrong diagnoses and wrong prescriptions, and uncritical commercial adoption threatens both human welfare and the scientific development of AI. He calls for transparent governance with sustained human oversight and accountability, so that people control the technology rather than being controlled by it. The article does not report any official response beyond the licensing board's statement, and it does not describe any further steps planned for the Utah pilot or for similar programs elsewhere.

Articles.Title: AI For People And Not For Profit – OpEd

stories.Headline: Study Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Integration in Sustainable Apparel Design and Production
stories.Summary:
A study published in the Journal of Industrial Ecology by Liu and Tang in 2026 evaluated how artificial intelligence can be used in sustainable apparel design and production. The authors reviewed AI tools used for concept generation, sewing-pattern engineering, virtual prototyping, production planning, consumer evaluation, and circular information systems. They organized the review by lifecycle stage, sustainability problem, and how well each tool had been validated. The findings were reported on November 6, 2026, by Scienmag and bioengineer.org.

The research drew on four separate sets of data covering design, specialist appraisal, consumer response, and production metrics. These included 4,200 garment-design records and assessments of 350 designs by 28 specialists. A consumer experiment tracked 858 participants who completed the study out of 864 recruited, and 426 enterprise pattern records with measured cutting-waste rates were also analyzed. In the consumer experiment, participants appeared to show higher purchase intention for co-created and labeled products, but lower intention at the higher price premium. The authors noted that the precision of one statistical reconstruction was limited by rounding in the reported inputs.

The clearest direct evidence of material savings came from manufacturing pattern engineering. Using ridge regression across the observed enterprise, quarter, and product mix, the model achieved a test root mean square error of 0.049 and a mean absolute error of 0.038, compared with a baseline root mean square error of 0.096 when predicting cutting-waste rates. To organize the results, the authors proposed an integration framework built on three pillars: data and technical integration, circular design performance, and validation and governance. It also uses four evaluation dimensions: digital plausibility, design feasibility, market viability, and verified sustainability performance. The authors themselves stated that direct sustainability verification remains limited to production-stage cutting waste and that broader lifecycle outcomes would need separate validation.

Articles.Title: Study Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Integration in Sustainable Apparel Design and Production

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence faces rejection in American museums; visitors cling to art and human creativity
stories.Summary:
Washington, DC, has become a focal point for a growing backlash, as several American museums have faced a wave of rejection for exhibitions built on artificial intelligence. Visitors have voiced clear reservations about displaying works that rely on digital technology instead of human creativity. The reporting describes the response as a widening debate over the limits of technology in art and culture. Questions have arisen about whether algorithm-made works hold real artistic value and whether they can express human experience, emotion, and ideas. These concerns come as AI tools spread quickly and can produce images that mimic the styles of well-known artists.

Many museum visitors argue that art is not defined only by its final form but also by the creative process and the personal effort behind it. They stress that human experience matters, and they question whether works made almost entirely by AI are authentic enough for major cultural institutions. Supporters of the technology see these experiments differently, describing them as a natural extension of artistic evolution that can open new horizons and offer fresh ways to present ideas. The debate reaches beyond museums to artists, critics, and cultural bodies. It also touches on intellectual property rights, the sources of images and data used to train these systems, and who bears responsibility for works produced with algorithmic help.

Museums now face the challenge of balancing technological progress with maintaining public trust. According to the reporting, they must clarify the tools used in producing exhibited works and how much a human artist was involved. Some creators also worry that the rapid output of modern software, which can produce large volumes of work quickly and cheaply, may shrink opportunities for traditional artists. The article notes that the American museum debate shows technological development does not automatically earn public acceptance. It suggests the relationship between art and AI still needs clear guidelines that protect creators' rights and preserve the authenticity of the artistic experience without stifling innovation.

Articles.Title: Artificial intelligence faces rejection in American museums; visitors cling to art and human creativity

stories.Headline: GPT-6.2 Astra & Fable 5.5 Exposed Overnight: AI Community’s Crazy November Is Coming
stories.Summary:
Late on November 1, 2026, clues about two unreleased AI models surfaced within hours of each other. Tech blogger @kimmonismus reported that the name "Claude Mythos 5.5" appeared in the HTML source of Anthropic's official website, in a product page's hidden title and image attributes. Developer @chetaslua later found the name six times in that HTML while the main text still referred to Mythos 5.1, and another user said Anthropic had since deleted the web content. Separately, the identifier "claude-fable-5-5" had appeared on October 13 in an Azure price configuration of the open-source LiteLLM API gateway, which was later removed, though third-party records remained.

The configuration information circulating online suggests Fable 5.5 could accept 1 million input tokens and produce up to 128,000 output tokens. Its listed prices are 10 US dollars per million input tokens, 50 US dollars per million output tokens and 0.25 US dollars for cache reads. Community members disagree on timing, with some expecting release this week, others next week, and others waiting until mid-November. Mythos is described as aimed at high-risk fields such as cybersecurity and biology with strictly limited access, while Fable applies added safeguards to the same underlying model for broader users.

Developer @notjazii posted a 36-second comparison on November 1 claiming that Fable 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 were given the same prompt to build 3D scenes. The Fable 5.5 output reportedly included changing seasons, growing cities, a shifting harbor day and night cycle, volcanic eruptions and rocket launches, while Opus 5.5 showed more static landscapes. Another author showed a 92-second Minecraft-style game that he said came from a single prompt in one to two hours, and a third developer showed an interactive sailing ship. None of these demos came with full prompts, call logs or source code, so the model identity and the single-prompt claims rest on the authors' own statements.

On the OpenAI side, user @TokenGremlin said that a Codex usage statistics screen showed GPT-6.2 Astra at 19.8 percent of one account's model usage, with GPT-6 Astra at about 80 percent, even though the selection menu still displayed GPT-6 Astra. Developer @Mr_Salio shared an API response in which the model field read gpt-6.2-astra, and user @ai_funss said an upgraded Codex CLI let him call the model with a 1M-token window. @TokenGremlin argues the new version improves design, technical ability and programming and may surpass Claude Opus 5.5, but the article notes this is unverified. The overall picture is that several rumors from both companies appeared at nearly the same time, and the article reports no official announcement from either company.

Articles.Title: GPT-6.2 Astra & Fable 5.5 Exposed Overnight: AI Community’s Crazy November Is Coming - 36氪

stories.Headline: Official Launch of AI Features for China-Market iPhones: Qwen Becomes Siri’s New Partner
stories.Summary:
Apple has announced that the first batch of Apple Intelligence features will launch for users in mainland China, ending a wait of roughly two years since the company first entered generative AI in 2024. According to the plan, the features will open for testing on November 4 through the latest iOS developer beta, and will reach Chinese users with the official iOS 27.3 release in December. The initial supported devices are limited to iPhones, including the iPhone 15 Pro series, iPhone 16 and later models, iPhone Air and iPhone Duo, with Simplified Chinese and English supported. Support for iPad and Mac will follow once the relevant approval procedures are completed.

The launch covers writing tools, photo editing, Genmoji, real-time translation, notification management, visual intelligence and upgraded basic Siri interactions. Writing tools can rewrite, proofread and summarize text across system and third-party apps, while the Photos app adds natural language search and a new Erase tool that runs on the device. Real-time translation works in Messages, Phone, FaceTime and AirPods, and the more advanced Siri that can understand personal context, screen content and cross-app actions is not part of this update. Apple has also clarified that its basic features run on its own models adapted for China and on the device, so personal data is not uploaded to Apple's servers.

For more complex tasks, Apple has brought in Alibaba's Tongyi Qianwen to expand the capabilities of Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence, and it says user requests handled by Qianwen will not be used for model training, advertising or behavior tracking. Users can choose whether to enable the feature, decide what information to share, and sign in with a Qianwen account or an Apple account. Apple has also set out rules for China-region features, saying that eligible users can keep using them while traveling abroad. Apple has not said when the more capable Siri will arrive in China.

Context matters here, since domestic phone makers have already made AI photo editing, translation and summaries standard features, so these tools are no longer rare. The broader aim, according to the coverage, is to move AI from answering questions toward a personal agent that completes tasks, a role that Apple's control of hardware, the operating system and the app ecosystem could support.
