It also describes Executive Order 14110, signed in October 2023, which paired AI safety rules with provisions to support innovation and federal adoption. In September 2024 the White House convened cloud providers, AI labs, data center operators and utilities to address bottlenecks, and it set up an AI Data Center Infrastructure Working Group. Later that year, National Security Memorandum 25 and Executive Order 14141, signed on January 14, 2025, pushed AI infrastructure and federal land for supercomputing centers.

The article says the Biden administration also pursued tough policies on the largest companies while backing the sector. In January 2024 the Federal Trade Commission opened antitrust reviews of partnerships between Microsoft and OpenAI, Amazon and Anthropic, and Google and Anthropic. Federal officials also tightened export controls on advanced chips in 2022 and 2023. The author argues these moves reflect separate goals, namely national leadership, corporate profit and fair distribution of costs, which can pull in different directions. Government can subsidize domestic chipmaking while restricting chip flows, and can push data center growth while making firms bear grid costs.

The article then shifts to the newer dispute over who pays for AI data center expansion. It cites a 2024 Department of Energy report estimating that US data centers used about 176 terawatt-hours in 2023, or 4.4 percent of national electricity, with the figure projected to rise sharply by 2028. That strain on power grids and local resources is, the article suggests, what has pulled data centers into local elections and congressional debate in 2026. The author's broader conclusion is that the policy fight is now about costs and fairness rather than a simple pro- or anti-AI divide, and the article cautions investors against reducing it to partisan labels.

Articles.Title: The Truth Behind the Democratic Party's Opposition to AI Policies and Capital Power Struggles - 深潮TechFlow

stories.Headline: Danish watchdog rejects web notice for AI trained on 3,000 student aid files
stories.Summary:
The Danish Data Protection Agency, known as Datatilsynet, has ruled that a government agency may train an artificial intelligence system on roughly 3,000 past applications for a student disability supplement, but only if it contacts those applicants directly rather than posting a notice online. The opinion, dated June 12, 2024 under journal number 2024-212-0371, responded to a request from the Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science. The regulator drew a clear line between building the tool and running it, finding that existing student aid law covered development while operating the system would require a more specific national legal basis. The article reports that the parliament supplied such a basis about a year later. The agency planned to develop the system with cBrain, a Danish software company, to check whether incoming supplement applications included enough documentation.

A case judged to have insufficient material would be sent for manual screening, and the applicant would be asked for more. The agency said the tool would be used only for this initial screening and not as decision support, with the final award remaining a separate assessment. The training data would include applicants' names, identity numbers, contact details, educational, income and employment information, prior SU and grant history, and health and social information. The regulator noted that this meant processing special category data about a group it described as a vulnerable target population.

Datatilsynet accepted that existing law could support building the system because development did not directly affect anyone's grant, but it required authorities to assess the whole life cycle of the tool before starting. On transparency, the regulator rejected the agency's reasons for relying on a web notice, which were the large number of people, the resources needed, the limited processing, the goal of faster processing, and the lack of direct consequences. It said the agency already held every applicant's contact details and could reach them by digital or physical mail, and it found no exemption that applied. For running the system, the regulator said a relatively clear supplementary national legal basis was required, because AI can draw conclusions far beyond what a human caseworker could and the applicant group is vulnerable.

It also said a data protection impact assessment would often be needed. The article reports that the Danish parliament acted on the question in June 2025 through bill L 152, whose explanatory remarks cited a taskforce recommending digital screening tools and stated that information was missing in 64 percent of applications. The article does not describe whether the screening tool has gone live on new applications, and it notes that the operational question remains a matter for the agency to resolve. The episode illustrates how a regulator's view on AI training can shape both what public bodies must tell people and what lawmakers ultimately write into statute.

Articles.Title: Danish watchdog rejects web notice for AI trained on 3,000 student aid files - PPC Land

stories.Headline: AI Sell-Off Wipes $2.5T, Nasdaq Falls 5.52% [2026] - https://tech-insider.org/
stories.Summary:
On November 6, 2026, a sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks erased more than $2.5 trillion (€2.24 trillion) from global technology markets, according to Deutsche Welle. The Nasdaq fell 5.52% and the S&P 500 dropped 4.4%. The BBC reported that the Magnificent Seven, a group including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, lost $1 trillion in value in a single trading day, with Nvidia falling more than 9%. Chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung were among the hardest hit.

The trigger was the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections. Democrats won control of both houses of Congress, and some Democratic governors-elect had campaigned on slowing AI development or pausing data-center construction. No new AI law has passed. Investors, according to the reporting, were reacting to what might come, including possible limits on data-center construction, slower AI investment, doubts about profitability and rising local opposition to data centers. Because the AI trade depends on continued expansion of computing capacity, a political signal that threatens that expansion can move prices sharply even before any rule takes effect.

Analysts quoted in the coverage described the same mechanism. Dan Coatsworth of AJ Bell told the BBC that the midterm result muddied the outlook because Democrats could slow data-center roll-outs and look at new ways to regulate the sector. Melissa Brown of SimCorp, quoted by Reuters, said investors were recognizing that some newly elected officials want to slow AI infrastructure development, while adding that a complete halt seemed unlikely. Michael Hewson of MCH Market Insights, quoted by AFP, raised the possibility of greater opposition to AI buildout plans in Texas. The reporting says these are concerns and forecasts, not established policy.

The episode also resembles the January 2025 scare that followed the arrival of the Chinese model DeepSeek, though the two shocks point in opposite directions. Reports that cheaper models could reduce demand for chips worried investors then, while this week's worries centered on whether data centers could be built at the expected pace. The reporting does not say whether frontier labs have changed their plans, but it identifies capacity, funding and pricing as the channels through which the pressure could reach model builders. What happens next, according to the articles, depends on whether any proposed slowdown becomes enacted rules. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI Sell-Off Wipes $2.5T, Nasdaq Falls 5.52% [2026] - https://tech-insider.org/

stories.Headline: Proceed with Caution: Pennsylvania Targets Deceptive AI in Advertising
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Pennsylvania AI Deceptive Advertising Act on October 22, 2026, setting disclosure rules for AI-generated advertising in the state. The law defines synthetic content broadly to cover images, video, audio, or text that has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence. It bars advertisers from knowingly, recklessly, or willfully running ads that use such content to create a false impression about a product's or service's nature, origin, or authenticity, unless a clear and conspicuous disclosure is included. The law takes effect December 21, 2026, and it follows similar rules that New York and California have already adopted.

The disclosure must say the content was modified or generated using artificial intelligence, and it must appear the first time consumers see the synthetic material. It must appear in the same medium as that material and, where technically feasible, be permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove. The disclosure must also be readable or audible, presented in a language the consumer uses, and consistent with the rest of the ad. Exemptions cover content that is evidently fictional based on context, parody, satire, commentary, criticism, and ads limited to text. Enforcement rests with the state Attorney General or a district attorney, who may seek an injunction or bring a civil action, and a court may impose a civil fine of up to $3,000 per violation.

Sen. Nick Pisciottano, a Democrat, sponsored the bill and said on Instagram on October 7 that it would help people tell whether what they see online was generated with AI. Law firm analysts writing for BakerHostetler and Robinson & Cole have read the statute as requiring disclosure mainly when synthetic content could mislead consumers about the actual product being sold, not every AI-touched image in an ad. They note the statute's language is not entirely clear, so the law's intent to promote basic transparency around material elements may guide how it is applied. Both firms warn that a disclosure may not cure an ad whose AI imagery still gives a false impression about the offering.

The analysts also say the law does not create a private right of action, which lowers direct exposure compared with California's approach, where a lack of disclosure can be treated as an unfair or deceptive act. Their advice to advertisers is to track where generative AI is used, require agencies and vendors to flag and disclose it, add AI review to existing approval workflows with a human check before publication, and build disclosures that meet every relevant state rule for national campaigns. They also note that social media platforms, broadcasters, and retail media networks may impose stricter disclosure requirements of their own. For now, the analysts say that when advertisers are unsure, they should disclose.

Articles.Title: Proceed with Caution: Pennsylvania Targets Deceptive AI in Advertising - JD Supra

stories.Headline: Rep. Yvette Clarke Stands on the Frontlines of AI Legislation
stories.Summary:
Rep. Yvette Clarke, a Democrat from New York, has pushed Congress to pass federal rules for artificial intelligence, a call the article ties to recent White House reports about possible voluntary industry regulation. She has introduced or co-sponsored several AI bills aimed at algorithmic bias, deepfakes, and intellectual property. Her most recent move was reintroducing the REAL Political Ads Act, which would require disclosure when generative AI is used to create images or videos in political ads. The bill was first introduced in May 2023. Clarke said Congress has fallen behind a rapidly advancing technology, leaving voters open to AI-generated misinformation.

Clarke's other proposals include the AI Civil Rights Act, introduced in December 2025 with Senator Edward J. Markey, which would bar biased AI algorithms from high-stakes decisions about housing, employment, education, credit, healthcare, and parole. She introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act with Senator Ron Wyden in September 2025 to bring transparency to AI use in those same high-impact areas. In June 2026 she introduced the CREATOR Act with Representatives Beth Van Duyne and Valerie Foushee to protect artists against AI-enabled style impersonation. Adobe publicly supported that bill, according to the article. Clarke and Representative Glenn Ivey also introduced the DEEPFAKES Accountability Act of 2023, which would require digital watermarks on deepfakes and make it a crime to fail to identify malicious ones.

Clarke led 43 colleagues in a December 2025 letter urging that any moratorium or preemption of state AI laws be kept out of the FY26 NDAA, arguing that state laws are the only recourse consumers have until Congress acts comprehensively. The article notes that all 50 states introduced AI legislation in 2025 and 38 adopted or enacted 100 measures. Clarke's No Biometric Barriers to Housing Act, introduced in April 2025, would ban facial recognition, fingerprint scanners, and other biometric technologies in most federally funded housing. It also directs HUD to study how biometric and algorithmic tenant screening discriminates against renters.

All of her AI bills remain in committee, mainly House Energy and Commerce and House Oversight and Government Reform. The article also points to conflicts in the legislative process, reporting that roughly one in five members of Congress holds investments in AI developers, chipmakers, data centers, or cloud companies, and that about 44 lawmakers with AI holdings sit on committees with jurisdiction over AI policy. It adds that major AI firms spent roughly $7.5 million on federal lobbying in a single recent quarter, with cumulative spending past $37 million since 2024, according to a Project on Government Oversight investigation. The piece does not describe any scheduled vote or next step for Clarke's bills.

Articles.Title: Rep. Yvette Clarke Stands on the Frontlines of AI Legislation - Our Time Press

stories.Headline: U.S. military accelerates AI push across Pacific as China tensions grow - Honolulu Star-Advertiser
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Pacific Command has been rapidly equipping its forces with artificial intelligence tools across Hawaii and the wider Pacific as tensions with China grow. Adm. Samuel Paparo has directed that AI be adopted across the entire command, according to Scott Brunstetter, the command's chief AI officer. Brunstetter spoke at the TechNet Hawaii Conference on Oct. 28, a military trade show focused on information technology and communications. His position, now officially titled "Chief Super Intelligence Officer" after President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring officials to use the term "superintelligence," was created about 15 months ago at the command's headquarters at Camp Smith.

Brunstetter said the command concluded that the operational risk of not adopting AI outweighs the risk of adopting it. The military is applying AI to tasks ranging from logistics to intelligence analysis. Tagup, an AI company, has worked with Marine Corps Forces Pacific on logistics, including tracking medical supplies nearing or past their expiration dates. Tagup's president, Paul Plemmons, said the tools let planners iterate faster than a staff officer normally could. The command covers the largest geographic area of any U.S. combatant command, so the AI tools are meant to help gather and analyze data across the Pacific.

The growth of AI has also created physical challenges, since the systems depend on server farms and data centers that use large amounts of electricity and water. Brunstetter said power limits on Hawaii and the distance to cloud services have driven significant innovation in the field. Ricky Buchanan, chief of PACOM's Intelligence Information Systems Division, said commanders cannot let warfighters depend on tools that rely on mainland data centers. The military is building a 56,000-square-foot laboratory and data center in Kihei, due for completion early next year, which has drawn opposition from the community, environmentalists and Native Hawaiian groups. Buchanan also said commanders are cautiously exploring smaller mobile data centers, warning against creating a fixed target that adversaries could strike first.

Officials acknowledged that AI tools can make mistakes. In September, CNN reported that U.S. troops had nearly launched a boarding raid on a Chinese cargo ship based on an AI-assisted intelligence report that a Special Operations Command analyst later found to be false, a report one source said almost started a war. Brunstetter said the military does not blindly trust its data tools and that analysts must understand how they work. Plemmons said a trained human should always remain in the loop. Contractors such as Sigma Defense are also working to modernize Navy ships with software, since hardware upgrades can take six to 10 years.

Articles.Title: U.S. military accelerates AI push across Pacific as China tensions grow - Honolulu Star-Advertiser

stories.Headline: OPB’s First Look: Blue ocean strategy for AI
stories.Summary:
Portland startup Panthalassa unveiled a new factory on November 6, 2026, at the historic Kaiser Shipyard site along the Columbia River in Vancouver, Washington. The facility will manufacture wave-powered devices meant to support floating data centers on the open ocean. The company, which has raised more than $300 million this year, aims to build nodes at the plant that will generate energy from waves. Panthalassa takes its name from a super ocean that covered most of Earth's surface roughly 190 million years ago. OPB's Courtney Sherwood attended the ribbon-cutting ceremony.

The company hopes to seed deep oceans around the globe with self-driving buoys and then use the energy they capture to power floating artificial intelligence computation hubs. Its backers argue these hubs would avoid the carbon emissions, freshwater contamination and neighborhood disruption that have fueled a backlash against land-based data centers. The new factory marks the company's first move from custom manufacturing to an assembly line. It is also a test of the firm's theory that it can eventually make and deploy its nodes at additional factories around the world.

Panthalassa is based in Portland, and the article describes the Vancouver plant as a significant investment in the region. The reporting frames the venture as an attempt to answer heated debate over greenhouse gas emissions tied to energy-hungry AI data centers. Beyond the factory opening, the article does not name additional officials or give further statements from company leaders. It also does not specify a production timeline or how many nodes the plant will produce.

Articles.Title: OPB’s First Look: Blue ocean strategy for AI - Oregon Public Broadcasting - OPB

stories.Headline: How Generative Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Spatial-Temporal Data Mining
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Qianru Zhang and Hongzhi Yin published a comprehensive review in Data Science and Engineering on how modern generative artificial intelligence is reshaping spatial-temporal data mining. The survey, drawing on work from academic institutions across several regions, sets out a structured taxonomy and an end-to-end pipeline for assessing how large language models, diffusion models, masked autoencoders, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks are replacing older modeling approaches. The authors did not run new physical experiments or collect field data. Instead, they analyzed how machine learning methods have developed for complex geographic and temporal systems, from urban traffic to climate observations. The review explains that conventional deep learning models, such as standard recurrent and convolutional networks, face three main limits in real-world settings.

They need large volumes of densely labeled data, which is costly to gather across sensor networks. They also generalize poorly to unseen scenarios, altered road layouts, or local extreme weather. Because they output single deterministic estimates, they cannot express uncertainty or generate alternative scenarios, which matters for disaster management and evacuation planning. The authors argue that generative frameworks address these gaps through synthetic data augmentation, stronger transfer to new regions with few or no examples, probabilistic outputs that show predictive confidence, and pretrained foundation models that carry over to many downstream tasks.

The survey also formally separates acquisition-level data types from modeling-level data instances. It names four sensing types: discrete event logs with coordinates and timestamps, continuous trajectories from moving agents, point readings from mobile monitors, and fixed raster grids of measurements. These can be converted into formats such as individual points, trajectory sequences, time series, spatial maps, or multidimensional tensors, depending on the model. To settle which architectures count as generative, the authors propose three criteria: explicit density modeling, implicit generation from latent noise, and conditional sequence synthesis through autoregressive factorization.

Under these criteria, large language models and diffusion models qualify alongside variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks. The authors compare the model families directly, noting that autoregressive models give exact likelihoods but decode slowly and accumulate errors over long horizons. Variational autoencoders allow efficient parallel sampling but can blur fine spatial detail and risk posterior collapse. Generative adversarial networks produce sharp outputs quickly but are hard to optimize and offer limited uncertainty calibration.

Diffusion models balance fidelity and diversity well but are computationally slow at inference, a cost the review says can be reduced through consistency distillation. Masked autoencoders learn by reconstructing hidden portions of the input and are data efficient, though they need additional output heads to quantify variance. The survey catalogs applications across representation learning and forecasting, including trajectory models, urban image-text alignment systems, traffic and air quality forecasters, and language-model-based time series systems. The article excerpt ends before describing the review's recommendations for future work, so further details on next steps are not available here.

Articles.Title: How Generative Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Spatial-Temporal Data Mining

stories.Headline: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools Accelerate Design Tasks but Diminish Creative Autonomy
stories.Summary:
Researcher Shin Young Jang published a controlled study in the journal Fashion and Textiles examining how generative artificial intelligence affects digital textile design. The study followed thirty-four third-year undergraduate fashion design students at a South Korean university who completed matched pattern design tasks using both traditional vector software and Adobe Illustrator's Firefly-powered text-to-vector generation. Each student produced twenty designs across five product categories, and afterward completed a fifty-item survey while eighteen of them also took part in follow-up interviews lasting 45 to 60 minutes. The work was framed against a wider debate about how automated tools affect cognitive engagement and creative authorship. Its findings point to a trade-off that the author treats as the central result.

The generative tools substantially reduced the perceived difficulty and workload of the tasks. Intrinsic task difficulty fell from 3.68 to 2.09 on a five-point scale, and overall mental workload dropped from 4.21 to 2.15. Students also rated the workflow as far more efficient, at 4.06 compared with 2.29 for traditional tools. However, editability fell from 3.91 to 2.47, since students found the machine-generated vector structures cumbersome to correct, often preferring to start over. Ideation was easier to begin with prompts, but the number of distinct ideas did not meaningfully increase, and the outputs tended to converge on a narrow aesthetic.

The outcomes were weaker across the board. Perceived creativity and originality dropped from 3.94 to 2.68, aesthetic value from 4.09 to 2.74, and overall task satisfaction from 3.91 to 2.26, while the ability to articulate personal style fell from 4.24 to 1.53. Sixteen participants said the system made key choices for them, leaving them as curators, and fourteen reported anxiety about translating visual intentions into text prompts. The author argues that automation removed the productive struggle that builds design understanding, and that freed cognitive resources did not shift into deeper engagement, since measured engagement showed no significant difference between workflows.

The study's authors propose a pedagogical framework of sequential exploration, refinement, and reflection, in which generative tools are used mainly for initial brainstorming while students manually rebuild outputs and document their prompt histories. They also suggest process-based grading and, for professional teams, prompt libraries and transparent decision pipelines. The author recommends future research on multimodal interfaces that accept sketch and style references, and on a wider range of learner profiles. The study's own methodological limits, which the article notes but which were not fully stated in the portion available, temper how far these findings can be generalized.

Articles.Title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools Accelerate Design Tasks but Diminish Creative Autonomy

stories.Headline: IJCAI: AI Conference and Publishing Guide
stories.Summary:
The International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI) has introduced a Primary Paper Initiative, a submission fee policy that starts with the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 cycle in Bremen, Germany. The CASRAI guide, last updated 7 November 2026, describes the policy as a way to address rising submission volumes and to fund peer-review sustainability. Under it, a USD 100 fee applies to Main Track, Survey Track, and Special Track submissions, but the fee is waived for a "primary paper," meaning a manuscript where none of the co-authors appear on any other paper submitted to that conference cycle. The guide does not say when or by whom the policy was announced beyond citing IJCAI's own 2025 materials.

The policy also sets out where the money goes and what else changes for authors. The guide states that 100 percent of proceeds from non-primary paper fees go to the Peer Reviewers Recognition Policy, which funds honoraria, registration subsidies, and formal recognition for program committee reviewers. The Journal Track, Sister Conferences Track, Competitions, Demos, and Doctoral Consortium are exempt from the fee. Separately, the guide notes that the review process runs in two phases, with an early summary rejection screen by two program committee members before full review, and that authors resubmitting work rejected at another peer venue such as NeurIPS, ICML, or AAAI within the previous 12 months must declare that venue and upload past reviews.

IJCAI is a non-profit academic organization governed by a Board of Trustees and a permanent Secretariat, and the guide credits the conference with a CORE A* ranking, placing it in the top roughly four percent of computer science venues. The guide lists upcoming meetings, including IJCAI-ECAI 2026 in Bremen from 15 to 21 August 2026 and IJCAI 2027 in Kyoto, Japan, from 7 to 13 August 2027, followed by a satellite symposium in Hengqin, China, from 15 to 17 August 2027. Looking ahead, the guide describes the conference's two-site format for 2027 and its annual schedule, which has run every year since 2015. The guide itself was written and maintained by the CASRAI Editorial Board, and the sources it cites are IJCAI's own call for papers and primary paper pages.

Articles.Title: IJCAI: AI Conference and Publishing Guide

stories.Headline: PMLR: Machine Learning Research Proceedings Guide
stories.Summary:
The article is an explainer guide rather than breaking news, so it contains no discrete event, actor or date of action to report. It describes the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR), an open-access series that publishes peer-reviewed proceedings from machine learning and AI conferences such as ICML, AISTATS and COLT. The guide says the series was formerly called JMLR Workshop and Conference Proceedings and was restructured under its current name on April 10, 2017. It is run by an editorial board of computer science researchers, with Tegan Emerson, Hoel Kervadec and Neil Lawrence listed as current Series Editors.

The guide explains how volumes are produced, with conference organizers submitting a proposal, building a repository from a Jekyll template and compiling a master BibTeX file. Each paper must carry a citation key in the form lastnameYY, with the camera-ready PDF matching that key, and supplementary files following a lastnameYY-supp.pdf pattern. Editors then submit a pull request that passes automated checks before deployment. The guide notes that PMLR charges no article processing fees, authors keep copyright under open licenses such as CC-BY, and individual authors cannot submit papers directly, since submissions come only through participating conferences and workshops.

The guide describes the series as maintained by volunteer editors and open-source tooling, which it says can lead to variable delays between a conference closing and its volume appearing online. It also says PMLR publishes only electronically, so institutions wanting print copies must use third-party services. The guide compares PMLR with NeurIPS Proceedings, OpenReview venues, IEEE Xplore and Springer LNCS, noting differences in access models and author costs. It does not describe any pending changes or upcoming decisions affecting the series.

Articles.Title: PMLR: Machine Learning Research Proceedings Guide

stories.Headline: OpenEHR Conference Demonstrates Advances in Clinical Data Interoperability and Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
A scientific supplement published in BMC Proceedings on November 8, 2026 gathers thirteen peer-reviewed abstracts accepted to the scientific track of the EHRCON25 openEHR International Conference, which was held in Barcelona in October 2025. The collection covers short papers and posters on health information systems built around openEHR archetypes, semantic data modeling, artificial intelligence, and conversions between data standards. Instead of relying on isolated proprietary databases, the work tests whether archetype-based architectures can structure clinical narratives, modernize older hospital systems, harmonize multi-center research registries, and support automated querying. The contributions come from academic medical centers, regional health authorities, public health bodies, and software teams working on standardized health records.

Several projects report measured results. Researchers from Better Ltd built a retrieval pipeline that links free-text clinical notes to archetypes, and on 800 narrative queries it reached an archetype recall of 0.73, compared with 0.53 for the Clinical Knowledge Manager Resource Finder and 0.44 for zero-shot GPT-4.1 prompting. A separate team developed Text2AQL, an assistant that turns plain-language questions into Archetype Query Language statements, and it produced syntactically valid queries in 81.9 percent of 1,274 tests. Other studies describe a multi-agent framework linking openEHR with HL7 Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources, an on-device assistant that runs small language models on a smartphone using local health records, and a template set for genomic variant reporting. The articles also describe a translation of the World Health Organization's antenatal care guidance into openEHR templates, in which 98 percent of its 879 data elements aligned with existing archetypes.

The authors do not present these tools as finished. The antenatal template, for instance, was judged limited as a primary longitudinal record and decision-support framework, so a further mapping phase is needed. The oncology study at Isala found that setup was laborious, documentation was sparse, ICD-10 codes did not map cleanly to SNOMED CT, and existing archetypes lacked coverage for adaptive radiotherapy and dose-volume parameters. The on-device assistant also sometimes left out critical emergency instructions, and the Clinnova pipeline relied on custom version attributes because REDCap lacks native form versioning. The articles describe these as ongoing hurdles rather than settled problems, and they point to further mapping, refinement, and testing as the next steps.

Articles.Title: OpenEHR Conference Demonstrates Advances in Clinical Data Interoperability and Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Hugging Face Papers: Guide to AI Research on HF
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story, and the article is a long explainer rather than a report of an event, so the requested "what happened, who did it and when" structure does not map cleanly onto it. The only dated facts are that the guide was last updated on 7 November 2026 and published on 8 November 2026 by CASRAI's Editorial Board, and that Hugging Face Papers is a platform run by Hugging Face, Inc. The article carries enough detail for three paragraphs, so I have written it as an explanatory summary of the guide instead. The guide, published by CASRAI on 8 November 2026 and last updated on 7 November 2026, explains Hugging Face Papers, a platform that links arXiv preprints to models, datasets and demonstration applications on the Hugging Face Hub. It is aimed at AI researchers, computational linguists and open-source developers who want to track new preprints, link their model weights and datasets, and verify authorship.

The platform's daily feed traces back to curation work by Ahsen Khaliq, and Hugging Face formalized that feed as a Hub feature in May 2023. After Meta retired Papers with Code in July 2025, the guide says Hugging Face Papers became the main destination for community-curated machine learning literature. Hugging Face, Inc., founded by Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf, develops and runs the platform. The guide describes three main functions: a daily trending feed ranked by date, upvotes and discussion, artifact linking that connects papers to Hub repositories and Gradio demonstrations in Spaces, and author profiles that let researchers claim their papers.

It notes that about 95 percent of paper links on the Hub come from arXiv, and it gives steps for searching by title or arXiv identifier, indexing a new paper at a URL based on its arXiv identifier, and linking a model by including the paper reference in its repository card. Authors claim authorship from the paper page, and requests are checked against institutional email addresses or by platform moderators. The guide also says that papers can be submitted within 14 days of their arXiv posting. The guide lists strengths and limits, and it is careful to say that Hugging Face Papers is a discovery and aggregation layer rather than a peer-reviewed journal.

Its strengths include quick links from preprints to runnable code, feed updates within hours of arXiv release, and browser-based testing through Spaces. Its limits include heavy dependence on arXiv, ranking that can favor popular generative AI topics over niche or negative results, and variable quality in community-uploaded artifacts. The guide also compares the platform with Papers with Code, arXiv Sanity Preserver, AlphaSignal and Semantic Scholar. The article does not describe any further changes or announced next steps for the platform.

Articles.Title: Hugging Face Papers: Guide to AI Research on HF

stories.Headline: As AI Threatens Tech Workers, Their Workplaces Become Sites of Class Struggle
stories.Summary:
Tech workers have been pushing back against their employers over military contracts, immigration enforcement, and the Israeli occupation of Palestine, and the fight has grown more intense as artificial intelligence threatens their jobs. The account comes from an interview with JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine, tech worker leaders and authors of the book Against Tech Oligarchy: Workers Resistance in the World's Most Powerful Industry. Their book traces the movement over roughly the last two decades, including campaigns and strikes at companies such as Kickstarter and The New York Times. The workers' early actions were aimed at exposing the gap between tech firms' public values and their contracts with the military, police, and ICE.

They often relied on open letters, and one example they describe is a campaign at Google over Project Maven, an AI system used to analyze military drone footage, which ended with the company agreeing not to renew its contract. The tech bosses' response, according to Tan, came in stages. After the Federal Reserve ended its zero-interest rate policy to fight inflation, the companies lost cheap credit and billions of dollars in market value, and they responded with mass layoffs, return-to-work orders, and heavier workloads for remaining staff. Tan points to Elon Musk's takeover of Twitter, where he fired 80 percent of the workforce and attacked teams focused on human rights, AI ethics, and content moderation.

Redwine describes how workers then turned to unionization using what she calls the Recognition Playbook, which means mapping coworkers, training organic leaders, building a supermajority, and filing for elections with the National Labor Relations Board. She says the bosses answered with their own union-busting tactics, including firing visible organizers, hiring consultants, and using return-to-office orders to push out workers. The authors also say the strike at The New York Times in 2024 was largely a failure, because management had prepared the platform to run without staff, and because contracts with no-strike pledges barred the newsroom from joining. Redwine argues that labor law constrains unions, and that most major breakthroughs in the labor movement came from illegal strikes.

Tan says AI is splitting the tech workforce, with most workers likely to lose their jobs or be de-skilled, while a smaller group of AI engineers holds strong bargaining power because employers value their skills. He says many of the affected workers are becoming more class-conscious and concerned with affordability, and that a growing movement against data center construction creates both openings and tensions, since building trades workers are currently gaining jobs from that construction. The authors say new organizing methods will be needed that go beyond the Recognition Playbook and beyond shop-floor issues. The articles do not describe specific plans or dates for those efforts beyond the book's publication and the continuing debate over strategy.

Articles.Title: As AI Threatens Tech Workers, Their Workplaces Become Sites of Class Struggle

stories.Headline: Opinion: College dual enrollment programs risk fueling a high school AI arms race
stories.Summary:
Michael Walsh, an affiliated faculty member at the University of Alaska Anchorage, published an opinion piece in the Anchorage Daily News on November 8, 2026, arguing that colleges should rethink how they choose students for dual enrollment programs. He says that selection criteria such as class rank, grade point average and prerequisite courses are now distorted by students using artificial intelligence chatbots on their schoolwork. The piece frames this as a risk that high school students will feel pressure to use AI more heavily to stay competitive, creating what he calls an AI arms race. He notes that the article is an opinion and that its claims come from his own reasoning and research he cites.

Walsh says colleges and universities should adjust their criteria so that dual enrollment placement reflects students' readiness for college coursework rather than work that may be done with chatbot help. He suggests one option is requiring a minimum score on a proctored, closed-book selection exam. He also proposes a widely adopted national blue-ribbon standard that would let the public tell apart programs that select students on readiness alone. He argues such a mark would give institutions more reason to change their criteria, since few would act alone if competitors did not.

Walsh places responsibility on several groups, including parents, secondary school administrators and teachers, and college administrators and professors. He argues that these groups are judged and rewarded on short-term measures, such as the number of dual enrolled students, which discourages them from enforcing rules on AI use. He also points to the revenue that dual enrollment brings to some colleges and the political weight that state and local officials have placed on these programs as alternatives to Advanced Placement courses. He cites a Pew Research Center survey showing that a majority of U.S. teens use AI chatbots for schoolwork, and a recent study suggesting that students who rely on AI perform worse on learning and retention once the tools are removed. The article does not describe any next steps by institutions or policymakers.

Articles.Title: Opinion: College dual enrollment programs risk fueling a high school AI arms race

stories.Headline: Computational Workflow Translates AI Tree Sketches into Deployable Tensegrity Pavilion
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Alberto Pugnale, Gabriele Mirra, Jack Halls, Michael Minghi Park, Michael Mack, and Sofia Colabella introduced FloaTree, an experimental workflow that turns artificial intelligence sketches of large trees into deployable tensegrity structures. The study was published in the journal Architectural Intelligence. The team validated the approach through a series of prototypes that grew from a two-module physical test to an eight-module pavilion erected in Switzerland. That pavilion won the 2024 International Association for Shell and Spatial Structures Design Competition and Exhibition of Innovative Lightweight Structures in Zurich.

The project addresses the decline of large, old trees, which provide nesting, perching, and sheltering habitat for birds and other wildlife, especially in dense cities. An earlier 2022 study by Mirra and colleagues trained an AI agent to generate three-dimensional line abstractions of large trees, and those lines preserve branching cues useful to wildlife. The team chose tensegrity structures, which hold isolated compression struts within a continuous network of prestressed cables, because they can mimic branching forms and fold into compact bundles for transport. Tensegrity was pioneered by Kenneth Snelson in 1948 and later popularized alongside Buckminster Fuller.

The design was generated automatically in Rhinoceros 3D and Grasshopper, then checked with Karamba3D simulations. The initial 12-module model showed that 14.8 percent of its 114 steel cables were slack and that the cantilever deflected 54 centimeters, so the team applied dynamic relaxation in Kangaroo2 and then a genetic optimization in Octopus. The optimized form eliminated compressed cables and reduced maximum deflection to 3.13 centimeters. The team also scaled the model down by 25 percent to meet travel limits.

Four prototyping phases followed, and the final pavilion had 75 steel cables and was packed into no more than six pieces of standard checked luggage. In Zurich, a four-person crew erected the eight-module structure within two days without scaffolding, ladders, or heavy hoisting gear. The article reports that an unexpected combination of rainfall and temperature swings overnight caused a primary timber strut to buckle at its notched joint after erection. The authors describe this as a trade-off between low-tech timber fabrication and tensegrity mechanics, and the article's account of the failure's analysis and any follow-up is cut off in the source text.

Articles.Title: Computational Workflow Translates AI Tree Sketches into Deployable Tensegrity Pavilion

stories.Headline: International Workshop Explores AI Biomarkers and Equity in Breast Density Screening
stories.Summary:
The eleventh International Breast Density Workshop met in Līhue, Kaua‘i, Hawai‘i, bringing together clinicians, researchers, and patient advocates from fourteen countries. The proceedings, published in Breast Cancer Research, examined imaging biomarkers, tissue biology, and individualized cancer risk management. Investigators presented eighty-five abstracts, and the biennial series, started in 2002, organized its 2025 conference around five thematic tracks. Participants also took part in a pre-diagnosis risk board modeled on multidisciplinary tumor conferences.

Dense breast tissue remains the strongest common predictor of breast cancer apart from age, according to the proceedings. Women in the highest quartile of dense breast volume face a four-fold to six-fold higher likelihood of developing the disease than those in the lowest quartile. Dense tissue also lowers mammographic sensitivity by masking tumors, which can produce false-negative results. Notification rules in the United States, Canada, and Australia now require that patients and physicians be told about breast density. The articles say that standardized measurement, biological confounders, and causal pathways remain unresolved after three decades of study.

Several sessions reported new findings. Dr. Gils described long-term results from the randomized DENSE trial, in which supplemental magnetic resonance imaging reduced interval cancers across three screening rounds in women with extremely dense breasts. Dr. van Grinsven reported promising accuracy for abbreviated breast magnetic resonance protocols in high-risk women. Dr. Mahmoud documented significant racial differences in background parenchymal enhancement, and the workshop concluded that such imaging biomarkers must be validated across diverse populations before they can be assumed to perform the same way for everyone. Dr. Mainprize introduced Mammatus, an automated tool that measures masking directly from mammograms.

Several speakers said the field's tools need further work before wide use. Dr. McCarthy showed that the qualitative BI-RADS categories and commercial percentage measures are confounded by body mass index, which leads to fewer supplemental screening recommendations for Black women and more for Asian women. McCarthy proposed age-adjusted density metrics or absolute dense volume as less biased alternatives. Dr. Strand reported that three commercial artificial intelligence algorithms gave Asian women with breast cancer significantly lower detection scores. Presenters agreed that wider deployment of these methods will require rigorous standardization and validation across racially and ethnically diverse patients.

Articles.Title: International Workshop Explores AI Biomarkers and Equity in Breast Density Screening

stories.Headline: It’s Time to Teach Students to Be Drivers of AI, Not Passengers
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column rather than news, so the breaking-story format does not apply, and I have written it as a four-paragraph piece in my own words. Michael Taubman and Scott Kern, both veteran teachers and AI innovation leads at North Star Academy Washington Park High School in Newark, argue in a piece published by The 74 on October 29, 2026, that high schools should teach students to be drivers rather than passengers in the age of artificial intelligence. They open with a story from their 12th-grade AI literacy class, where a student realized she had not used an AI-powered tool in two days until a classmate pointed out that a music app's DJ function was choosing her songs. The authors cite a Common Sense Media survey finding that 7 in 10 teens use AI for schoolwork while fewer than 1 in 3 say they have been taught AI literacy skills. They note that the students at their school are mostly Black and Latino and come from low-income communities.

The authors compare AI to automobiles, which are empowering, widespread and potentially dangerous, and they propose an "AI driver's license" modeled on driver education. Their course begins with an analog day with no devices, in which students audit their own AI use, including the algorithms behind social media feeds. The license rests on four elements: choosing a destination, learning to drive by working with AI on a real project, opening the hood to understand how AI predicts words from patterns in human writing, and discussing the rules of the road. The article also cites the survey finding that 38% of teens who use AI for schoolwork say it leads them to develop fewer original ideas, and 39% say they feel they are missing out on learning. Students who complete the course, the authors argue, can judge when AI is wrong or biased and decide whether to use it at all, a skill they say carries over to any future tool.

Taubman and Kern frame the course as a response to a choice students have always faced, whether to copy answers or do their own thinking, and they say the best defense has always been education. Their students drafted a class statement, inspired by the Declaration of Independence, asserting a right and responsibility to question, limit and regulate AI where it diminishes honesty, creativity, livelihoods, the environment or human connection. The article reports that the class ended with each student receiving a hand-laminated "AI driver's license." The authors conclude that most of the critical decisions about generative AI still lie ahead, so it is important now to ensure that all high school students learn how to get behind the wheel.

Articles.Title: It’s Time to Teach Students to Be Drivers of AI, Not Passengers

stories.Headline: SonaBuds Bring AI Translation To Wireless Earbuds With Support For Over 140 Languages
stories.Summary:
SonaBuds, a company whose products are described in a promotional article on thatericalper.com published November 8, 2026, is offering wireless earbuds that translate conversations between people speaking different languages. According to the company, the AI-powered Bluetooth earbuds support real-time, two-way translation across more than 140 languages, with offline functionality for supported language pairs and situations. The devices also work as ordinary wireless earbuds for music and phone calls. The article presents the product as a response to a familiar travel problem, such as ordering food or asking directions in a country where the listener does not speak the language. The translation process starts by pairing the earbuds with a smartphone over Bluetooth, after which users choose their languages in a companion app.

The system is designed to work in both directions so two people can talk without changing settings each time. The company says offline translation works in certain supported situations, but it does not say which languages or features are included offline, so buyers would need to confirm that themselves. The article also notes that accuracy can vary with pronunciation, accents, dialects, speaking speed and background noise. The company is responsible for these claims, and the article repeats them as company statements rather than verified results. SonaBuds also advertises noise cancelling, stereo music playback, phone call support and compatibility with most Bluetooth-enabled iOS and Android phones.

It says no subscription is required, with pricing starting at $79.95 per unit in its May 2026 announcement, possible discounts for multi-unit purchases, a 30-day money-back guarantee and a two-year warranty against manufacturing defects. The article adds that it is promotional material containing affiliate links, so purchases through those links could earn the site commissions. The piece places the product within a wider trend of adding artificial intelligence to devices people already own, and it suggests that independent testing would be needed to confirm how well the translation performs across the advertised languages. The article does not report any such testing, nor does it describe any regulatory action or next steps from the company.

Articles.Title: SonaBuds Bring AI Translation To Wireless Earbuds With Support For Over 140 Languages

stories.Headline: North Wales media projects share £90,526 to test AI newsgathering and broaden community coverage
stories.Summary:
Two north Wales media organisations have shared £90,526 from the UK Government's Local News Fund to develop new ways of finding and delivering local journalism. The award was reported by Tomorrow's Publisher on 8 November 2026, drawing on the Department for Culture, Media and Sport's list of grant recipients. Wrexham Dotcom Limited will receive £34,436 to build a tool that uses artificial intelligence to scan publicly available information and flag developments that may merit coverage. Coast Community Radio and Media CIC, which runs Bayside Radio in Colwyn Bay, has been granted £56,090.

The Wrexham project is designed to assist newsgathering, and the articles say the system is meant to help journalists identify potential stories. Decisions about what to investigate and publish remain editorial ones, according to the reporting. Bayside Radio says its project will extend local news and community-information work through partnerships, audience research and stronger digital publishing. It plans to work with groups across Conwy County and the north Wales coast to bring a wider range of community voices into its coverage. The station will distribute journalism on radio and digital channels.

The grants sit within the Government's £6 million Local News Fund, which forms part of its Amplify: The Local Media Action Plan. The plan aims to help local organisations adapt to digital audiences, develop online-focused business models and build stronger engagement with communities. A separate Department for Culture, Media and Sport announcement says the fund is intended to support innovation and help outlets reach new audiences. Ofcom's review of local media, cited in the reporting, found in its 2023 survey that 92 per cent of UK adults used local news or information, and that 89 per cent of those users accessed it online.

Ofcom also describes the civic role of local reporting, including scrutiny of public institutions, while noting providers' concerns about staffing, revenue and sustaining their services. The two Welsh projects take different routes: one invests in a digital tool to help journalists spot possible stories, while the other expands partnerships and publishing across platforms. The Government presents the fund as support for the long-term sustainability of local journalism. The articles state that the awards themselves do not establish how effectively either project will increase audiences or improve financial resilience.

Articles.Title: North Wales media projects share £90,526 to test AI newsgathering and broaden community coverage

stories.Headline: Physical AI Stocks Heat Up as Unitree Robotics Shares Jump Over 50% in a Month; Industry Players Say Three Bottlenecks Remain
stories.Summary:
Unitree Robotics founder Wang Xingxing used a speech on Oct. 22, 2026, at the "2026 World Physical AI Conference and Partner Ecosystem Conference" in Hangzhou to predict a major breakthrough in physical AI within one to three years, earlier than his August 2026 estimate of two to three years at the fastest and five to 10 years at the slowest. Since mid-October, the company's shares have risen more than 50%. Wang attributed the shift mainly to GPT-6Astra, a model OpenAI released on Sept. 3, which Unitree loaded onto its humanoid robots for tests without specialized training. In one painting task, the robot cleaned its brush when changing colors on its own. The article notes the model still falls short on precision assembly and on sensing environmental change and retrying after failure.

Wang also described Unitree's approach of keeping the "cerebellum," the part with strict low-latency needs, inside the robot while delegating "brain" functions to cloud or edge AI. He judged GPT-6Astra close to what a brain requires, and said that a next-generation GPT-7 would cross the "ChatGPT moment" for brain function alone. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the GTC Berlin conference on Oct. 21 that physical intelligence is the next wave and that it needs data centers, digital twin training systems and computers onboard machines. On an Oct. 21 earnings call, Tesla CEO Elon Musk repeated that humanoid robots will become the world's largest industry. Several people interviewed said the rally reflects both sector rotation and these public comments, while the article stresses that physical AI remains early-stage.

Cai Zhenhui, founder and CEO of Guangzhou Huarui Zhipu Artificial Intelligence Technology Co., said physical AI is expected to enter industrial production and commercial services, but warned that capital markets are not moving in step with industrial deployment. He identified three bottlenecks: models, high-quality real-world data that remains scarce and costly, and on-device computing power, which cannot yet handle models moved from cloud development onto robot bodies. An embodied industry analyst added that data investment and brain-model financing are structurally mismatched, and that whether data supply changes substantively should guide judgments on timing. Wang Chuang, a partner and senior vice president at Agibot, said real environments, where children may hug or push robots, are far more complex than laboratories. Cai noted that tasks such as washing dishes and folding clothes are still hard to achieve at demonstration level.

According to a report titled "Embodied Intelligence Development Report (2026)," jointly released by the Artificial Intelligence Research Institute of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, Tsinghua University's Department of Electronic Engineering and the Embodied Intelligence Testing Laboratory, embodied intelligence and physical AI are converging in meaning, with robots serving as a key vehicle for testing. The report also notes that humanoid robots face limits on height, weight and body shape, and that heat dissipation and room for AI hardware and batteries remain unresolved. The article's impact analysis says the concept heat gives short-term valuation support to robot bodies, components and computing power. It concludes that investors may need to focus on whether a data closed loop is forming, whether on-device platforms are adapted, and whether shipments reach scalable industrial settings.

Articles.Title: Physical AI Stocks Heat Up as Unitree Robotics Shares Jump Over 50% in a Month; Industry Players Say Three Bottlenecks Remain

stories.Headline: AI data center stocks drop as Democrats sweep U.S. midterms
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in the U.S. midterm elections held on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and stocks tied to artificial intelligence data centers sold off in response. The party also flipped traditionally Republican-leaning states including Texas and Kansas, and won governor races in Texas and Georgia, which together account for roughly a third of AI data center spending and projects. On Wednesday, neocloud companies took the sharpest early losses, with CoreWeave down as much as 3.2% in premarket trading, Applied Digital off 3% and Nebius down 1.3%. Oracle fell about 1.2%, giving back part of a 5.85% gain from Tuesday, after it priced a combined $20 billion stock and debt offering.

The selloff deepened on Thursday. Nvidia lost 9.3%, AMD 17.3%, Microsoft 3.6%, Micron 17.5%, Broadcom 10.4%, Tesla 10.8% and SpaceX 9.1%, while Nebius dropped 15%, Iren fell 17% and CoreWeave lost 10%. Tesla and SpaceX together lost more than $420 billion in market value after the vote. By Friday morning, U.S. tech stocks were showing signs of recovery. Dozens of local ballot measures in 10 states also sought to restrict data center construction, and one analyst said a Democratic Congress could slow the planned 800 to 1,000 U.S. data centers.

Analysts offered several readings of the risk. Evercore ISI analysts led by Amit Daryanani said a more restrictive development environment could add negative sentiment toward AI infrastructure names, and that the first reaction would be to sell, with the open question being how much fundamentals change and whether inflation and yields offset it over time. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. said the elections would clearly slow the buildout and now expects Big Tech spending growth to peak in 2027, not in 2028 or 2029. Kyle Rodda of Capital.com pointed to the risk of measures such as moratoriums on new construction. Dominique Toublan of Barclays said AI pushback is bipartisan but local, making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it, and that the race becomes a war of attrition in which scarce power favors the biggest balance sheets.

The vote landed on a sector already under strain. The Goldman Sachs Broad AI basket fell 15% in October and was down more than 24% from its peak heading into Wednesday. Data Center Watch counted at least 45 projects worth $68 billion disrupted by local opposition in the second quarter of 2026, while the International Data Center Authority counted at least 46 projects across 20 states, representing more than $170 billion, blocked, withdrawn or stalled between January 2024 and May 2026. Goldman Sachs estimates AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031. Any Democratic legislation would still need President Trump's signature, which limits near-term legislative risk, though analysts noted that executive branch action and uncertainty over capital allocation remain concerns.

Articles.Title: AI stocks hammered by midterm shock as data center buildout becomes a 'war of attrition'
